comment: The conformance MAP — OWASP ASVS 5.0.0 (345 requirements), OWASP MASVS 2.1 (24 controls) and the EU Cyber Resilience Act Annex I (23 points) — as reviewed policy. tools/check-conformance-map.mjs judges it and runs as the third script of the docs-sync chain step. Harness-owned and sha-pinned by check-gate-integrity.mjs: widening a grade is a CODEOWNERS-reviewed act that appears in a PR diff.

READ THIS FIRST — WHAT THIS FILE DOES NOT CLAIM. It never says the generated application is ASVS Level 1, 2 or 3, MASVS-verified, or CRA-conformant, and no sentence in it may. Verification levels attach to a VERIFICATION OF AN APPLICATION performed by an assessor against that application; a template cannot hold one and a generator cannot confer one — the same inversion the Essential Eight register refuses. CRA conformity is a manufacturer’s legal act (Annex I obligations, a conformity assessment, a declaration, CE marking) that no code tree performs, and no harmonised standard for the CRA had been cited in the Official Journal as of the verified date — so this map has a shelf life, tracked as the calendar obligation conformance-cra-hens-citation. What this file IS: a per-requirement statement of which live control in this harness bears on the requirement, how much of it that control reaches, and what is left — so an assessor starts from an honest ledger and a consumer never mistakes a template for a verification.

THE GRADES. covered: a live control’s subject IS the requirement and its residual is stated. partial: a live control bears on part of it, and the note says which part and what is missing. not-covered: nothing in the tree bears on it — honestly unbuilt, or the consumer’s to build; the note says what would be needed. not-applicable: the surface the requirement governs is absent from the generated system, with a written negativeProof stating why (and, above the documentation tier, a negativeCanary that would red if the surface reappeared). Grades are conservative by rule: absence of a surface is never coverage, where two grades are defensible the lower is taken, and a control already carrying one row’s weight is named again only where its subject genuinely spans both. Rows with `module` set are CONDITIONAL on that opt-in module being enabled and say so in the note.

THE FIELDS. control names a LIVE control — a validate-chain or Stop-chain step, a shipped CI job, a write-guard rule id, or a Stop-step-demanded reviewer verdict — and the gate reds a control nothing runs. canary is the tests/canary/injections.json registry KEY under which the control’s can-fail proof is registered (steps ∪ lanes ∪ hookRules); it is resolved FACTORY-SIDE by scripts/check-conformance-evidence.mjs because the registry never ships. proof is the file that proves it, in prose. evidenceTier follows the Essential Eight register’s bar: simulated-activity may rest only on a registered canary; covered may never rest on documentation alone. reviewedOn is the date the row was last judged against the tree.

THE SOURCE TEXTS ARE VERBATIM and the counts are asserted from the source rather than typed: 345 ASVS rows across 17 chapters at tag v5.0.0 (an earlier planning figure of 369 was wrong and is recorded here so nobody re-derives it), 24 MASVS controls at v2.1.0, and Annex I Part I (points 1, 2 and 2(a)–(m)) plus Part II (points 1–8) of Regulation (EU) 2024/2847. Generated from this file: docs/compliance/controls-crosswalk.md and docs/security/threat-model.md (tools/gen-conformance-docs.mjs, regen-diffed by the same gate).

unmappedControls.format: Source formatting (biome) has no subject in ASVS, MASVS or CRA Annex I — it is the harness’s own consistency floor, not an application security requirement.
unmappedControls.wiring: Hook/settings/lockfile wiring is the harness’s self-integrity check — that ITS enforcement is installed — and no requirement in the three standards asks an application to prove its development harness is wired.
unmappedControls.suppressions: The inline-suppression census governs how the enforcement layer may be silenced; it is a control ON the controls, and none of the standards enumerates it as an application requirement.
unmappedControls.provenance: Citation discipline on decision sites is a development-process control; CRA Annex I Part II asks for vulnerability handling and documentation, not for cited authorities on decision lines, and ASVS/MASVS do not ask for it at all.
unmappedControls.boundaries: Package-layering and export-wall closure is architectural hygiene (verticals ⊥ verticals, the reversibility wall); ASVS 5.0 dropped its architecture chapter and no remaining row demands module boundaries.
unmappedControls.native-deps: The reviewed native-module allowlist is Expo build hygiene; MASVS-CODE speaks to third-party components generally and is mapped through the dependency lanes, not through this allowlist.
unmappedControls.prompts: Prompt-file hash locking governs LLM prompt provenance — no row in the three standards addresses it.
unmappedControls.licenses: Licence compliance is a legal obligation outside all three security standards.
unmappedControls.types-drift: Freshness of the generated Supabase type mirror is a correctness control with no security-requirement subject.
unmappedControls.migrations: Append-only migration discipline and the DML/ADR markers are change-management hygiene; the schema controls that DO map (RLS, grants, audit) are claimed by schema-rls and tenancy, and claiming this step too would count one artefact twice.
unmappedControls.parity: Web/mobile feature parity has no security-requirement subject.
unmappedControls.build: That the tree compiles is a precondition of every other control, not a requirement any standard states.
unmappedControls.styleguide: Design-token discipline has no security-requirement subject.
unmappedControls.perf-budget: Bundle and interaction budgets have no security-requirement subject; the effect-cleanup leak scan is availability hygiene, not a standard’s row.
unmappedControls.e2e: The e2e step asserts spec PRESENCE for routes; the security-bearing e2e specs themselves are claimed by the web-e2e lane rows.
unmappedControls.docs-sync: docs-sync is the step that RUNS the two conformance registers and the documentation-drift closures; it is the judge of this map, so it may not be named as evidence inside it.
unmappedControls.diff-coverage: Per-file coverage floors are a test-quality control with no security-requirement subject; ASVS 5.0 carries no testing chapter.
unmappedControls.duplication: Token-clone detection has no security-requirement subject.
unmappedControls.i18n: The catalog-key rule and the Intl ban have no security-requirement subject.
unmappedControls.test-quality: Assertion-free/focused/disabled test detection is a test-quality control with no security-requirement subject.
unmappedControls.mobile-perf: Maestro-flow and startup-budget closure has no security-requirement subject.

requirements.text: Verify that input is decoded or unescaped into a canonical form only once, it is only decoded when encoded data in that form is expected, and that this is done before processing the input further, for example it is not performed after input validation or sanitization.
requirements.note: The wire boundary decodes once by construction — the tRPC router runs with no transformer (packages/api/src/trpc.ts records the decision), so a request body is JSON-decoded exactly once by the framework and the decoded value is then zod-parsed — but no gate asserts that ordering, and no control anywhere addresses canonicalization of encoded forms (percent-decoding, unicode normalization) before validation. A consumer who decodes inside a handler after validation is caught by nothing.

requirements.text: Verify that the application performs output encoding and escaping either as a final step before being used by the interpreter for which it is intended or by the interpreter itself.
requirements.note: For the dominant interpreter the encoding is performed by the interpreter itself: React 19 and React Native escape interpolated values at render time, and the one React bypass is denied at write time by the dangerously-set-inner-html write-guard rule (WRITE_GLOBAL_CHECKS in template/base/.claude/hooks/lib/guard-rules.mjs), whose denial is proven can-fail by tests/hooks/hook-contract.test.mjs. Honest reach of that rule: pretool-write-guard scans only Edit/Write tool calls, and only on JS/TS-extension files (.ts/.tsx/.mts/.cts/.js/.jsx/.mjs/.cjs) — a shell-redirected write, a hand-authored commit, or a non-JS file is not content-scanned, and no validate-chain step or ESLint rule (no react/no-danger, no react plugin at all in eslint.config.mjs) scans the committed tree for the token, so an occurrence that arrives outside the tool channel reaches human review uncaught by machine. Interpreters other than HTML (HTTP header fields, URLs, SQL, shell) are outside this rule's subject and are graded on their own rows.

requirements.text: Verify that output encoding for an HTTP response, HTML document, or XML document is relevant for the context required, such as encoding the relevant characters for HTML elements, HTML attributes, HTML comments, CSS, or HTTP header fields, to avoid changing the message or document structure.
requirements.note: HTML element and attribute contexts are encoded by React's renderer, and the sole raw-HTML sink (dangerouslySetInnerHTML) is write-guard-denied with a can-fail test. As depth, the security-headers validate step pins a nonce + 'strict-dynamic' CSP by evaluated value, so markup that escaped encoding still does not execute as script (template/stack/apps/web/e2e/security-headers.spec.ts reads the live header). Not reached: HTML comment and CSS contexts, and HTTP header fields written by consumer route handlers — no control encodes or scans those; XML documents are not produced by the seeded tree. The guard's agent-write-only reach stated at 1.1.2 applies here too.

requirements.text: Verify that when dynamically building URLs, untrusted data is encoded according to its context (e.g., URL encoding or base64url encoding for query or path parameters). Ensure that only safe URL protocols are permitted (e.g., disallow javascript: or data:).
requirements.note: No control encodes untrusted data at URL build sites, and no protocol allowlist exists in application code. Depth that exists but is not this requirement: the enforcing CSP (security-headers step) prevents javascript: navigation from executing script in browsers, and the expo-policy gate holds extra.apiOrigin to https-or-loopback — neither encodes a query or path parameter, neither judges an href a consumer renders, and the mobile Linking/deep-link surface is ungoverned.

requirements.text: Verify that output encoding or escaping is used when dynamically building JavaScript content (including JSON), to avoid changing the message or document structure (to avoid JavaScript and JSON injection).
requirements.note: No control encodes or escapes at a JavaScript- or JSON-building site, and nothing scans consumer code for string-built script or JSON. Facts of the seeded tree, not controls: no <script string, Function constructor or string-argument timer appears in apps/ or packages/ (grep on template/stack), and payloads move as JSON through the transformer-less tRPC router serialized by JSON.stringify. Depth that exists but is not this requirement — the same distinction the 1.2.2 row draws — is the web CSP: script-src is nonce + 'strict-dynamic' with 'unsafe-eval' a banned token, asserted by evaluated value against tools/security-headers.json by the security-headers step and read off the live document response by template/stack/apps/web/e2e/security-headers.spec.ts. That policy stops injected script from EXECUTING in a browser; it does not encode anything at a build site, and the Hermes mobile runtime and Node server have no CSP equivalent. Grading a consequence-mitigation as partial coverage of an encoding requirement would be inflation, so the grade is not-covered with the CSP recorded as depth.

requirements.text: Verify that data selection or database queries (e.g., SQL, HQL, NoSQL, Cypher) use parameterized queries, ORMs, entity frameworks, or are otherwise protected from SQL Injection and other database injection attacks. This is also relevant when writing stored procedures.
requirements.note: Every statement the seeded DALs issue goes through the supabase-js PostgREST builder — values ride as builder arguments (packages/verticals/notes/src/data/notes.ts is the worked pattern) and PostgREST compiles them to parameterized SQL server-side — and the query-shapes step closes the DAL statement census by execution: tools/gen-query-shapes.mjs drives every exported DAL function through a recording Proxy (tools/lib/query-recorder.mjs; a DAL export with no probe, or a probe that records no chain, fails generation), a builder method outside the reviewed KNOWN_METHODS set reds by name (tests/gates/check-query-shapes.test.mjs proves the red), and the contracts step regen-diffs the manifest byte-fresh. SECURITY DEFINER functions must pin search_path both at write time (the security-definer-no-search-path write-guard rule) and tree-wide (the schema-rls step's definer discipline in tools/check-rls-manifest.mjs). Residuals, stated precisely: parameterization is the platform's property and no gate asserts it; the reviewed grammar includes .or(), which takes a PostgREST FILTER STRING — the seeded keyset tie-break interpolates cursor values into it (notes.ts keysetTieBreak) and is safe only because domain/cursor.ts strict-parses the cursor first, and no gate judges what a consumer interpolates into an .or() string; a raw-SQL path issued beside a recorded builder chain (a postgres() client, an .rpc() body) is invisible to the census; the migrations are NOT purely static SQL — the audit and auth-trail partition-maintenance functions use EXECUTE format() with %I on internally derived names, and no gate judges dynamic-SQL quoting inside PL/pgSQL; a consumer-authored Edge Function or RPC that concatenates SQL is outside every check; and the bash-guard destructive-sql rule governs the agent's shell, never application code.

requirements.negativeProof: The generated system makes no operating-system calls: apps and packages contain no child_process/exec/spawn call sites (verified against template/stack), compute is managed serverless, and the mobile app is a client on user-owned devices. The absence is unenforced — no lint or guard rule denies child_process — so a consumer who adds process execution re-opens this requirement with no harness control behind it.

requirements.text: Verify that the application escapes special characters in regular expressions (typically using a backslash) to prevent them from being misinterpreted as metacharacters.
requirements.note: The dynamic-regex sites in the seeded tree practice the requirement — packages/platform/supabase/src/cookies.ts escapes every regex metacharacter before embedding a key, and mfa-flow.ts builds only from a numeric length constant — but a specimen is not a control: no lint or gate enforces escaping when a string reaches a RegExp constructor, so future code is held to nothing. The grade is what the enforcement earns, not what the specimens show.

requirements.text: Verify that the application is protected against CSV and Formula Injection. The application must follow the escaping rules defined in RFC 4180 sections 2.6 and 2.7 when exporting CSV content. Additionally, when exporting to CSV or other spreadsheet formats (such as XLS, XLSX, or ODF), special characters (including '=', '+', '-', '@', '\t' (tab), and '\0' (null character)) must be escaped with a single quote if they appear as the first character in a field value.
requirements.negativeProof: No CSV or spreadsheet export ships: the export surface tracked by tools/data-flow.json is JSON-shaped, and no code path emits CSV, XLS, XLSX or ODF. If a consumer adds spreadsheet export, RFC 4180 escaping and formula-prefix quoting have no harness control behind them — the data-flow gate closes export column names against the schema, never the emitted format.

requirements.text: Verify that all untrusted HTML input from WYSIWYG editors or similar is sanitized using a well-known and secure HTML sanitization library or framework feature.
requirements.negativeProof: The dangerously-set-inner-html write-guard rule (WRITE_GLOBAL_CHECKS in template/base/.claude/hooks/lib/guard-rules.mjs) denies any Edit/Write tool call whose content carries the token on a JS/TS-extension file, and tests/hooks/hook-contract.test.mjs proves the denial can fail. It does not scan shell-redirected writes, hand commits, or non-JS files. No WYSIWYG editor, HTML input surface, or HTML sanitization library ships (none in the pnpm-workspace.yaml catalog).
requirements.note: There is no untrusted HTML input to sanitize: the template renders user text through approved components (raw text outside AppText is lint-red on mobile), never HTML strings, and the only React HTML-string sink is write-guard-denied, so the surface this requirement sanitizes cannot arrive through the governed agent channel. Residual: the guard reaches agent-mediated writes only; a consumer who hand-commits an HTML rendering path (a markdown-to-HTML pipeline, a WebView with html source) re-opens the requirement and must bring their own sanitizer — the harness ships none.

requirements.text: Verify that the application avoids the use of eval() or other dynamic code execution features such as Spring Expression Language (SpEL). Where there is no alternative, any user input being included must be sanitized before being executed.
requirements.note: The seeded tree calls no eval() or Function constructor (grep on template/stack apps/ and packages/), and the web surface enforces the avoidance at runtime: 'unsafe-eval' is a banned CSP token in tools/security-headers.json — the security-headers step reds it by evaluated value (tests/gates/check-security-headers.test.mjs 'RED: unsafe-eval in script-src' proves that red), and template/stack/apps/web/e2e/security-headers.spec.ts asserts the live document header omits it — so eval in the browser throws under the shipped policy. Not reached: server-side Node code and the Hermes mobile runtime have no CSP; the typescript-eslint strictTypeChecked preset the tree lints under carries no-implied-eval (Function constructor, string-argument timers) but no rule bans bare eval(), so a consumer-added eval on those surfaces is caught by nothing. Expression-language engines (SpEL and kin) do not exist in this stack.

requirements.text: Verify that data being passed to a potentially dangerous context is sanitized beforehand to enforce safety measures, such as only allowing characters which are safe for this context and trimming input which is too long.
requirements.proof: tools/check-contract-drift.mjs (the `contracts` validate-chain step; its factory red-proof is tests/gates/check-contract-drift.test.mjs)
requirements.note: The over-long half is enforced: every z.string() in the shared wire contract (@app/contracts) must carry .max(N) — the contracts step's bounded-wire-strings closure (G18 in tools/check-contract-drift.mjs) reds an unbounded field, with exemptions a reviewed, write-guard-protected tools/dto-bounds-allow.json entry — so input that is too long is refused at the boundary rather than trimmed. Evidence limit, stated: tests/gates/check-contract-drift.test.mjs exercises the tsconfig-reference and inventory halves of that gate only; no test in tests/ or the selftest workflow plants an unbounded z.string() and asserts the red, so the G18 closure is verified by reading the gate, not by a can-fail proof — hence the documentation tier and no canary named. The character-safety half is not enforced: no control constrains input to characters safe for a downstream context, and any zod refinement beyond the length bound is the consumer's authoring choice that no gate closes. Grading rides the enforced half only.

requirements.text: Verify that user-supplied Scalable Vector Graphics (SVG) scriptable content is validated or sanitized to contain only tags and attributes (such as draw graphics) that are safe for the application, e.g., do not contain scripts and foreignObject.
requirements.negativeProof: tools/check-essential-eight.mjs (second script of the docs-sync validate step) machine-asserts the no-upload posture: `[storage] enabled = false` in supabase/config.toml and no upload-shaped route anywhere in the tree — an upload surface appearing reds the chain.
requirements.note: No user-supplied SVG can arrive: Supabase storage is disabled, no upload route exists, and icons render from a closed glyph set through the design system. The negative is machine-asserted (docs-sync reds if storage is enabled or an upload route appears). A consumer who enables uploads must bring SVG sanitization themselves — none ships, and the docs-sync assertion will have already forced that decision into a red they must clear.

requirements.text: Verify that the application sanitizes or disables user-supplied scriptable or expression template language content, such as Markdown, CSS or XSL stylesheets, BBCode, or similar.
requirements.negativeProof: No Markdown, BBCode, XSL, or user-supplied stylesheet rendering ships; user text renders through the AppText/primitive layer as text. Only the HTML-string sink is machine-denied (the dangerously-set-inner-html write-guard rule); a markdown renderer that emits React elements directly would pass every gate, so beyond that one sink the absence of scriptable template-language rendering is unenforced.

requirements.text: Verify that the application protects against Server-side Request Forgery (SSRF) attacks, by validating untrusted data against an allowlist of protocols, domains, paths and ports and sanitizing potentially dangerous characters before using the data to call another service.
requirements.negativeProof: The seeded server code calls no service at a URL influenced by untrusted data: outbound calls go to the project's own Supabase URL and, for the rate limiter, the Upstash REST URL, both from validated env (@app/env; packages/platform/ratelimit/src/index.ts is the one server-side fetch() and its base is the configured url option), and telemetry sinks are the reviewed tools/observability.json register. Adjacent, not coverage: the resilience step requires every outbound transport construction site to carry a reviewed tools/resilience.json row — a census of seams, not an allowlist of destinations. No allowlist-of-protocols/domains/ports mechanism ships for consumer-added outbound fetches, so SSRF protection for any such feature is entirely the consumer's to build — grading this covered on absence of the surface would be the inflation the register refuses.

requirements.text: Verify that regular expressions are free from elements causing exponential backtracking, and ensure untrusted input is sanitized to mitigate ReDoS or Runaway Regex attacks.
requirements.note: No control bounds regular-expression complexity or scans for exponential backtracking — no regex-safety lint ships and no gate's subject is ReDoS. The seeded dynamic-regex sites are linear-time by inspection (an escaped literal key in cookies.ts; a fixed-length digit match in mfa-flow.ts), but inspection is not enforcement. This is a control the harness could ship (the eslint plugin class exists), which is why the grade is not-covered rather than not-applicable.

requirements.text: Verify that the application uses memory-safe string, safer memory copy and pointer arithmetic to detect or prevent stack, buffer, or heap overflows.

requirements.note: Every line the template owns runs on managed runtimes (Node/V8 server-side, Hermes on device); the chapter's own preamble scopes this section to systems languages and unmanaged code, which the owned tree does not contain. Native code exists only inside third-party dependencies (React Native, Expo modules), whose memory safety is their vendors' and is not claimed here. A consumer adding a native module with C/C++ inherits this requirement against that module, with only the reviewed-allowlist channel (native-deps) between them and it.

requirements.text: Verify that sign, range, and input validation techniques are used to prevent integer overflows.
requirements.negativeProof: JavaScript numbers do not overflow into adjacent memory — arithmetic degrades into floats/Infinity and BigInt is arbitrary-precision — so the memory-corruption class this section targets has no analogue in the owned code. The adjacent honest gap, stated rather than hidden: nothing enforces range validation on numeric wire fields (the contracts step bounds strings with .max(), not numbers), so a semantically absurd numeric input is refused only where a consumer wrote a zod bound. That gap belongs to the validation chapter's rows, not this memory-safety one.

requirements.text: Verify that dynamically allocated memory and resources are released, and that references or pointers to freed memory are removed or set to null to prevent dangling pointers and use-after-free vulnerabilities.
requirements.negativeProof: Same enforced absence as 1.4.1: the cng-android/cng-ios write-guard rules and the native-deps step's CNG-purity closure keep hand-authored unmanaged code out of the tree, so no owned code frees memory manually.
requirements.note: Memory is garbage-collected on every owned surface; there is no free(), no pointer arithmetic, no manual allocation with use-after-free semantics. The JS-adjacent residual — leaked listeners and subscriptions — has its own real control (the perf-budget step's effect-cleanup pairing scan over addEventListener/setInterval/subscribe and their teardown twins), but that control's subject is resource leaks, not memory unsafety, and it is deliberately not claimed as coverage here.

requirements.text: Verify that the application configures XML parsers to use a restrictive configuration and that unsafe features such as resolving external entities are disabled to prevent XML eXternal Entity (XXE) attacks.
requirements.negativeProof: The application parses no XML: no XML parser is resolved in the workspace catalog and no surface accepts XML input — the API is JSON-only through the transformer-less tRPC router. XML that exists in the toolchain (Android manifest manipulation at prebuild) processes trusted build inputs in CI, not untrusted data at runtime. Unenforced absence: a consumer adding an XML parser must disable external-entity resolution themselves, and nothing here would red the dependency arriving.
requirements.note: The application parses no XML: no XML parser is resolved in the workspace catalog and no surface accepts XML input — the API is JSON-only through the transformer-less tRPC router. XML that exists in the toolchain (Android manifest manipulation at prebuild) processes trusted build inputs in CI, not untrusted data at runtime. Unenforced absence: a consumer adding an XML parser must disable external-entity resolution themselves, and nothing here would red the dependency arriving.

requirements.text: Verify that deserialization of untrusted data enforces safe input handling, such as using an allowlist of object types or restricting client-defined object types, to prevent deserialization attacks. Deserialization mechanisms that are explicitly defined as insecure must not be used with untrusted input.
requirements.note: No gate's subject is deserialization safety. Facts of the seeded tree, favourable by construction but unenforced: untrusted data deserializes as JSON.parse followed by zod parsing against hand-authored DTOs in @app/contracts (every seeded procedure that takes input carries .input(<zod schema>) — packages/api/src/routers/notes.ts and system.ts), and client-defined object types cannot be revived because the router deliberately runs no transformer (packages/api/src/trpc.ts records the decision), so no Date/Map/Set/class revival path exists. What no machine holds: that every procedure carries a zod .input() (no gate, lint rule or test asserts it); that the transformer stays absent (no test or gate reads the tRPC init); prototype-pollution keys in parsed JSON; and any consumer-added route handler that deserializes differently. The contracts step's closures — action-inventory regen-diff, tsconfig references, the .max() bound on wire strings — are adjacent to this requirement, not its subject, and its test file proves none of them against a deserialization mutation, so naming it as the control here was inflation.

requirements.text: Verify that different parsers used in the application for the same data type (e.g., JSON parsers, XML parsers, URL parsers), perform parsing in a consistent way and use the same character encoding mechanism to avoid issues such as JSON Interoperability vulnerabilities or different URI or file parsing behavior being exploited in Remote File Inclusion (RFI) or Server-side Request Forgery (SSRF) attacks.
requirements.note: Nothing asserts that the parsers handling the same data type behave consistently. In practice each runtime uses its engine's single JSON.parse and WHATWG URL, and one router serves both clients — a shape that reduces parser divergence by construction — but no gate's subject is parser consistency, and the V8/Hermes/PostgREST trio are three JSON implementations no control compares. The harness could ship a cross-surface parser-behaviour fixture; it has not, so the grade is not-covered.

requirements.text: Verify that the application's documentation defines input validation rules for how to check the validity of data items against an expected structure. This could be common data formats such as credit card numbers, email addresses, telephone numbers, or it could be an internal data format.
requirements.note: The single home for input-structure expectations is @app/contracts (packages/contracts/src/index.ts): hand-authored zod DTOs where every seeded wire string carries .min/.max bounds, and the contracts validate-chain step (tools/check-contract-drift.mjs) enforces the two closures it can decide — every z.string() in @app/contracts carries .max(N) or a reviewed tools/dto-bounds-allow.json entry, and the generated action inventory is regen-diffed so the declared contract cannot drift from the router that enforces it. That makes the definition machine-checked rather than prose, which is stronger than documentation in one direction and weaker in another: the template ships no written catalogue of common data formats, the spec-first template (specs/_template.md) has no validation-rules section, and the field-level rules for every consumer-added feature are the consumer's to author. Partial covers the seeded surface and the bound closure only.

requirements.text: Verify that the application's documentation defines how to validate the logical and contextual consistency of combined data items, such as checking that suburb and ZIP code match.
requirements.note: No shipped surface documents cross-field contextual consistency rules: specs/_template.md carries no combined-data (or any validation) section, and no doc describes how combined items must cohere. For accuracy about the code: the seeded DTOs are not purely field-independent — @app/contracts NoteUpdateInput carries an object-level .refine (a patch must name at least one of body/title/isArchived) and @app/notes schemas.ts adds a normalised-title refinement — but both are presence/normalisation checks on one shape, not a contextual rule of the suburb/ZIP kind where one value constrains another, and neither is documented as a rule. Which combinations must cohere is the consumer's domain, so the rules cannot be seeded — but the harness could ship a spec-template prompt and a worked cross-field .refine/.superRefine specimen and does not today, which is why this is not-covered rather than not-applicable.

requirements.text: Verify that expectations for business logic limits and validations are documented, including both per-user and globally across the application.
requirements.note: For the limit families the harness owns, the documented expectation and the running implementation are held equal by value: tools/db-limits.json (per-role statement/lock/idle timeouts and the per-org quota machinery, judged by the db-limits step against the applied migration text — every declared knob must be applied by a migration at exactly the declared value and under the declared ceiling, and a knob on the register's `unavailable` list reds if it appears; the matrix closure is ONE-directional though — an ALTER ROLE SET of a knob the register does not declare passes silently unless it is on that list), tools/rate-limit-budget.json (per-identity buckets with written reasons, closed BOTH ways against the generated action inventory by the rate-limits step: an unmapped mutation reds and a mapping to a vanished procedure reds), and the seeded quota_defaults rows in the quota migration. Per-org and global ceilings are therefore documented and diff-enforced for those families. What is not documented is any consumer domain business limit — transfer amounts, order counts, workflow ceilings — which is the half the requirement chiefly means; the registers document the harness's infrastructure limits, not the application's business rules, and per-USER (as opposed to per-org) business limits exist only as the rate buckets' identity resolution.

requirements.text: Verify that input is validated to enforce business or functional expectations for that input. This should either use positive validation against an allow list of values, patterns, and ranges, or be based on comparing the input to an expected structure and logical limits according to predefined rules. For L1, this can focus on input which is used to make specific business or security decisions. For L2 and up, this should apply to all input.
requirements.note: The worked pattern parses every procedure input against a zod DTO before any handler runs: seeded DTOs use positive structural validation (uuid ids, bounded strings, bounded coerced integer page limits, an enum-closed cursor shape), the contracts step's G18 closure holds every wire z.string() to .max(N) or a reviewed tools/dto-bounds-allow.json entry, and the named canary asserts by test that unbounded or malformed input is refused (its 'bounds every wire string' and rejection cases go red if a bound is dropped). The database mirrors the seeded bounds as CHECK constraints (notes_title_length, notes_body_length in supabase/migrations/20260101000100_notes.sql), so the structural floor also binds the direct PostgREST path. Residuals that keep this partial: no gate asserts that a consumer-added procedure declares an input schema at all, and no machine can judge whether a field's allow-list or pattern SEMANTICS are right for the consumer's domain — the L1 scope (input feeding the seeded business/security decisions) is closed, the L2 'all input' scope is the consumer's.

requirements.text: Verify that the application is designed to enforce input validation at a trusted service layer. While client-side validation improves usability and should be encouraged, it must not be relied upon as a security control.
requirements.note: The design places validation server-side by construction: DTO parsing lives in @app/contracts/@app/api, which run only on the server — the mobile app consumes @app/api as an import-type-only devDependency (the boundaries step holds that wall), so there is no client-resident copy of the enforcement to mistake for the control, and client-side form validation in the seeded screens is UX only. Beneath the application layer the seeded schema carries its own CHECK constraints and RLS WITH CHECK predicates, which bind even a client that POSTs to PostgREST directly with the publishable key — the path the tRPC-layer validation never sees. Partial rather than covered for exactly that path: no gate asserts that a consumer-added table carries CHECK constraints mirroring its wire bounds, so on new surfaces the trusted-layer floor for direct-path writes is only what the consumer writes into the migration.

requirements.text: Verify that the application ensures that combinations of related data items are reasonable according to the pre-defined rules.
requirements.note: No shipped control validates that combinations of related data items are reasonable under domain rules. The seeded verticals do demonstrate the seam — @app/contracts NoteUpdateInput carries an object-level .refine (an empty patch is refused) and @app/notes schemas.ts adds a normalised-title refinement — but those are presence and normalisation checks, not a rule relating one field's value to another's, and the migrations carry no multi-column CHECK on domain data. There is no gate closure over combined-data rules, no worked contextual-consistency specimen, and the rules themselves are the consumer's domain knowledge (the same gap as 2.1.2's documentation half). A worked specimen and an enforcement seam are shippable and absent, so not-covered.

requirements.text: Verify that the application will only process business logic flows for the same user in the expected sequential step order and without skipping steps.
requirements.note: The template ships no general mechanism asserting that multi-step business flows execute in order without skipped steps. The nearest seeded specimen is the invitation flow (supabase/migrations/20260201000000_tenancy_spine.sql): create_invitation stores only a sha256 token digest and returns the plaintext exactly once, redemption must be performed by the invited holder, and a redeemed token cannot be replayed because its row no longer exists — a two-step flow whose order is enforced by its own data design. That is one flow's construction, not a control whose subject is flow sequencing; consumer-added flows get no state-machine scaffold and no gate here.

requirements.text: Verify that business logic limits are implemented per the application's documentation to avoid business logic flaws being exploited.
requirements.note: For the limits the harness documents, documentation and implementation cannot disagree silently: the db-limits step folds the migrations' ALTER ROLE matrix in statement order and requires every knob declared in tools/db-limits.json to be applied at the declared value and under its ceiling (a later RESET reds), and asserts the per-org quota machinery's exact shape (AFTER INSERT FOR EACH STATEMENT with REFERENCING NEW TABLE executing private.enforce_org_quota, the AFTER DELETE release twin, no WHEN clause, no RESTRICTIVE policy over a STABLE count); the rate-limits step diffs the budget by value against the code that runs. The overflow error is SQLSTATE 53400 mapped to quotaExceeded — deliberately not rateLimited, so a client never retries a limit that waiting cannot clear — but that mapping is proven by the unit test packages/platform/supabase/src/errors.test.ts, not by the gate: the db-limits step only requires the register to carry an errorCode key and does not read the migration's RAISE. The named pgTAP canary asserts the trigger shape from pg_trigger and that authenticated holds no write privilege on org_usage/org_quota — a tenant that can raise its own limit has none. Residual: these are the harness's own limit families; a consumer's domain business limits have the quota-metric pattern to copy but no closure asserting they were implemented at all, and no live test drives an actual 53400 overflow through PostgREST (the register's 'verified: 53 rows against a limit of 5' is a hand run, not a suite).

requirements.text: Verify that transactions are being used at the business logic level such that either a business logic operation succeeds in its entirety or it is rolled back to the previous correct state.
requirements.note: The seeded verticals get all-or-nothing behaviour by construction: every business operation is a single SQL statement, and the quota check and audit row fire from triggers inside the writing transaction, so a refused quota rolls back the write and its audit trace together. But no shipped control's subject is transactional integrity of multi-step operations — nothing asserts that a consumer procedure composing several statements wraps them in one transaction, and the primary client path (supabase-js over PostgREST) offers no client-side transaction to compose with, which makes the discipline easy to lose exactly where it starts mattering. Grading the atomic-by-construction specimen as coverage would claim a property no gate holds; not-covered.

requirements.text: Verify that business logic level locking mechanisms are used to ensure that limited quantity resources (such as theater seats or delivery slots) cannot be double-booked by manipulating the application's logic.
requirements.note: The one limited-quantity resource the template ships — the per-org quota — is allocated through a concurrency-correct mechanism: enforce_org_quota performs a single upsert on the org's usage row (ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE takes the row lock and applies the delta against the latest committed value, so concurrent allocating statements serialize against the counter; ORDER BY org_id fixes lock order across multi-org statements), and the db-limits step structurally refuses both fail-open shapes that are each one word away (a FOR EACH ROW trigger, and a RESTRICTIVE policy over a STABLE count, which the planner hoists to one pre-statement evaluation so a single multi-row INSERT of any size passes wholesale). The write-guard hook rules pg-advisory-session-lock, pg-session-timeout-set and pg-prepared-statement (.claude/hooks/lib/guard-rules.mjs — edit-time deny rules, not a chain step) refuse the pooled-connection locking primitives that break under a transaction-mode pooler (a session-scoped advisory lock leaks on any error path; the sanctioned form is pg_advisory_xact_lock), and the db-limits step repeats the session-advisory-lock scan over the tree. Residuals: the named pgTAP canary asserts trigger shape and privileges, not concurrency — no test drives two concurrent allocating statements against one org — and domain resources of the theater-seat kind are consumer tables; they inherit the pattern and the guard rules, but no closure asserts that a consumer allocation flow locks at all.

requirements.text: Verify that high-value business logic flows require multi-user approval to prevent unauthorized or accidental actions. This could include but is not limited to large monetary transfers, contract approvals, access to classified information, or safety overrides in manufacturing.
requirements.note: No maker-checker machinery ships: no pending-approval schema, no second-actor procedure pattern, and nothing in the seeded verticals models a high-value flow. The nearest shipped machinery is deliberately not this control: the privilege-lifecycle migration (supabase/migrations/20260815000000_privilege_lifecycle_jit.sql) makes revalidate_member an others-only act (the policy's WITH CHECK requires user_id <> auth.uid(), so a privileged seat's continuation is signed by a different, higher-ranked actor) and gates a lapsed owner's self-revalidation on a verified second FACTOR (aal2) — a second proof from the same user, not approval by a second user; both govern seat lifecycle, not a business transaction. CODEOWNERS review governs the repository's enforcement surfaces, not the generated application's business flows. A generic two-person-rule module is shippable and absent.

requirements.text: Verify that anti-automation controls are in place to protect against excessive calls to application functions that could lead to data exfiltration, garbage-data creation, quota exhaustion, rate-limit breaches, denial-of-service, or overuse of costly resources.
requirements.note: Three shipped layers, each with a different reach: per-procedure rate buckets enforced at the tRPC router and Server Action seams (the budget is reviewed by value in tools/rate-limit-budget.json and closed both directions against the generated action inventory, so a new mutation cannot land unmapped — an unknown name resolves to the write bucket, never to unlimited; the named canary proves the router refuses with a 429 BEFORE any handler runs, against a database that throws if touched); the per-org quota trigger; and the per-role statement timeouts, the latter two binding every path including direct PostgREST (tests/rls/resource-limits.test.ts proves the ceilings are in force through PostgREST, not merely present in the catalog). Honest scope, restated from the gate's own catalog entry: the buckets do not bind a client that calls PostgREST directly with the publishable key and its own JWT, and they do not bind sign-in or sign-up, which go to GoTrue — on those paths the quota and the timeouts are the only harness ceilings (GoTrue's own default endpoint limits apply but the template neither declares nor reviews them: supabase/config.toml carries no [auth.rate_limit] section), and they are coarser than per-caller limits. The limiter FAILS OPEN by recorded decision (docs/adr/20260204-rate-limiting.md) when its backend is unavailable, degrading to an in-process limiter (the budget multiplied by instance count; on a serverless platform that discards the process, still effectively removed). No CAPTCHA or human-verification control ships in any layer.

requirements.text: Verify that business logic flows require realistic human timing, preventing excessively rapid transaction submissions.
requirements.note: No shipped control measures inter-step timing or enforces human-plausible pacing on any flow. The rate buckets bound sustained throughput over 60-second windows (the seeded write bucket is 60/minute), which caps volume but does not distinguish a scripted burst inside the budget from a human, and nothing enforces a minimum interval between the steps of any business flow. Per-flow timing is buildable as consumer logic on the existing rate-limit seam (the port receives the procedure path and resolved identity); unshipped.

requirements.text: Verify that application documentation states the expected security features that browsers using the application must support (such as HTTPS, HTTP Strict Transport Security (HSTS), Content Security Policy (CSP), and other relevant HTTP security mechanisms). It must also define how the application must behave when some of these features are not available (such as warning the user or blocking access).
requirements.note: No shipped document states the browser security features the generated application requires of its users' browsers, or how the application behaves when one is absent. The docs the template seeds (docs/harness/**, SECURITY.md) address developers and vulnerability reporters, not browser-capability expectations. The harness could seed such a page beside the reviewed header policy in tools/security-headers.json, which already records the posture the page would describe, so this is not-covered rather than not-applicable.

requirements.text: Verify that security controls are in place to prevent browsers from rendering content or functionality in HTTP responses in an incorrect context (e.g., when an API, a user-uploaded file or other resource is requested directly). Possible controls could include: not serving the content unless HTTP request header fields (such as Sec-Fetch-*) indicate it is the correct context, using the sandbox directive of the Content-Security-Policy header field or using the attachment disposition type in the Content-Disposition header field.
requirements.note: X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff ships on every response the Next app produces, by exact value (the security-headers validate step evaluates apps/web/lib/security-headers.ts and diffs its returned values against tools/security-headers.json; the web-e2e lane's Playwright spec asserts the header on a real response). The Next API surface serves JSON only, and there is no user-uploaded-resource surface at all ([storage] enabled = false in supabase/config.toml, no upload route). What does NOT ship: Sec-Fetch-* context validation exists only on the cookie-authenticated tRPC path (packages/api/src/csrf.ts refuses cross-site shapes), no Content-Disposition or CSP sandbox discipline exists for direct resource requests, the seeded Supabase Edge Function (supabase/functions/delete-account) returns JSON outside the header module with no nosniff of its own, and nothing machine-checks a consumer-added file-serving route for any of the requirement's named controls.

requirements.text: Verify that content intended to be displayed as text, rather than rendered as HTML, is handled using safe rendering functions (such as createTextNode or textContent) to prevent unintended execution of content such as HTML or JavaScript.
requirements.note: React JSX text rendering escapes by construction (the textContent-equivalent path), and the one escape hatch is denied by the dangerously-set-inner-html write-guard rule (.claude/hooks/lib/guard-rules.mjs), whose deny is proven to fire by the factory's hook-contract suite and registered in tests/canary/injections.json. The residual is the guard's reach: it fires on agent edits through the PreToolUse hook — a human commit made outside the harness never meets it, and no ESLint twin (react/no-danger) ships in the flat config — so the merged-tree half rests on the web-security-reviewer's read rather than on a tree-wide gate.

requirements.text: Verify that the application avoids DOM clobbering when using client-side JavaScript by employing explicit variable declarations, performing strict type checking, avoiding storing global variables on the document object, and implementing namespace isolation.
requirements.note: No control has DOM clobbering as its subject. Strict TypeScript everywhere and React's component model mean the seeded code declares its variables and touches the document object nowhere, but that is incidental hygiene, not enforcement: nothing asserts namespace isolation, bans id/name attribute collisions with global names, or lints for clobbering-prone patterns in consumer-authored client code.

requirements.text: Verify that cookies have the 'Secure' attribute set, and if the '__Host-' prefix is not used for the cookie name, the '__Secure-' prefix must be used for the cookie name.
requirements.note: The Secure half holds: all three cookie writers (the browser jar in apps/web/lib/supabase/client.ts, the proxy.ts rewrite, and the server jar) derive Secure from the serving scheme, so every https response carries it — the derivation exists because a hard-coded true makes plain-http local development drop the cookie entirely — and cookies.test.ts, riding the unit Stop-chain step, proves the shared codec forwards the host's secure flag rather than stripping it. The prefix half does NOT hold: the session cookie is @supabase/ssr's sb-<project-ref>-auth-token name, which the server reader and the CSRF ambient-cookie matcher both key on, and neither the __Host- nor the __Secure- prefix is used. No gate asserts cookie attributes on the wire.

requirements.text: Verify that each cookie's 'SameSite' attribute value is set according to the purpose of the cookie, to limit exposure to user interface redress attacks and browser-based request forgery attacks, commonly known as cross-site request forgery (CSRF).
requirements.note: The one cookie the seed writes — the chunked Supabase session — defaults to SameSite=Lax in the shared codec (packages/platform/supabase/src/cookies.ts), with the purpose reasoning recorded at the constant: Strict would land every magic-link and OAuth return on a signed-out render, None invites cross-site delivery the app never needs. cookies.test.ts asserts the attribute in the write set. Graded partial rather than covered because the value is a codec default applied to whatever is written through it, not a per-cookie reviewed register: no gate inventories cookies or judges a consumer-added cookie's SameSite against its purpose. The CSRF exposure SameSite=Lax leaves open is independently closed by the Fetch-Metadata guard (see 3.5.1).

requirements.text: Verify that cookies have the '__Host-' prefix for the cookie name unless they are explicitly designed to be shared with other hosts.
requirements.note: The session cookie carries no __Host- prefix. Its name is the @supabase/ssr convention (sb-<project-ref>-auth-token, chunked as .0/.1), which the cookie-jar reader, the shared chunking codec, and the CSRF ambient-cookie matcher in packages/api/src/csrf.ts all key on. The cookie's attributes (Path=/, no Domain, Secure over https) would satisfy the prefix's preconditions, so adopting it is a rename decision, not an architectural one — but it has not been made, and the cookie is not explicitly designed for cross-host sharing, so the requirement is simply unmet.

requirements.text: Verify that if the value of a cookie is not meant to be accessible to client-side scripts (such as a session token), the cookie must have the 'HttpOnly' attribute set and the same value (e. g. session token) must only be transferred to the client via the 'Set-Cookie' header field.
requirements.note: The session cookie is deliberately NOT HttpOnly, and on this architecture it cannot be: sign-in runs browser-side (the password never crosses an extra hop), so the browser both writes and reads the cookie via document.cookie, and a user agent ignores HttpOnly on a script write. The trade is stated bluntly at both writers (packages/platform/supabase/src/cookies.ts, apps/web/lib/supabase/client.ts) together with the compensating mitigations — Secure, SameSite=Lax, the fail-closed CSRF guard on the ambient-credential path, and a short-lived rotating token. The requirement's subject (a session token invisible to script, delivered only via Set-Cookie) is unmet; a consumer who needs it must move sign-in server-side first, which the codec documents as the path to reclaiming the attribute.

requirements.text: Verify that when the application writes a cookie, the cookie name and value length combined are not over 4096 bytes. Overly large cookies will not be stored by the browser and therefore not sent with requests, preventing the user from using application functionality which relies on that cookie.
requirements.note: This exact failure mode is why the cookie codec exists: a Supabase session does not fit in one cookie, so packages/platform/supabase/src/cookies.ts chunks every value at CHUNK_BYTES = 3180 bytes per chunk — under RFC 6265's 4096-byte floor with headroom for the name and attributes, which count against the same budget — measured in UTF-8 BYTES rather than UTF-16 units, and all three seeded writers (the browser jar in apps/web/lib/supabase/client.ts, proxy.ts, and the server jar via cookie-server.ts) go through it. cookies.test.ts (unit Stop-chain step and the CI unit job) proves the byte-measured chunking, the code-point-safe splits, and the stale-chunk expiry — but every case passes an explicit small limit (2, 4, 6, 64, 100), and the only default-limit case (an 8000-byte session round-trips as more than one chunk) proves the constant is below 8000, not below 4096. Partial rather than covered because the shipped constant is a source value no test or gate pins: raising it past the budget passes the suite green, and a consumer writing cookies through some other path is outside the codec's guarantee entirely.

requirements.text: Verify that a Strict-Transport-Security header field is included on all responses to enforce an HTTP Strict Transport Security (HSTS) policy. A maximum age of at least 1 year must be defined, and for L2 and up, the policy must apply to all subdomains as well.
requirements.note: strict-transport-security: max-age=63072000; includeSubDomains; preload — two years (over the one-year floor) with the subdomain clause the L2-and-up half requires — ships on every path via next.config.ts headers(), deliberately NOT via the proxy, so the header does not depend on a request-interception layer running. The security-headers validate step asserts the exact value by evaluating the module (a shortened max-age is a proven red in tests/gates/check-security-headers.test.mjs), and the web-e2e lane's Playwright spec asserts includeSubDomains on a real response. Honest limit, stated by the gate itself: neither can prove the PRODUCTION response — a header-stripping CDN in front of a correct config is invisible from here. The seeded delete-account Edge Function answers on Supabase's own hostname, where HSTS is the platform's header, not this config's. Preload-list membership is 3.7.4's row, not this one.

requirements.text: Verify that the Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) Access-Control-Allow-Origin header field is a fixed value by the application, or if the Origin HTTP request header field value is used, it is validated against an allowlist of trusted origins. When 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *' needs to be used, verify that the response does not include any sensitive information.
requirements.note: The surface EXISTS in the seed, so this is not not-applicable: supabase/functions/delete-account/index.ts answers OPTIONS and stamps a fixed 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *' (plus Allow-Headers authorization/apikey/x-client-info/content-type, Allow-Methods POST/OPTIONS) on every response, because the web app calls it cross-origin from the browser (apps/web/lib/account/delete-account.ts via functions.invoke) and the Expo client through supabase-js. Read against the requirement's own clauses: the value is fixed rather than Origin-reflected, and the wildcard responses carry nothing sensitive — bodies are {ok:true} or an error code, and the function refuses without a bearer Authorization it verifies itself, so no ambient credential rides the wildcard. The Next app itself emits no Access-Control-Allow-Origin on any response, and Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy: same-origin (gate-asserted) blocks no-cors embedding besides. Not-covered because all of that is inspection, not enforcement: no gate asserts the function's header is fixed, no check reds a sensitive field arriving in a wildcard response, and a consumer-added reflected-Origin or wildcard route in the Next app meets no machine check.

requirements.text: Verify that HTTP responses include a Content-Security-Policy response header field which defines directives to ensure the browser only loads and executes trusted content or resources, in order to limit execution of malicious JavaScript. As a minimum, a global policy must be used which includes the directives object-src 'none' and base-uri 'none' and defines either an allowlist or uses nonces or hashes. For an L3 application, a per-response policy with nonces or hashes must be defined.
requirements.note: Every document response the proxy sees carries a per-response nonce CSP with 'strict-dynamic' — the L3 shape, not merely the L2 minimum — minted per request in proxy.ts, with object-src 'none' held by exact value and the nonce's reach proven end-to-end: the Playwright spec asserts a real minted nonce, asserts Next actually STAMPED it onto its bootstrap scripts via the IDL property, and collects securitypolicyviolation events so a policy that blanks the app cannot ship green. Three honest deviations keep this partial. First, base-uri is 'self' where the requirement's verbatim minimum says 'none' (a same-origin base tag remains expressible). Second, the CSP is applied by proxy.ts, so a response the proxy never produces — its matcher exclusions, or the CVE-2025-29927 class of interception bypass — carries the static headers but no CSP; the static half deliberately does not share that dependency. Third, proxy.ts mints the nonce only when the request carries sec-fetch-dest: document, so a client that sends no Fetch Metadata receives a document with no CSP at all. style-src's structural 'unsafe-inline' is a recorded decision in tools/security-headers.json; script-src's CSP2-fallback 'unsafe-inline' is documented in the module and policed by the gate's rule that refuses it unless 'strict-dynamic' is present.

requirements.text: Verify that all HTTP responses contain an 'X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff' header field. This instructs browsers not to use content sniffing and MIME type guessing for the given response, and to require the response's Content-Type header field value to match the destination resource. For example, the response to a request for a style is only accepted if the response's Content-Type is 'text/css'. This also enables the use of the Cross-Origin Read Blocking (CORB) functionality by the browser.
requirements.note: x-content-type-options: nosniff ships on every response the Next app produces ('/:path*' in next.config.ts headers(), request-independent, not routed through the proxy). The security-headers step asserts the exact value by evaluating the shipped module rather than grepping its text, and the web-e2e spec asserts the header on a real browser response. Partial on the requirement's 'all HTTP responses': the seeded Supabase Edge Function (supabase/functions/delete-account/index.ts) builds its own JSON responses with a hand-written header set that carries no nosniff — whether the platform's gateway adds one is not something any check here verifies — and no gate scans a consumer-added Edge Function or Route Handler that sets its own headers. Residual on the Next half: the gate proves the config and the lane proves its own build; a production CDN stripping headers is invisible to both, which the gate states as its own limit.

requirements.text: Verify that the application sets a referrer policy to prevent leakage of technically sensitive data to third-party services via the 'Referer' HTTP request header field. This can be done using the Referrer-Policy HTTP response header field or via HTML element attributes. Sensitive data could include path and query data in the URL, and for internal non-public applications also the hostname.
requirements.note: referrer-policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin ships on every response, asserted by exact value by the gate and on the wire by the e2e spec. The choice is grounded in this app's own URL shape: paths carry org slugs, so a full-URL Referer to a third party leaks tenant identity — the header sends the full URL same-origin only, origin-only cross-origin, nothing over a downgrade. Residual: per-element referrerpolicy attributes are not governed, and an internal-only deployment wanting to suppress even the hostname (no-referrer) would relax nothing by accident — tools/security-headers.json is write-guard-protected (guard rule security-headers-policy), listed in gate-integrity's ESCAPE_LISTS so an edit must be committed rather than left dirty at gate time, and under CODEOWNERS — so the change lands as a reviewed diff.

requirements.text: Verify that the web application uses the frame-ancestors directive of the Content-Security-Policy header field for every HTTP response to ensure that it cannot be embedded by default and that embedding of specific resources is allowed only when necessary. Note that the X-Frame-Options header field, although supported by browsers, is obsolete and may not be relied upon.
requirements.note: frame-ancestors 'none' rides every document response the proxy mints a CSP for, and X-Frame-Options: DENY rides every response as the legacy companion; the gate asserts both values AND their agreement, so the answer does not depend on which control the browser honours, and deleting the directive is a proven double red in the gate's test suite. Partial on the requirement's own wording: 'every HTTP response' — the CSP is minted in proxy.ts, whose matcher excludes static assets and /api/trpc, and only when the request carries sec-fetch-dest: document, so those responses (and any document fetched by a client without Fetch Metadata) carry only the X-Frame-Options fallback the requirement calls obsolete. None of the excluded paths serves a navigable document in the seed, but the verbatim clause is not met response-for-response.

requirements.text: Verify that the Content-Security-Policy header field specifies a location to report violations.
requirements.note: The ENFORCING Content-Security-Policy carries no reporting directive. Reporting rides the report-only twin: every document response also carries Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only holding the identical policy plus report-uri /api/csp-report, so anything the enforcing policy blocks necessarily violates the twin and reaches the in-app collector (app/api/csp-report/route.ts ships). The gate asserts the twin carries its report-uri — dropping it is a proven red in the gate's test suite — and the e2e lane separately collects securitypolicyviolation events in a real browser. Residuals stated plainly: the location is on the twin rather than on the header field the requirement names, report-uri is the deprecated (though still honoured) mechanism and no report-to/Reporting-Endpoints wiring ships, and the collector is in-app — a CSP failure that takes the app down can take its own reporting endpoint with it.

requirements.text: Verify that all HTTP responses that initiate a document rendering (such as responses with Content-Type text/html), include the Cross‑Origin‑Opener‑Policy header field with the same-origin directive or the same-origin-allow-popups directive as required. This prevents attacks that abuse shared access to Window objects, such as tabnabbing and frame counting.
requirements.note: cross-origin-opener-policy: same-origin ships on every response — a superset of the document-response requirement — via the request-independent next.config.ts half, asserted by exact value by the gate and on a real response by the e2e spec. The seed opens no cross-origin popups, so the same-origin-allow-popups relaxation is not needed; a consumer who needs it edits tools/security-headers.json, which is write-guard-protected and commit-enforced by gate-integrity's escape-list rule, so the relaxation lands as a reviewed diff. Non-document responses (the JSON API, the delete-account Edge Function) are outside the requirement's subject. Residual: the standing CDN caveat — the gate proves the config, the lane proves its build, neither proves production.

requirements.text: Verify that, if the application does not rely on the CORS preflight mechanism to prevent disallowed cross-origin requests to use sensitive functionality, these requests are validated to ensure they originate from the application itself. This may be done by using and validating anti-forgery tokens or requiring extra HTTP header fields that are not CORS-safelisted request-header fields. This is to defend against browser-based request forgery attacks, commonly known as cross-site request forgery (CSRF).
requirements.note: The ambient-credential path is guarded by Fetch Metadata, not tokens: packages/api/src/csrf.ts refuses any cookie-bearing request whose Sec-Fetch-Site is outside {same-origin, same-site, none} — a forbidden header name page script cannot forge — falling back to Origin-vs-self for pre-Fetch-Metadata clients and FAILING CLOSED when a cookie-bearing request carries neither signal. The host applies it in app/api/trpc/[trpc]/route.ts on the raw request BEFORE building the cookie client, so a cross-site request can never reach the getUser() refresh it could otherwise abuse to rotate-and-withhold a victim's token; the bearer path (mobile) needs and gets no guard, because a keychain token is not ambient. csrf.test.ts proves the refusals and rides the unit Stop-chain step. Partial for one stated reason: the seeded Server Actions (apps/web/app/actions/notes.ts and orgs.ts) rely on Next's own built-in Origin/Host enforcement for POSTed actions — real, but framework-internal and asserted by no gate in this tree. Sign-in itself is not a Server Action: it runs browser-side against the Supabase origin with the publishable key, a non-ambient path this guard does not and need not cover.

requirements.text: Verify that, if the application relies on the CORS preflight mechanism to prevent disallowed cross-origin use of sensitive functionality, it is not possible to call the functionality with a request which does not trigger a CORS-preflight request. This may require checking the values of the 'Origin' and 'Content-Type' request header fields or using an extra header field that is not a CORS-safelisted header-field.
requirements.negativeProof: The conditional does not hold: the application does not rely on the CORS preflight mechanism for request-forgery prevention. The Next app emits no CORS headers and its forgery defence is the Fetch-Metadata guard graded at 3.5.1, which examines every cookie-bearing request whether or not it would have triggered a preflight (simple-request shapes included). The one CORS-enabled endpoint the seed ships — the delete-account Edge Function, which answers OPTIONS with a fixed wildcard — is protected by a bearer Authorization it verifies itself, not by the preflight: a request that skips the preflight arrives without the token and is refused 401 before any state changes. Nothing enforces the absence: a consumer who later builds a preflight-reliant endpoint takes on this requirement with no machine check behind it.

requirements.text: Verify that HTTP requests to sensitive functionality use appropriate HTTP methods such as POST, PUT, PATCH, or DELETE, and not methods defined by the HTTP specification as "safe" such as HEAD, OPTIONS, or GET. Alternatively, strict validation of the Sec-Fetch-* request header fields can be used to ensure that the request did not originate from an inappropriate cross-origin call, a navigation request, or a resource load (such as an image source) where this is not expected.
requirements.note: State-changing procedures ride POST: tRPC's fetch adapter maps mutations to POST, the route handler mounts only GET and POST (any other verb 405s from the framework before the router), and Server Actions are POST by construction. Authenticated queries ride GET, which is where the requirement's stated alternative carries the row: the Sec-Fetch-Site validation in packages/api/src/csrf.ts is applied to EVERY cookie-bearing request regardless of method, refusing cross-site calls and (fail-closed) signal-less ones, proven by csrf.test.ts on the unit Stop step. Partial because the method mapping itself is framework behaviour no gate asserts — nothing reds a consumer procedure that performs a write inside a query — and the Sec-Fetch guard's subject is cross-site provenance, not the navigation/resource-load contexts the alternative also names.

requirements.text: Verify that separate applications are hosted on different hostnames to leverage the restrictions provided by same-origin policy, including how documents or scripts loaded by one origin can interact with resources from another origin and hostname-based restrictions on cookies.
requirements.negativeProof: Hosting topology — which applications share a hostname — is a deployment decision made in the operator's DNS and platform consoles, not in any file this template generates; the harness produces one application and cannot ship hostname separation between applications it does not know exist. What the tree does record: the CSRF guard deliberately treats same-site siblings (app.example.com beside api.example.com) as first-party, a choice the operator inherits when they co-host other applications on sibling subdomains of the same registrable domain — co-hosting an UNTRUSTED application there weakens the guard, and that trade lives with the operator.

requirements.text: Verify that messages received by the postMessage interface are discarded if the origin of the message is not trusted, or if the syntax of the message is invalid.
requirements.negativeProof: No postMessage listener or sender exists anywhere in the web application (grep-verified across apps/web at review time), so there is no message-handling surface to validate. The absence is not enforced: no guard rule or gate reds a consumer-added message listener, so this row's subject arrives ungoverned the moment one is written. COOP: same-origin (gate-asserted) narrows the cross-window surface — a cross-origin opener cannot retain a handle to this app's window — but does not validate messages on a listener a consumer adds.
