requirements.text: Verify that JSONP functionality is not enabled anywhere across the application to avoid Cross-Site Script Inclusion (XSSI) attacks.
requirements.negativeProof: The security-headers validate step asserts, by exact value on every response, x-content-type-options: nosniff and cross-origin-resource-policy: same-origin — so a cross-origin <script src> pointed at any app response is refused twice over (MIME enforcement against a JSON Content-Type, and CORP blocking the no-cors embed), which is the exploitation path a JSONP ban exists to close.
requirements.note: No JSONP endpoint exists: the API surface is tRPC JSON over GET/POST (plus a bearer-only JSON Edge Function that sets its own headers and is outside the negativeProof's reach), no route interprets a callback parameter, and no response wraps data in executable script. The negativeProof headers red the exploitation shape rather than the endpoint's appearance — nothing statically scans for a consumer-added callback-echoing route, so the enforced half is the browser-side refusal, and the absence of the server-side surface is architectural fact at review time.

requirements.text: Verify that data requiring authorization is not included in script resource responses, like JavaScript files, to prevent Cross-Site Script Inclusion (XSSI) attacks.
requirements.note: Script resources are build-time static chunks carrying no per-user data — authorized data rides JSON API responses that the gate holds to cache-control: private, no-store with a Vary naming the session cookie and acting-org selector (both explicit proven reds in the gate's test suite), and every response carries cross-origin-resource-policy: same-origin, which blocks the cross-origin script-tag inclusion XSSI needs (held by the gate's exact-value static-header comparison, whose red is proven on another header rather than on CORP specifically). Partial because the guarantee's first half is architectural rather than asserted: nothing scans script-typed responses for embedded authorized data, and the RSC payload Next inlines into the DOCUMENT — which is same-origin-readable by design and not a script resource — is the nearest thing to data-in-markup no gate examines.

requirements.text: Verify that authenticated resources (such as images, videos, scripts, and other documents) can be loaded or embedded on behalf of the user only when intended. This can be accomplished by strict validation of the Sec-Fetch-* HTTP request header fields to ensure that the request did not originate from an inappropriate cross-origin call, or by setting a restrictive Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy HTTP response header field to instruct the browser to block returned content.
requirements.note: The requirement names two acceptable implementations and the tree ships both: cross-origin-resource-policy: same-origin on every response (the restrictive-CORP option, held by the gate's exact-value comparison against tools/security-headers.json — the comparison's red is proven in the gate's test suite via a weakened HSTS value; there is no CORP-specific case, and the e2e spec does not read CORP on the wire), and Sec-Fetch-Site validation on the cookie-authenticated API path (packages/api/src/csrf.ts, proven by csrf.test.ts). The seed additionally has no authenticated media to embed — no storage, no user files. Residual: CORP governs no-cors embedding only in browsers that honour it; a consumer who intentionally serves embeddable cross-origin resources must relax tools/security-headers.json — write-guard-protected and commit-enforced by gate-integrity's escape-list rule — as a reviewed diff, at which point the intentionality the requirement asks about becomes their recorded decision.

requirements.text: Verify that client-side assets, such as JavaScript libraries, CSS, or web fonts, are only hosted externally (e.g., on a Content Delivery Network) if the resource is static and versioned and Subresource Integrity (SRI) is used to validate the integrity of the asset. If this is not possible, there should be a documented security decision to justify this for each resource.
requirements.negativeProof: The security-headers validate step asserts the CSP by value: default-src 'self' as a required directive, connect-src must contain 'self' and may not contain '*', default-src may not contain '*', object-src 'none' — so an externally hosted resource of any type NOT named by a more specific directive falls to default-src 'self' and is refused by the deployed policy. The module additionally ships style-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline', font-src 'self', img-src 'self' blob: data:, but those three per-type values are emitted, not gate-asserted: a widening there passes the gate green.
requirements.note: No client-side asset is hosted externally: every script, style and font is first-party, bundled and served from the app's own origin (apps/web/app/layout.tsx loads no external stylesheet, font or script), so there is nothing for SRI to attest. Honest limits of the negativeProof: the gate pins default-src and connect-src but not style-src/font-src/img-src, and script-src carries an https: CSP2 fallback while 'strict-dynamic' ignores host allowlists by design, so the CSP does not make external SCRIPT loading impossible for code the app itself ships — it makes it a decision of nonce-trusted first-party code. The moment a consumer adds a CDN asset, the SRI-or-documented-decision obligation is theirs, and no gate checks integrity attributes.

requirements.text: Verify that the application only uses client-side technologies which are still supported and considered secure. Examples of technologies which do not meet this requirement include NSAPI plugins, Flash, Shockwave, ActiveX, Silverlight, NACL, or client-side Java applets.
requirements.note: The client stack is current React/Next/Expo and contains none of the named legacy technologies; three real controls hold adjacent ground: object-src 'none' (security-headers, by value) refuses the plugin-document embedding every named example needs; the version-sync step's end-of-life census reds any package the resolved lockfile records as vendor-deprecated unless dispositioned in tools/eol.json, diffed by value in both directions (tests/gates/eol.test.mjs proves the no-row red; the section rides a ramp on upgrading installs and is live on fresh scaffolds); and the same step's framework floor holds the pinned frameworks at or above reviewed patched releases (tests/gates/framework-floor.test.mjs), with review lapse riding the scheduled floor-review job. Partial because 'considered secure' is a judgement no gate makes, and a client-side technology arriving other than through npm resolution (a pasted script, a consumer-authored applet-era embed) is unseen by all three.

requirements.text: Verify that the application will only automatically redirect the user to a different hostname or domain (which is not controlled by the application) where the destination appears on an allowlist.
requirements.negativeProof: Every seeded redirect is an internal literal path — the sign-in/sign-up gates, the protected layout's /sign-in bounce, and the org picker's slug route (grep-verified at review time); no redirect destination derives from request data and no cross-hostname redirect exists, so there is no open-redirect surface to allowlist. The absence is not enforced: nothing reds a consumer-added redirect(searchParams.get('next')), and typedRoutes checks Link hrefs against the route table but does not constrain redirect() strings to same-origin.

requirements.text: Verify that the application shows a notification when the user is being redirected to a URL outside of the application's control, with an option to cancel the navigation.
requirements.negativeProof: The same absence as 3.7.2 from the other side: the application performs no navigation to URLs outside its control, so there is nothing to interpose a notification on, and no exit-interstitial component ships because there is no surface to hang one from. A consumer who introduces outbound links or redirects takes on both this row and 3.7.2 together, with no seeded component or gate waiting for them.

requirements.text: Verify that the application's top-level domain (e.g., site.tld) is added to the public preload list for HTTP Strict Transport Security (HSTS). This ensures that the use of TLS for the application is built directly into the main browsers, rather than relying only on the Strict-Transport-Security response header field.
requirements.negativeProof: Preload-list membership is an act the operator performs at hstspreload.org for a domain the template does not know; no repository artefact can register it, and no offline check could verify membership without violating the hermeticity rule. What the tree does ship, held by value by the security-headers step: the preload-ELIGIBLE header (max-age=63072000, includeSubDomains, preload), with the hstsPreload decision recorded in tools/security-headers.json precisely because it is close to irreversible — a consumer serving any subdomain over plain HTTP must change it BEFORE first deploy. The submission itself, and the responsibility for its near-irreversibility, are the operator's.

requirements.text: Verify that the application behaves as documented (such as warning the user or blocking access) if the browser used to access the application does not support the expected security features.
requirements.note: This row inherits 3.1.1's gap and adds behaviour to it: the documentation of expected browser security features does not exist, and no feature-detection, warning or blocking surface ships for a browser that lacks them (the app relies on modern-browser behaviour — CSP3 strict-dynamic, Fetch Metadata — degrading silently rather than as documented). The harness could ship both halves — the statement and a detection surface — so this is not-covered rather than not-applicable.

requirements.text: Verify that every HTTP response with a message body contains a Content-Type header field that matches the actual content of the response, including the charset parameter to specify safe character encoding (e.g., UTF-8, ISO-8859-1) according to IANA Media Types, such as "text/", "/+xml" and "/xml".
requirements.proof: tests/gates/check-security-headers.test.mjs (registry fixture for the security-headers step — mutates the shipped apps/web/lib/security-headers.ts and watches the gate red; Canary 21) + apps/web/e2e/security-headers.spec.ts (web-e2e lane live half, held present by check-web-e2e.mjs; asserts x-content-type-options nosniff on a real response)
requirements.note: Control: security-headers (validate step: node tools/check-security-headers.mjs). The Next runtime stamps a matching Content-Type on every framework-generated response (text/html; charset=utf-8 for pages, application/json for the tRPC fetch adapter's output), and the one hand-built response in the tree — the tRPC route's CSRF 403 — sets application/json explicitly, a type whose encoding is UTF-8 by definition with no charset parameter to carry. What the harness actually enforces is the ADJACENT half, not this requirement: the security-headers step diffs x-content-type-options: nosniff BY VALUE against tools/security-headers.json so the declared type is authoritative in the browser, and the web-e2e spec reads that header off a real response. No gate verifies that any response's Content-Type matches its body or carries a charset parameter, no canary injects a wrong or absent Content-Type, and a consumer's hand-built Response with a wrong or missing type would pass every gate — the correctness is the framework's default, inherited rather than asserted. Graded partial for the adjacent nosniff control only.

requirements.text: Verify that only user-facing endpoints (intended for manual web-browser access) automatically redirect from HTTP to HTTPS, while other services or endpoints do not implement transparent redirects. This is to avoid a situation where a client is erroneously sending unencrypted HTTP requests, but since the requests are being automatically redirected to HTTPS, the leakage of sensitive data goes undiscovered.
requirements.note: Vercel terminates TLS for every deployment and transparently redirects plain-HTTP requests to HTTPS across the whole host, /api/trpc included — the exact behavior this requirement says non-user-facing endpoints must not have — and that redirect is platform policy nothing in this tree can scope per endpoint. The mitigations the tree holds run the other way: the security-headers step pins a two-year preload HSTS by value so a browser stops issuing plain-HTTP requests at all, and the expo-policy step reds a cleartext or non-https extra.apiOrigin so the shipped mobile client cannot erroneously dial http. The residual the requirement targets — a non-browser API consumer whose unencrypted requests are silently upgraded instead of failing loudly — remains, and it is a property of the deployment platform rather than of anything a gate here reaches.

requirements.text: Verify that any HTTP header field used by the application and set by an intermediary layer, such as a load balancer, a web proxy, or a backend-for-frontend service, cannot be overridden by the end-user. Example headers might include X-Real-IP, X-Forwarded-*, or X-User-ID.
requirements.note: The tree consumes two intermediary-set headers, and no gate protects either from end-user override. apps/web/lib/rate-limit-runtime.ts reads x-forwarded-for (first hop) as the anonymous rate-limit key, recording on the function that the value is trustworthy only to the extent the platform overwrites it and that a verified userId always outranks it — so a spoofed value on a self-terminated deployment degrades anonymous limiting, never another caller's budget. apps/web/lib/supabase/server.ts reads x-forwarded-proto to decide whether the session cookie is written with Secure — a security decision riding an intermediary header, safe only because Vercel overwrites it. Neither read is asserted by any chain step, Stop step or test, and the web-security-reviewer's checklist (triggered on apps/web/lib/rate-limit*.ts and apps/web/lib/supabase/**) names neither forwarded header. The nearest test — packages/api/src/envelope.test.ts proving an x-org-id naming an org the caller does not hold is not an elevation, riding the unit Stop step — is about a CLIENT-set header the design deliberately looks up in the caller's own seats, which is a different property from the one this requirement names. Whether intermediary headers can be overridden is a fact of the deployment platform, and nothing here reaches it.

requirements.text: Verify that only HTTP methods that are explicitly supported by the application or its API (including OPTIONS during preflight requests) can be used and that unused methods are blocked.
requirements.note: Both shipped Route Handlers export an explicit method set — the tRPC adapter mounts GET and POST only ('No other verb is mounted — an unhandled method returns 405 from Next', stated in the route file itself) and app/api/csp-report mounts POST only — and the App Router returns 405 for any unexported method by construction. That blocking is a framework guarantee inherited by the tree, not a harness assertion: no gate or test drives an unsupported verb and asserts the 405, and no OPTIONS/preflight handling is exercised. The web-security-reviewer is owed a PASS on any diff under apps/web/app/api/** (tools/reviewer-triggers.json, enforced by the reviewer-verdicts Stop step), but its checklist has no item about the HTTP method surface — the closest is the CSRF item's 'state-changing GET' — so a handler that widened its verb set would not be something that reviewer is instructed to flag. The Supabase Data API's own method surface (PostgREST, pg_graphql) is vendor behavior outside the tree's reach.

requirements.text: Verify that per-message digital signatures are used to provide additional assurance on top of transport protections for requests or transactions which are highly sensitive or which traverse a number of systems.
requirements.negativeProof: The requirement is conditional on a traffic class the scaffold does not ship: every request runs client to the single tRPC endpoint to Postgres under TLS, and no flow is relayed onward through further systems where transport protection would lapse. Whether any of a consumer's future flows are 'highly sensitive' enough to warrant per-message signatures is their product decision, and nothing in the harness enforces this absence or would notice such a flow arriving unsigned. The opt-in e2ee module's AEAD envelope binds row identity for data at rest and is not a per-message request signature; no signing infrastructure for requests exists or is claimed.

requirements.text: Verify that all application components (including load balancers, firewalls, and application servers) determine boundaries of incoming HTTP messages using the appropriate mechanism for the HTTP version to prevent HTTP request smuggling. In HTTP/1.x, if a Transfer-Encoding header field is present, the Content-Length header must be ignored per RFC 2616. When using HTTP/2 or HTTP/3, if a Content-Length header field is present, the receiver must ensure that it is consistent with the length of the DATA frames.

The nearest control the tree holds is keeping the framework on a patched line: the version-sync step's framework floor (tools/framework-floor.json) reds a resolved next version below its reviewed floor — a patch posture against known defects, not a verification of framing behavior — and it floors next only; Node is held to a MAJOR agreement across .nvmrc/.node-version/engines/eas.json, not to a patched-release floor. An operator who fronts the deployment with their own load balancer or terminates HTTP themselves owes this requirement at that proxy.

requirements.text: Verify that, if the application (backend or frontend) builds and sends requests, it uses validation, sanitization, or other mechanisms to avoid creating URIs (such as for API calls) or HTTP request header fields (such as Authorization or Cookie), which are too long to be accepted by the receiving component. This could cause a denial of service, such as when sending an overly long request (e.g., a long cookie header field), which results in the server always responding with an error status.
requirements.proof: tests/gates/check-contract-drift.test.mjs (registry fixture for the contracts step — exercises the inventory-freshness and tsconfig-reference halves; it does NOT inject an unbounded z.string(), so the G18 sweep has no injection canary)
requirements.note: Control: contracts (validate step: node tools/check-contract-drift.mjs — G18 bounded wire strings). G18 (tools/check-contract-drift.mjs, the contracts step) walks packages/contracts/src and reds any z.string() whose fluent chain carries no .max(), with reviewed exceptions in tools/dto-bounds-allow.json (write-guarded and gate-integrity-hashed; the gate does not red a stale allow entry, so the escape list is closed one way only) — so every wire string a client can place into a request body or query input carries a size cap at the contract boundary. The honest residuals: the mobile tRPC client uses httpBatchLink, whose queries ride GET with inputs serialized into the URL, and no maxURLLength is configured — nothing computes the assembled batch-URL length, so batching many individually-bounded queries can still exceed a receiving intermediary's limit; non-string payload growth (arrays of bounded strings) is bounded only by each procedure's own input schema; cookie-header growth is not bounded by any gate; and the receiving components' specific limits (Vercel, Supabase) are not knowable from the tree. requirements.text: Verify that a query allowlist, depth limiting, amount limiting, or query cost analysis is used to prevent GraphQL or data layer expression Denial of Service (DoS) as a result of expensive, nested queries.
requirements.proof: tests/rls/resource-limits.test.ts (rls-isolation Stop step; proves the ceilings are in force through PostgREST)
requirements.note: Control: db-limits (validate step: node tools/check-db-limits.mjs — per-role statement_timeout ceilings and the [api].max_rows pin). The shipped supabase/config.toml exposes graphql_public through the Data API ([api].schemas), so on a Supabase project the pg_graphql endpoint is a live query surface, and no query allowlist, depth limit, or cost analysis governs it. What binds an expensive query there is time-limiting at the data layer: the per-role statement_timeout ceilings the db-limits step holds against the resource-limits migration apply to graphql.resolve() exactly as to any statement the role runs, and tests/rls/resource-limits.test.ts proves the ceilings are in force through PostgREST — a blunt backstop that bounds a nested query's cost rather than refusing it. The [api].max_rows = 1000 pin the same gate holds bounds PostgREST REST reads but NOT the GraphQL endpoint (a GraphQL query returns as one jsonb value from an rpc, so the row cap never sees the nested rows); pg_graphql applies its own per-collection row cap by vendor default, and neither that default nor any depth or cost limit is asserted here. Worth a reviewer's attention: the comment above [api].schemas says only public is exposed while the value also names graphql_public — a comment/value drift this row's research surfaced.

requirements.text: Verify that GraphQL introspection queries are disabled in the production environment unless the GraphQL API is meant to be used by other parties.
requirements.note: graphql_public sits in the shipped exposed-schema list, and pg_graphql serves schema introspection to any caller presenting the publishable key; nothing in the tree disables it and no gate reds it staying enabled. This is graded not-covered rather than not-applicable because the harness could close it — nothing in the tree consumes GraphQL (the API surface in use is tRPC plus PostgREST, and a tree-wide grep finds no GraphQL client), so dropping graphql_public from [api].schemas would remove the surface at no cost to the scaffold. RLS still governs the rows behind the endpoint, so what introspection reveals is schema shape, never data; that bounds the exposure; it does not close the requirement.

For L1, this can focus just on files which are used to make specific business or security decisions. For L2 and up, this must apply to all files being accepted.

requirements.text: Verify that file names served (e.g., in HTTP response header fields or email attachments) are encoded or sanitized (e.g., following RFC 6266) to preserve document structure and prevent injection attacks.
requirements.negativeProof: supabase/config.toml seeds [storage] enabled = false and tools/check-essential-eight.mjs (docs-sync chain step) reds if that setting is enabled or absent. No shipped gate registers App Router route handlers (tools/check-web-routes.mjs registers page.* files; tools/check-route-manifest.mjs excludes api/ routes) and none judges header-field encoding, so the absence of served file names is a reviewed claim, not a machine-decided one.
requirements.note: Not applicable: no file names are served in response header fields, and the scaffold sends no email attachments — auth email is Supabase-templated OTP text (supabase/config.toml, template = "Your code is {{ .Code }}"). Nothing in the harness would judge RFC 6266 encoding on a future download surface, and no registry gate would even notice a new route handler that serves one; the obligation transfers whole to the consumer who adds it, and this row must be re-graded in that change.

requirements.text: Verify that files obtained from untrusted sources are scanned by antivirus scanners to prevent serving of known malicious content.
requirements.negativeProof: supabase/config.toml seeds [storage] enabled = false and tools/check-essential-eight.mjs (docs-sync chain step) reds if that setting is enabled or absent, and if a file-acceptance shape appears on either surface — so a file-ingestion path cannot arrive without a red gate and a reviewed diff.
requirements.note: Not applicable at the organisation boundary: antivirus scanning is a running operational service that a template cannot ship or evidence, and this tree obtains no files from untrusted sources for one to scan — Supabase Storage is disabled at seed and no ingestion path exists. If a consumer's operator enables Storage, malware scanning of ingested objects becomes their operational control to deploy and evidence; the harness's contribution ends at redding the surface's unreviewed appearance, which forces this row's re-grade in the enabling change.

requirements.text: Verify that application documentation defines how controls such as rate limiting, anti-automation, and adaptive response, are used to defend against attacks such as credential stuffing and password brute force. The documentation must make clear how these controls are configured and prevent malicious account lockout.
requirements.note: Control: validate-chain step rate-limits (tools/check-rate-limits.mjs). The documentation exists as reviewed, machine-diffed data rather than prose: tools/rate-limit-budget.json carries every bucket with a written reason, an explicit fail-open decision (availability over lockout, with the degraded-mode cost stated), and an honest-scope paragraph, and the rate-limits gate holds the running code equal to it by value in both directions. What the documentation itself states, and this row therefore cannot claim past: the budgets bind the tRPC and Server Action seams only — sign-in and sign-up go to GoTrue, whose own rate limits are a platform fact configured in the deployed project's Dashboard, invisible to every gate here. No application-side lockout mechanism exists, so the anti-lockout half is discharged by absence at the app seams and by whatever the deployed GoTrue does, which is documented nowhere here. The failed-attempt observability at the GoTrue seam lives in a SEPARATE record (auth_trail.events, docs/adr/20260816-auth-event-trail.md — the rate-limit ADR itself only defers sign-in to "Supabase Auth's own limits and the platform WAF"), is proven live by a real failed sign-in in tests/rls/auth-trail.test.ts, and observes rather than prevents.

requirements.text: Verify that a list of context-specific words is documented in order to prevent their use in passwords. The list could include permutations of organization names, product names, system identifiers, project codenames, department or role names, and similar.
requirements.note: No context-specific word list ships, and the platform offers no enforcement point for one: GoTrue exposes no hook at password-creation time (its only password hook fires at verification), so a server-side denylist cannot be wired into the shipped auth service. A consumer discharging this row would document the list and enforce it client-side in the sign-up form, labelled advisory — a direct API caller bypasses any client-side check, and that limit belongs in the same documentation.

requirements.text: Verify that, if the application includes multiple authentication pathways, these are all documented together with the security controls and authentication strength which must be consistently enforced across them.
requirements.proof: tools/check-auth-posture.mjs (the `auth-posture` validate-chain step; its factory red-proof is tests/gates/check-auth-posture.test.mjs)
requirements.note: Control: validate-chain step auth-posture (tools/check-auth-posture.mjs). The scaffold ships exactly one pathway — email/password against GoTrue with an offered TOTP step-up — reached identically by web and mobile, and the pathway census is machine-held for the local config: tools/auth-posture.json is diffed against supabase/config.toml by value in both directions, and both the unknown-key and unknown-section closures red, so a new local auth surface (a provider section, an anonymous-sign-in flip, a phone factor) cannot land undocumented. Consistent strength across surfaces is structural: both clients hit the same GoTrue and the same RLS policies, and the aal2 rail — a RESTRICTIVE policy — binds in the database on public.notes ONLY (supabase/migrations/20260812000000_mfa_aal2.sql states the notes-only scope plainly; profiles, orgs, memberships, invitations and admin_elevations carry no aal2 policy, and nothing in packages/api or the protected web layout reads the aal claim), so consistent authentication STRENGTH is machine-held for one table and rests on "one GoTrue, one policy set" for the rest. The residual is the deployed project: providers enabled in the Dashboard never appear in any file a gate can read, so the documented-together property is proven for the local posture only.

requirements.text: Verify that user set passwords are at least 8 characters in length although a minimum of 15 characters is strongly recommended.
requirements.note: Nothing shipped pins a minimum password length. GoTrue's local default minimum is 6 characters, the config key (minimum_password_length) is real and CLI-accepted — the 0.6.0 spike recorded in check-auth-posture.mjs proved a config carrying it brings the stack up — yet neither supabase/config.toml nor the tools/auth-posture.json floor sets it, so the seeded local stack accepts 6-character passwords today. The deployed project's password policy is a Dashboard setting no gate can see. The natural discharge is a posture-floor row pinning the key at 8 or above; the seeded forms perform no client-side length validation either.

requirements.text: Verify that users can change their password.
requirements.note: No change-password surface ships. The seeded account surfaces are sign-in, sign-up, the MFA factor management page/screen, and account deletion (the delete-account Edge Function, seeded for Apple 5.1.1(v)); none of them changes a password. GoTrue's updateUser({password}) exists for a consumer to build against, but until a screen calls it the capability is the platform's, not the application's.

requirements.text: Verify that password change functionality requires the user's current and new password.
requirements.note: No password-change surface ships (see 6.2.2), and the platform default does not satisfy this row on its own: GoTrue's updateUser accepts a new password on the strength of the session alone. The reauthentication requirement is a real config.toml key (auth.email.secure_password_change, CLI default false) that neither supabase/config.toml nor the tools/auth-posture.json floor sets — and because the floor's unknown-key census is closed and a consumer cannot mint a tunable, pinning it locally is a harness floor row, not a consumer edit; the deployed project's equivalent is a Dashboard setting no gate sees. A consumer building the change screen owes both halves: the surface, and the reauthentication posture (a floor row locally, the Dashboard remotely).

requirements.text: Verify that passwords submitted during account registration or password change are checked against an available set of, at least, the top 3000 passwords which match the application's password policy, e.g. minimum length.
requirements.note: No common-password check ships in the tree and none is pinned in configuration. The hosted platform's leaked-password protection (a HaveIBeenPwned check at signup and password change) is the natural discharge, but it is a paid-plan Dashboard toggle on the deployed project — invisible to every local gate, and absent from the local GoTrue entirely. Nothing client-side performs a top-N check either.

requirements.text: Verify that passwords of any composition can be used, without rules limiting the type of characters permitted. There must be no requirement for a minimum number of upper or lower case characters, numbers, or special characters.
requirements.proof: tools/check-auth-posture.mjs (the `auth-posture` validate-chain step; its factory red-proof is tests/gates/check-auth-posture.test.mjs)
requirements.note: Control: validate-chain step auth-posture (tools/check-auth-posture.mjs). No composition rule exists anywhere in the tree — the seeded forms validate nothing about password shape, and the local GoTrue runs with password_requirements unset — and the absence is enforced in the one direction a gate can hold: the auth-posture backward census reds any [auth*] key appearing in supabase/config.toml that the reviewed registers do not name, so a composition requirement cannot be introduced into the local config silently. The residual is the deployed project, where a Dashboard-set password policy could impose composition rules without any tree diff; graded partial rather than covered for exactly that gap.

requirements.text: Verify that password input fields use type=password to mask the entry. Applications may allow the user to temporarily view the entire masked password, or the last typed character of the password.
requirements.note: The seeded surfaces do what the row asks as written — the design-system Input renders type=password on web when its secure prop is set (packages/design-system/src/Input.tsx) and the mobile sign-in sets secureTextEntry — but no gate, test, or reviewer trigger holds the property: the credential form paths are outside every security reviewer's MUST-BE-USED set, and no unit or e2e assertion checks masking, so a diff dropping the secure prop would land with every control green. Graded not-covered because this register grades enforcement, not the current state of an unguarded file; the note records only that today the inputs are masked.

requirements.text: Verify that "paste" functionality, browser password helpers, and external password managers are permitted.
requirements.note: The seeded inputs permit all three as written: the web Input is a plain controlled input with no paste interception and no autocomplete suppression, and the mobile sign-in sets textContentType='password', which is what enables the iOS password-manager AutoFill bar. But permission-by-default is not a control — nothing would red a later onPaste handler or an autocomplete="off", and no test asserts the affordance. Graded not-covered on enforcement grounds, with the current permissive state recorded here.

requirements.text: Verify that the application verifies the user's password exactly as received from the user, without any modifications such as truncation or case transformation.
requirements.note: The tree's own half holds trivially — both clients pass the raw string to signInWithPassword with no transformation — but the verifier is GoTrue, and its bcrypt storage truncates input beyond 72 bytes, which is a modification this requirement's letter forbids for very long passwords. That is an upstream property no local control can change, pin, or test; recorded here rather than graded around.

requirements.text: Verify that passwords of at least 64 characters are permitted.
requirements.note: GoTrue accepts passwords up to its 72-character bcrypt bound, so 64-character passwords pass against today's platform, and the seeded inputs impose no maxLength. But the bound is the vendor's fact, not a control this tree holds: nothing pins it, nothing tests it, and a platform change would be invisible here. Not-covered records that the property is currently true and entirely unheld.

requirements.text: Verify that a user's password stays valid until it is discovered to be compromised or the user rotates it. The application must not require periodic credential rotation.
requirements.negativeProof: Neither GoTrue nor anything in this tree implements periodic password expiry — there is no rotation mechanism to configure, so the prohibition holds by construction of the platform. Graded not-applicable rather than covered because the register refuses absence-as-coverage: no control enforces that a rotation scheme never appears, and a consumer who built one application-side would violate this row without any gate noticing.
requirements.note: Neither GoTrue nor anything in this tree implements periodic password expiry — there is no rotation mechanism to configure, so the prohibition holds by construction of the platform. Graded not-applicable rather than covered because the register refuses absence-as-coverage: no control enforces that a rotation scheme never appears, and a consumer who built one application-side would violate this row without any gate noticing.

requirements.text: Verify that the documented list of context specific words is used to prevent easy to guess passwords being created.
requirements.note: Depends wholly on 6.1.2, which is not-covered: no list is documented, and GoTrue offers no password-creation hook that could enforce one server-side. The enforcement half of this row therefore has neither the list nor a place to apply it.

requirements.text: Verify that passwords submitted during account registration or password changes are checked against a set of breached passwords.
requirements.note: The hosted platform's leaked-password protection is exactly this check, and it is a paid-plan Dashboard toggle on the deployed project that no gate in this tree can see, pin, or prove enabled. Nothing ships in-tree. Same disposition as 6.2.4, which is the top-N subset of the same platform feature.

requirements.text: Verify that controls to prevent attacks such as credential stuffing and password brute force are implemented according to the application's security documentation.
requirements.note: Control: validate-chain step rate-limits (tools/check-rate-limits.mjs). Implemented-according-to-documentation is literally the gate's shape: check-rate-limits evaluates the running limiter module and diffs it against the reviewed budget by value, so code and documentation cannot drift apart silently, and the vitest suite proves the limiter itself can fail. The stuffing surface this cannot reach is the one the documentation names: sign-in goes to GoTrue, whose rate limits live in the deployed project's platform configuration. What the tree adds at that seam is observation, not prevention — auth_trail.events records every password and MFA verification attempt including failures, via GoTrue's own hooks, proven end-to-end by a real failed sign-in in tests/rls/auth-trail.test.ts.

requirements.text: Verify that default user accounts (e.g., "root", "admin", or "sa") are not present in the application or are disabled.
requirements.negativeProof: No default-account surface exists to disable: GoTrue creates no application user accounts on its own, and the seeded fixtures are deliberately credential-less — supabase/seed.sql's header states NO CREDENTIALS and its five auth.users rows carry no password hash, so they cannot authenticate even locally; the seed itself runs only against local/CI stacks, never a deployed project. Nothing machine-enforces the seed staying credential-less (a hand-added password hash would be caught only by review), which is why this is a not-applicable with a stated reason rather than a covered.
requirements.note: No default-account surface exists to disable: GoTrue creates no application user accounts on its own, and the seeded fixtures are deliberately credential-less — supabase/seed.sql's header states NO CREDENTIALS and its five auth.users rows carry no password hash, so they cannot authenticate even locally; the seed itself runs only against local/CI stacks, never a deployed project. Nothing machine-enforces the seed staying credential-less (a hand-added password hash would be caught only by review), which is why this is a not-applicable with a stated reason rather than a covered.

requirements.text: Verify that either a multi-factor authentication mechanism or a combination of single-factor authentication mechanisms, must be used in order to access the application. For L3, one of the factors must be a hardware-based authentication mechanism which provides compromise and impersonation resistance against phishing attacks while verifying the intent to authenticate by requiring a user-initiated action (such as a button press on a FIDO hardware key or a mobile phone). Relaxing any of the considerations in this requirement requires a fully documented rationale and a comprehensive set of mitigating controls.
requirements.note: Control: Stop-chain step rls-isolation (tests/rls/run-rls.mjs, running supabase/tests/mfa_aal2.test.sql). The rails ship; the word MUST does not, and the database enforcement covers one table. TOTP enrolment is offered at sign-up on both surfaces, challenge screens and factor management exist on both, and a RESTRICTIVE policy on public.notes refuses any statement from a user who holds a verified factor but presents an aal1 token. That scope is stated plainly in the migration itself (which data warrants a second factor is a product decision): profiles, orgs, memberships, invitations and admin_elevations carry NO aal2 policy, and nothing in packages/api or the protected web layout reads the aal claim, so an enrolled user's aal1 session still reaches every other table and every protected route. The rail's fail-closed shape is proven by a 25-assertion pgTAP suite the rls-isolation Stop step runs; the fail-open mutation (the published upstream policy swapped in) was run once and recorded in the CHANGELOG (6 of the then-23 assertions failed), and no gate re-runs it. What cannot be closed here: GoTrue's MFA configuration has no required field, so a user who declines enrolment still authenticates with a password alone — mandatory MFA is an application/product decision handed to the consumer, stated in the config and posture registers rather than implied. The L3 half is explicitly unavailable: WebAuthn is pinned off in tools/auth-posture.json because the platform silently downgrades it when its billing is unconfirmed, and no hardware-backed factor exists on this stack today.

requirements.text: Verify that, if the application includes multiple authentication pathways, there are no undocumented pathways and that security controls and authentication strength are enforced consistently.
requirements.proof: tools/check-auth-posture.mjs (the `auth-posture` validate-chain step; its factory red-proof is tests/gates/check-auth-posture.test.mjs)
requirements.note: Control: validate-chain step auth-posture (tools/check-auth-posture.mjs). For the local posture the no-undocumented-pathways closure is machine-held in the direction that matters: every [auth*] key and every config section in supabase/config.toml must appear in a reviewed register, so an added provider section, anonymous sign-in flip, or new factor reds rather than landing quietly. Consistency of strength is structural — web and mobile traverse one GoTrue and one set of RLS policies, and the aal2 rail binds in the database on public.notes only (see 6.3.3) — for that table it covers even a pathway nobody wrote; for every other table, strength consistency is only "one GoTrue, one policy set". The residual: authentication pathways enabled in the deployed project's Dashboard (OAuth providers, magic links) produce no tree diff and are invisible to this gate; the deployed census is the consumer's to keep.

requirements.text: Verify that users are notified of suspicious authentication attempts (successful or unsuccessful). This may include authentication attempts from an unusual location or client, partially successful authentication (only one of multiple factors), an authentication attempt after a long period of inactivity or a successful authentication after several unsuccessful attempts.
requirements.note: No user-facing notification channel for authentication events exists — the scaffold ships no transactional-email or push infrastructure wired to auth activity. The substrate a consumer would build on does exist: auth_trail.events captures successful and failed password and MFA verification attempts server-side via GoTrue's hooks (the seam no client can see), but that trail is deliberately reader-less — its consumer is an operator with database access, and it notifies nobody. Detection heuristics (unusual location, partial success, inactivity) and the delivery channel are both unbuilt.

requirements.text: Verify that email is not used as either a single-factor or multi-factor authentication mechanism.
requirements.note: The seeded clients never offer email-based authentication — both forms use signInWithPassword and the MFA rail is TOTP — but the platform pathway exists regardless of what the forms render: GoTrue's magic-link/email-OTP grant rides the enabled email provider, no shipped config key disables it, and a caller driving the API directly can authenticate a deployed project's user by email link. Closing it is a Dashboard/product act on the deployed project that no local gate can observe, which is why this row is graded on the platform's reachable surface rather than the scaffold's UI.

requirements.text: Verify that users are notified after updates to authentication details, such as credential resets or modification of the username or email address.
requirements.proof: tools/check-auth-posture.mjs (the `auth-posture` validate-chain step; its factory red-proof is tests/gates/check-auth-posture.test.mjs)
requirements.note: Control: validate-chain step auth-posture (tools/check-auth-posture.mjs). One update class is held: email change requires confirmation on BOTH the old and new address — auth.email.double_confirm_changes is pinned true in the tools/auth-posture.json floor precisely because an email change with no notice to the old address is an account-takeover primitive, and the gate reds the key drifting in the LOCAL config; the deployed project's value is a Dashboard/remotes setting no gate sees. Nothing else notifies: password changes, factor enrolments and unenrolments produce no user-facing message (the auth trail records verification events operator-side, and factor lifecycle is not in it). The covered slice is one update kind out of several, hence partial.

requirements.text: Verify that valid users cannot be deduced from failed authentication challenges, such as by basing on error messages, HTTP response codes, or different response times. Registration and forgot password functionality must also have this protection.
requirements.note: Control: Stop-chain step mobile-unit (jest-expo, running apps/mobile/__tests__/sign-in.test.tsx). The seam this tree owns holds the discipline and proves it: both sign-in and sign-up render ONE non-enumerating failure sentence for every failure mode and never forward the provider's message — asserted by can-fail tests on the mobile suite for both forms ('a rejected credential shows ONE non-enumerating sentence, never the provider message'; sign-up's mirror), with the web forms sharing the same deliberate structure. What the form discipline cannot reach: an attacker talks to GoTrue directly, so enumeration resistance ultimately rests on the vendor's responses and timing at the token, signup, and recovery endpoints — behavior nothing here measures (no timing-channel test exists), and the deployed posture (email confirmations on, which is what blunts signup-time enumeration) lives in the Dashboard outside any gate's sight. No forgot-password surface ships (see 6.4.3), so its protection is unbuilt rather than unproven.

requirements.text: Verify that system generated initial passwords or activation codes are securely randomly generated, follow the existing password policy, and expire after a short period of time or after they are initially used. These initial secrets must not be permitted to become the long term password.
requirements.negativeProof: No system-generated initial authentication secret exists: accounts are created by self-service signup with a user-chosen password, and no admin-provisioning flow mints temporary credentials. The nearest analogue in the tree is an authorization artifact, not an authentication one, and it happens to be the worked pattern this row would want: invitation tokens are CSPRNG-generated (gen_random_uuid), stored digest-only (sha256, returned in plaintext exactly once), expire after 7 days, and are consumed by a race-safe DELETE so a redeemed token cannot be replayed (supabase/migrations/20260201000000_tenancy_spine.sql).
requirements.note: No system-generated initial authentication secret exists: accounts are created by self-service signup with a user-chosen password, and no admin-provisioning flow mints temporary credentials. The nearest analogue in the tree is an authorization artifact, not an authentication one, and it happens to be the worked pattern this row would want: invitation tokens are CSPRNG-generated (gen_random_uuid), stored digest-only (sha256, returned in plaintext exactly once), expire after 7 days, and are consumed by a race-safe DELETE so a redeemed token cannot be replayed (supabase/migrations/20260201000000_tenancy_spine.sql).

requirements.text: Verify that password hints or knowledge-based authentication (so-called "secret questions") are not present.
requirements.negativeProof: Absent everywhere: GoTrue offers no password-hint or security-question feature, and the scaffold ships none. Nothing machine-enforces the absence — a consumer could build KBA application-side without any gate noticing — so this is recorded as an absence with its reason rather than claimed as a control.
requirements.note: Absent everywhere: GoTrue offers no password-hint or security-question feature, and the scaffold ships none. Nothing machine-enforces the absence — a consumer could build KBA application-side without any gate noticing — so this is recorded as an absence with its reason rather than claimed as a control.

requirements.text: Verify that a secure process for resetting a forgotten password is implemented, that does not bypass any enabled multi-factor authentication mechanisms.
requirements.note: No forgot-password flow ships — neither form links to one and no reset screen exists. The platform's recovery grant exists regardless (a direct API caller can trigger GoTrue's recovery email against a deployed project), so the pathway is reachable without being built or reviewed here. One partial mitigation is worth recording without over-claiming it: the RESTRICTIVE aal2 policy on public.notes means an enrolled user's recovery-minted aal1 session reads and writes nothing in NOTES — but profiles, orgs, memberships and invitations carry no aal2 policy and remain fully reachable to that session, so recovery DOES bypass MFA into most of an enrolled user's data; whether it can bypass MFA into changing the credential itself is GoTrue's behavior, unverified by anything in this tree.

requirements.text: Verify that if a multi-factor authentication factor is lost, evidence of identity proofing is performed at the same level as during enrollment.
requirements.negativeProof: Identity proofing on factor loss is a running organisation's support process — who may attest to a user's identity, against what evidence, recorded where — and no repository can ship it. What the tree contributes is the constraint that makes the process necessary: no in-app recovery or backdoor exists, and GoTrue requires an aal2 session to unenrol a verified factor (vendor behavior, pinned and tested by nothing here), so a user who has lost the factor cannot self-recover and recovery necessarily goes through the operator's console (the vendor's admin API can unenrol a factor), which is exactly where the organisation's proofing procedure must sit.

requirements.text: Verify that renewal instructions for authentication mechanisms which expire are sent with enough time to be carried out before the old authentication mechanism expires, configuring automated reminders if necessary.
requirements.negativeProof: No expiring authentication mechanism exists in the stack: passwords do not expire (6.2.10), TOTP secrets do not expire, and no certificate- or hardware-based authenticators ship (WebAuthn is pinned off). With no expiring mechanism class there is nothing to send renewal instructions for. A consumer introducing one (client certificates, expiring hardware tokens) inherits this row whole.
requirements.note: No expiring authentication mechanism exists in the stack: passwords do not expire (6.2.10), TOTP secrets do not expire, and no certificate- or hardware-based authenticators ship (WebAuthn is pinned off). With no expiring mechanism class there is nothing to send renewal instructions for. A consumer introducing one (client certificates, expiring hardware tokens) inherits this row whole.

requirements.text: Verify that administrative users can initiate the password reset process for the user, but that this does not allow them to change or choose the user's password. This prevents a situation where they know the user's password.
requirements.note: No administrative user-management surface ships in-tree — service_role is confined to ADR-governed Edge Functions and the only one seeded is delete-account — so the admin-initiated reset an operator actually performs happens on the vendor's console, and there the requirement's guarantee does not hold: the Dashboard and the admin API allow an operator to SET a user's password directly, not merely trigger a reset. The harness could ship a constrained reset-initiation surface (an ADR'd function that only sends the recovery email) and does not; until then the reset path is the vendor console with its choose-the-password capability intact, an organisation-side residual recorded rather than closed.

requirements.text: Verify that lookup secrets, out-of-band authentication requests or codes, and time-based one-time passwords (TOTPs) are only successfully usable once.
requirements.note: Of the three mechanism classes only TOTP exists here (no lookup secrets, no out-of-band factors — phone MFA is pinned off), and TOTP single-use is the vendor's verifier behavior: whether GoTrue refuses a replayed code inside its validity window is not documented in anything this tree pins and is proven by no test here. The in-tree single-use precedent (invitation tokens consumed by DELETE) is an authorization artifact and is not claimed for this row.

requirements.text: Verify that, when being stored in the application's backend, lookup secrets with less than 112 bits of entropy (19 random alphanumeric characters or 34 random digits) are hashed with an approved password storage hashing algorithm that incorporates a 32-bit random salt. A standard hash function can be used if the secret has 112 bits of entropy or more.
requirements.negativeProof: No lookup secrets exist: GoTrue's TOTP implementation has no recovery codes, and the scaffold mints none. Two adjacent artifacts are deliberately not claimed: the invitation token (an authorization credential, stored as a plain sha256 digest — consistent with this row's own rule, since a v4 UUID carries about 122 bits of entropy) and the opt-in e2ee module's Recovery code, which is key-escrow material for client-side encryption, not an authentication secret, and ships only when the module is enabled.
requirements.note: No lookup secrets exist: GoTrue's TOTP implementation has no recovery codes, and the scaffold mints none. Two adjacent artifacts are deliberately not claimed: the invitation token (an authorization credential, stored as a plain sha256 digest — consistent with this row's own rule, since a v4 UUID carries about 122 bits of entropy) and the opt-in e2ee module's Recovery code, which is key-escrow material for client-side encryption, not an authentication secret, and ships only when the module is enabled.

requirements.text: Verify that lookup secrets, out-of-band authentication code, and time-based one-time password seeds, are generated using a Cryptographically Secure Pseudorandom Number Generator (CSPRNG) to avoid predictable values.
requirements.negativeProof: write-guard rule math-random-key-material + ESLint no-insecure-random-in-crypto-scope (crypto-scoped — see note for the limit)
requirements.note: No authentication secret is generated by code in this tree: TOTP seeds are minted by GoTrue (vendor-side, unverifiable here), lookup secrets and out-of-band codes do not exist, and the one in-tree secret generation — the invitation token — uses gen_random_uuid(), which draws from Postgres's strong-random source. The named guards enforce CSPRNG discipline where key-shaped material is born in JS, and their honest limit is that they are scoped to crypto surfaces and key-shaped names: a hand-rolled OTP generator elsewhere in app code would not trip them and would fall to review.

requirements.text: Verify that lookup secrets and out-of-band authentication codes have a minimum of 20 bits of entropy (typically 4 random alphanumeric characters or 6 random digits is sufficient).
requirements.negativeProof: validate-chain step auth-posture pins auth.mfa.phone.* (including otp_length 6) so the class cannot be enabled without a reviewed diff
requirements.note: Neither mechanism class exists: no lookup secrets ship and out-of-band authentication is pinned off. The disabled phone factor's keys are nonetheless written out and reviewed by value — including otp_length = 6, which meets this row's arithmetic — precisely so that enabling the factor is a reviewed diff arriving with its entropy posture already on the table rather than a one-line flip.

requirements.text: Verify that out-of-band authentication requests, codes, or tokens, as well as time-based one-time passwords (TOTPs) have a defined lifetime. Out of band requests must have a maximum lifetime of 10 minutes and for TOTP a maximum lifetime of 30 seconds.
requirements.note: Out-of-band mechanisms are absent (phone MFA pinned off), so the 10-minute half is moot; the TOTP half is live and unheld: GoTrue verifies TOTP with the standard 30-second period as its behavior, but no config key pins the period or the accepted skew window, nothing in the tree can read the vendor's verifier parameters, and no test exercises code expiry. The property is believed true of the platform and is proven by nothing here.

requirements.text: Verify that any authentication factor (including physical devices) can be revoked in case of theft or other loss.
requirements.note: Control: Stop-chain step mobile-unit (jest-expo, running apps/mobile/__tests__/security-screen.test.tsx). The factor class that exists — enrolled TOTP — is user-revocable through shipped surfaces on both platforms: the web security page and the mobile security screen list factors and unenrol them, and the mobile suite proves the flow can fail ('lists enrolled factors by name and removes one on unenroll', plus the failed-unenroll case). Partial, not covered, for three residuals: the web factors panel has no equivalent unit test of its own; revocation when the user has LOST the factor (GoTrue requires an aal2 session to unenrol a verified factor — vendor behavior, unpinned here — so that user cannot self-revoke) is the operator's act through the vendor's admin surface, outside the tree; and no physical-device factor class exists to revoke (WebAuthn pinned off).

requirements.text: Verify that biometric authentication mechanisms are only used as secondary factors together with either something you have or something you know.
requirements.negativeProof: validate-chain step expo-policy (tools/check-expo-policy.mjs) — a biometric surface needs iOS usage strings reviewed into tools/expo-permissions.json, and app.config.ts is a mobile-security-reviewer trigger path
requirements.note: No biometric authentication mechanism exists: the platform keychain use inside LargeSecureStore protects the session store and is not an authentication factor, and no Face ID/Touch ID gate ships. The absence cannot be reversed silently on mobile — a biometric capability arrives with new permission usage strings, which must land in the reviewed permission register the expo-policy gate closes, and the config diff owes a mobile-security-reviewer verdict. A web biometric flow (WebAuthn platform authenticators) is pinned off with the rest of WebAuthn in the auth-posture floor.

requirements.text: Verify that time-based one-time passwords (TOTPs) are checked based on a time source from a trusted service and not from an untrusted or client provided time.
requirements.note: Structurally sound and unproven: TOTP verification happens server-side in GoTrue against the server's clock — the clients only forward the six digits, and no code path in this tree evaluates a TOTP against device time — but the verifier's time source is the vendor's implementation detail, pinned by nothing and tested by nothing here. The architectural fact is recorded; the vendor's half is not claimed.

requirements.text: Verify that authentication mechanisms using the Public Switched Telephone Network (PSTN) to deliver One-time Passwords (OTPs) via phone or SMS are offered only when the phone number has previously been validated, alternate stronger methods (such as Time based One-time Passwords) are also offered, and the service provides information on their security risks to users. For L3 applications, phone and SMS must not be available as options.
requirements.negativeProof: validate-chain step auth-posture (tools/check-auth-posture.mjs): tools/auth-posture.json pins auth.mfa.phone.enroll_enabled and verify_enabled false by value, in both directions; the floor file is harness-owned and sha-pinned by check-gate-integrity.mjs
requirements.note: PSTN/SMS authentication is not offered, and the absence is a machine-held posture rather than a default: both phone-factor keys are explicitly false in config and pinned false in the reviewed floor, so flipping either reds the auth-posture gate until the floor itself changes in a CODEOWNERS-reviewed harness diff. The posture notes record the reason (phishable by construction; SIM-swap surface), which is the user-risk information half of this row applied at the strongest point — refusal. The stronger alternative (TOTP) is the factor that IS enabled. A deployed project enabling phone MFA Dashboard-side would bypass the local pin; that residual belongs to the consumer.

requirements.text: Verify that out-of-band authentication requests, codes, or tokens are bound to the original authentication request for which they were generated and are not usable for a previous or subsequent one.
requirements.negativeProof: validate-chain step auth-posture: the phone factor (the only out-of-band class the platform offers as MFA) is pinned off; see 6.6.1
requirements.note: No out-of-band authentication mechanism ships, so there is no request binding to verify. The caveat recorded at 6.3.6 applies here too: GoTrue's email magic-link grant is an out-of-band-shaped pathway that remains reachable on a deployed project regardless of the seeded UI, and whether its tokens are bound to an originating request is the vendor's behavior, unexamined by anything in this tree.

requirements.text: Verify that a code based out-of-band authentication mechanism is protected against brute force attacks by using rate limiting. Consider also using a code with at least 64 bits of entropy.
requirements.negativeProof: validate-chain step auth-posture: auth.mfa.phone.* pinned off, and the disabled factor's rate key (max_frequency = 5s, the CLI's real default — the published docs say 10s and are wrong) is pinned by value too
requirements.note: No code-based out-of-band mechanism is enabled. The register deliberately pins even the disabled factor's rate-limiting key, so if a consumer enables phone MFA the change arrives as a reviewed diff already carrying a rate posture rather than inheriting an unreviewed default. GoTrue's own OTP endpoint rate limits on a deployed project are platform facts outside any local gate.

requirements.text: Verify that, where push notifications are used for multi-factor authentication, rate limiting is used to prevent push bombing attacks. Number matching may also mitigate this risk.
requirements.negativeProof: No push-notification authentication mechanism exists: GoTrue offers no push-approval MFA factor, and the harness's opt-in push-notifications module is product messaging infrastructure, not an authentication mechanism — enabling that module creates no auth surface. With the mechanism absent, push-bombing rate limiting has no subject.
requirements.note: No push-notification authentication mechanism exists: GoTrue offers no push-approval MFA factor, and the harness's opt-in push-notifications module is product messaging infrastructure, not an authentication mechanism — enabling that module creates no auth surface. With the mechanism absent, push-bombing rate limiting has no subject.

requirements.text: Verify that the certificates used to verify cryptographic authentication assertions are stored in a way protects them from modification.
requirements.negativeProof: validate-chain step auth-posture: auth.mfa.web_authn.enroll_enabled and verify_enabled pinned false — the one device-bound cryptographic mechanism the platform could offer cannot be enabled without a reviewed floor diff
requirements.note: No cryptographic device authentication mechanism (smart card, FIDO key, WebAuthn) ships, so no verification certificates exist to protect. WebAuthn is pinned off with the recorded reason that the platform silently downgrades it when billing is unconfirmed — a config line claiming a disabled factor would be worse than the absence. The adjacent-but-different artifact is noted to prevent conflation: JWT session assertions are verified against the project's published keys (getClaims/JWKS), whose custody is the vendor's, and that is 6.8's subject, not this row's.

requirements.text: Verify that the challenge nonce is at least 64 bits in length, and statistically unique or unique over the lifetime of the cryptographic device.
requirements.negativeProof: validate-chain step auth-posture: WebAuthn pinned off (see 6.7.1)
requirements.note: No challenge-response cryptographic authentication exists, so there is no challenge nonce to measure. If a consumer enables WebAuthn (a reviewed floor change plus the platform's paid add-on), nonce generation would be GoTrue's implementation, and this row would move to the vendor-behavior class alongside 6.5.1 and 6.5.8 rather than becoming coverable here.

requirements.text: Verify that, if the application supports multiple identity providers (IdPs), the user's identity cannot be spoofed via another supported identity provider (eg. by using the same user identifier). The standard mitigation would be for the application to register and identify the user using a combination of the IdP ID (serving as a namespace) and the user's ID in the IdP.
requirements.negativeProof: validate-chain step auth-posture (tools/check-auth-posture.mjs): the config section census is closed in both directions, so an [auth.external.*] provider section appearing in supabase/config.toml reds as an unknown section
requirements.note: A single identity provider is configured (GoTrue's email/password), so cross-IdP spoofing has no subject; a provider section cannot be added to the local config unreviewed. If a consumer federates providers (a Dashboard act on the deployed project, invisible here), the row's standard mitigation is in fact GoTrue's internal model — identities are keyed by (provider, provider-subject) — but that is the vendor's design, recorded as context and not claimed as this tree's control.

requirements.text: Verify that the presence and integrity of digital signatures on authentication assertions (for example on JWTs or SAML assertions) are always validated, rejecting any assertions that are unsigned or have invalid signatures.
requirements.proof: tools/eslint-rules/index.mjs — the custom rule named in the note, wired in eslint.config.mjs and run by the `lint` step (factory red-proof tests/gates/eslint-custom-rules.test.mjs)
requirements.note: Control: validate-chain step lint (custom ESLint rule no-unverified-session, tools/eslint-rules/index.mjs). The failure mode this row exists for — trusting a decoded-but-unverified assertion — is machine-banned in first-party server code: getSession() returns the cookie's JWT without signature verification, and the AST rule reds any server-side member call of it (with a write-guard tripwire beside it for edit fragments), leaving getUser() (verified against the auth server) and getClaims() (verified against the published key) as the only identity reads; the data path's own verification is the platform's — PostgREST/GoTrue verify the JWT signature before auth.uid() resolves, so a forged token matches no rows. Partial rather than covered because the rejection behavior itself is the vendor's and untested in-tree: no test presents a tampered or unsigned token and asserts refusal (the RLS suites authenticate with genuine GoTrue-signed tokens), and the lint rule's 'use client' exemption means a browser component reading its own session is deliberately out of scope.

requirements.text: Verify that SAML assertions are uniquely processed and used only once within the validity period to prevent replay attacks.
requirements.negativeProof: No SAML exists anywhere in the stack: the auth service speaks JWT/OIDC-shaped flows, the scaffold configures no SAML SSO (a hosted enterprise SSO feature on the deployed platform), and no assertion-consuming endpoint ships. Nothing machine-enforces the absence — a consumer enabling the platform's SAML SSO would inherit this row whole, with replay protection being the vendor's implementation to verify.
requirements.note: No SAML exists anywhere in the stack: the auth service speaks JWT/OIDC-shaped flows, the scaffold configures no SAML SSO (a hosted enterprise SSO feature on the deployed platform), and no assertion-consuming endpoint ships. Nothing machine-enforces the absence — a consumer enabling the platform's SAML SSO would inherit this row whole, with replay protection being the vendor's implementation to verify.

requirements.text: Verify that, if an application uses a separate Identity Provider (IdP) and expects specific authentication strength, methods, or recentness for specific functions, the application verifies this using the information returned by the IdP. For example, if OIDC is used, this might be achieved by validating ID Token claims such as 'acr', 'amr', and 'auth_time' (if present). If the IdP does not provide this information, the application must have a documented fallback approach that assumes that the minimum strength authentication mechanism was used (for example, single-factor authentication using username and password).
requirements.note: Control: Stop-chain step rls-isolation (tests/rls/run-rls.mjs, running supabase/tests/mfa_aal2.test.sql). The mechanism this row describes is exactly what ships, applied to the built-in provider: authentication strength is read from the token's assurance claim and verified where it matters — client-side the sign-in flow reads the assurance level and routes enrolled users to the challenge (packages/platform/supabase/src/mfa-flow.ts, its own vitest suite beside it), and server-side a restrictive database policy evaluates the JWT's aal claim on every statement, so for public.notes — and only that table: the migration states the notes-only scope, and no procedure, Server Action or layout reads the aal claim — a caller expecting aal2 strength gets it enforced below the application; the pgTAP suite proves the policy fails closed rather than open, including the NULL-claim arm. The honest caveats: GoTrue is the application's own auth service rather than a 'separate' IdP, so the row's literal subject — a federated external provider — does not exist here (this is the worked pattern, not federation coverage), and the client-side fallback when the assurance read fails is to proceed (documented in the form, safe only because the database rail still refuses aal1), which is a fallback the DATA layer makes conservative rather than a documented minimum-strength assumption at the session layer.

requirements.text: Verify that the user's session inactivity timeout and absolute maximum session lifetime are documented, are appropriate in combination with other controls, and that the documentation includes justification for any deviations from NIST SP 800-63B re-authentication requirements.
requirements.note: The two parameters this requirement asks to see documented do not exist in the tree: the seeded supabase/config.toml sets no [auth.sessions] inactivity_timeout or timebox, and GoTrue's default leaves a session refreshable indefinitely, so there is neither an inactivity timeout nor an absolute lifetime to document. What does exist is adjacent, not the subject: auth.jwt_expiry is 3600 seconds with a reviewed bound (300 to 86400) and a written justification in tools/auth-posture.json, but that is the access-token life between refreshes, not a session lifetime. The auth-posture gate's closed section census means a future [auth.sessions] block reds until one of the two registers names it (the harness-owned tools/auth-posture.json knownSections or the consumer's write-guarded tools/auth-tunables.json additionalSections — the second is the consumer's own reviewed act, so review is forced but not harness review), which pushes the eventual decision through a diff but does not create the documentation this row asks for.

requirements.text: Verify that the documentation defines how many concurrent (parallel) sessions are allowed for one account as well as the intended behaviors and actions to be taken when the maximum number of active sessions is reached.
requirements.note: No concurrent-session policy is configured or documented anywhere in the tree: GoTrue's default admits unlimited parallel sessions per account, the seeded supabase/config.toml sets no per-user session cap, and neither tools/auth-posture.json nor tools/auth-tunables.json carries a row for one. Deciding how many parallel sessions a product tolerates, and what happens at the cap, is the consumer's risk analysis; the harness ships the reviewed-register surface where that decision would be recorded but does not make it.

requirements.text: Verify that all systems that create and manage user sessions as part of a federated identity management ecosystem (such as SSO systems) are documented along with controls to coordinate session lifetimes, termination, and any other conditions that require re-authentication.
requirements.negativeProof: tools/check-auth-posture.mjs (auth-posture chain step) closes supabase/config.toml's section census in both directions against the union of tools/auth-posture.json knownSections (harness-owned, sha-pinned) and tools/auth-tunables.json additionalSections (consumer-owned, write-guard-protected, seeded empty) — neither names any federation section ([auth.external.*], a third-party IdP section, or any other), so a federation block appearing in config reds the gate until one of the two registers records it in a reviewed diff (both files sit under the /tools/** CODEOWNERS rule; a consumer widening additionalSections is a reviewed human commit, not a harness release). The register keys under [auth*] are diffed the same way, so an unnamed key reds too.
requirements.note: The generated system contains no federated identity management ecosystem to document: the seeded supabase/config.toml enables email/password and TOTP MFA only, no OAuth provider, SAML or SSO section exists, and both seeded entries in additional_redirect_urls are the first-party web callback and mobile deep link. A consumer who enables SSO re-opens this row on their side of the boundary, and the register carries nothing they could inherit for it.

requirements.text: Verify that the application performs all session token verification using a trusted, backend service.
requirements.proof: apps/web/e2e/authenticated.spec.ts (quality-gate.yml job web-e2e) — the signed-out server render must refuse a protected route.
requirements.note: Control: no-unverified-session ESLint rule (tools/eslint-rules/index.mjs, enforced by the lint chain step) plus schema-rls (tools/check-rls-manifest.mjs) — server identity resolves only via getUser()/getClaims(), and every data access is authorized by RLS keyed on auth.uid() from the JWT the platform gateway verifies.. Session-token verification happens server-side on both rails: RLS predicates key on auth.uid(), which resolves from JWT claims verified before any row is readable, and application code resolves identity with getUser() (an auth-server round trip) or getClaims() (signature verification against the published key). getSession(), which returns the stored JWT unverified — attacker-controlled input on a server — is red under the no-unverified-session lint rule, and apps/web/proxy.ts is wired and documented as a cookie-refresh pass, never an authorization boundary (CVE-2025-29927). The residual is scope, not mechanism: the lint rule matches the .auth.getSession member shape, so a consumer building a novel token path that never touches the Supabase client is caught by the web-security-reviewer's mandatory pass on auth seams, not by a machine.

requirements.text: Verify that the application uses either self-contained or reference tokens that are dynamically generated for session management, i.e. not using static API secrets and keys.
requirements.proof: apps/web/e2e/authenticated.spec.ts (quality-gate.yml job web-e2e) — sign-in must mint a fresh sb-* session cookie the server accepts; sign-out must leave none.
requirements.note: Control: auth-posture (tools/check-auth-posture.mjs) — pins auth.enable_refresh_token_rotation true and refresh_token_reuse_interval 10 by value in both directions, and asserts the browser-session cookie transport (tools/lib/session-transport.mjs: the browser client writes the cookie jar every server reader reads, with the reviewed attributes at every writer); the write-guard rules expo-public-secret-name and next-public-secret-name (.claude/hooks/lib/guard-rules.mjs) plus the expo-policy gate's EXPO_PUBLIC_ source scan (tools/check-expo-policy.mjs) red a secret-shaped name in either client-inlined env channel, and secrets (tools/check-secrets.mjs) reds a credential VALUE (e.g. the supabase-secret-key pattern) anywhere in the tree.. The only session rail in the tree is GoTrue's: sign-in mints a fresh self-contained access JWT plus a rotating reference refresh token, and both surfaces (the cookie-backed web client and the LargeSecureStore-backed mobile client) carry that dynamically generated pair — no static API secret authenticates any user session. The publishable key riding every request authenticates the app to the gateway, not a user, and RLS admits no rows to it without a verified JWT; a secret-shaped name in an EXPO_PUBLIC_/NEXT_PUBLIC_ channel is refused by name shape (write-guard + expo-policy), and a checked-in secret-key value by the secrets gate. What is proven live is the web half only (the browser lane's cookie assertion); the mobile session pair is held in LargeSecureStore and asserted by unit tests, not a device run. Nothing structurally prevents a consumer from hand-rolling a static-key auth scheme in new code; that lands on the web-security-reviewer's mandatory paths rather than a gate.

requirements.text: Verify that if reference tokens are used to represent user sessions, they are unique and generated using a cryptographically secure pseudo-random number generator (CSPRNG) and possess at least 128 bits of entropy.
