requirements.note: The reference tokens representing sessions here are GoTrue's refresh tokens, minted upstream and outside this tree: no code in the template generates a session token, and no in-tree control can measure the uniqueness or entropy of the vendor's generator without a live probe the harness's hermeticity rule refuses. The register therefore declines to claim CSPRNG provenance or the 128-bit floor on the vendor's behalf — verifying it belongs to an assessment of the deployed platform, not this repository. The adjacent in-tree facts: where the template does mint a secret-bearing token (public.invitations), it stores only a sha256 digest and returns the plaintext exactly once, and the crypto-scope rules (no-insecure-random-in-crypto-scope, the math-random-key-material write-guard) red insecure randomness at the sites where in-tree key material is born.

requirements.text: Verify that the application generates a new session token on user authentication, including re-authentication, and terminates the current session token.
requirements.proof: tests/gates/check-auth-posture.test.mjs — the posture closure reds on a drifted or missing key in either direction.
requirements.note: Control: auth-posture (tools/check-auth-posture.mjs) — pins auth.enable_refresh_token_rotation true, refresh_token_reuse_interval 10 and enable_anonymous_sign_ins false, by value in both directions.. The half that holds: no session identifier predates authentication (an anonymous visitor holds no token at all, and anonymous sign-ins are pinned off), every sign-in mints a fresh token pair, and refresh-token rotation with reuse detection is pinned, so a replayed pre-rotation refresh token invalidates the family. The half that does not: re-authentication does not terminate the previous session token — GoTrue leaves a user's other sessions valid until expiry, no in-tree surface ends the prior session at sign-in, and the seeded [auth] block carries no session cap that would force it. The partial grade is the lower of the two defensible readings.

requirements.text: Verify that there is an inactivity timeout such that re-authentication is enforced according to risk analysis and documented security decisions.
requirements.note: No inactivity timeout exists: supabase/config.toml sets no [auth.sessions] inactivity_timeout, GoTrue's default never expires a session for inactivity, and no documented risk analysis in the tree says what the timeout should be — which this requirement makes the prerequisite. The platform offers the enforcement as a config key; choosing a value against the product's risk profile is the consumer's act. The auth-posture gate's closed section census reds an [auth.sessions] block until either register names it (the harness floor's knownSections or the consumer's write-guarded tools/auth-tunables.json additionalSections), so the choice will pass through a reviewed diff when it is made, but nothing in the tree makes it.

requirements.text: Verify that there is an absolute maximum session lifetime such that re-authentication is enforced according to risk analysis and documented security decisions.
requirements.note: No absolute session lifetime exists: no [auth.sessions] timebox is configured, so a session that keeps refreshing lives indefinitely — the seeded jwt_expiry of 3600 seconds bounds the ACCESS token between refreshes, not the session. The same boundary reasoning as 7.3.1 applies: the platform can enforce a timebox, the value is a product risk decision the consumer must document and set, and the harness currently neither seeds nor requires one.

requirements.text: Verify that when session termination is triggered (such as logout or expiration), the application disallows any further use of the session. For reference tokens or stateful sessions, this means invalidating the session data at the application backend. Applications using self-contained tokens will need a solution such as maintaining a list of terminated tokens, disallowing tokens produced before a per-user date and time or rotating a per-user signing key.
requirements.proof: apps/web/e2e/authenticated.spec.ts — after sign-out the sb-* cookie jar must be empty and a hard navigation to a protected route must land on /sign-in.
requirements.note: Control: web-e2e (quality-gate.yml job web-e2e, judged by tools/check-web-e2e.mjs) — the sign-out spec; auth-posture bounds auth.jwt_expiry to 300–86400 seconds, capping the post-termination validity window.. Termination is real at the backend for the reference half: both sign-out surfaces (apps/web/app/(protected)/sign-out-button.tsx, apps/mobile/app/actions.tsx) call auth.signOut() with no scope argument — supabase-js's documented default is 'global', which asks GoTrue to revoke the user's refresh tokens server-side, though no in-tree test asserts the scope or the server-side revocation itself — the browser-lane spec proves the cookie jar is emptied and the next server render refuses, and account deletion removes the GoTrue user outright. The residual is exactly the one this requirement names for self-contained tokens: an access JWT captured before termination still verifies against the published key until jwt_expiry (seeded 3600 seconds, floor-bounded to at most 86400) — the tree maintains no terminated-token list, no per-user not-before cutoff, and no signing-key rotation lever, so getClaims() and the data API accept a revoked session's JWT for up to that window. A bounded window is a mitigation, not the revocation the requirement describes, hence partial. The `web-e2e` job is (path-filtered), so this is proven periodically or per-touching-PR rather than on every commit.

requirements.text: Verify that the application terminates all active sessions when a user account is disabled or deleted (such as an employee leaving the company).
requirements.proof: apps/web/__tests__/delete-account.test.ts — server-side deletion must precede the local session drop, and a failed deletion must not sign the user out.
requirements.note: Control: expo-policy (tools/check-expo-policy.mjs, check 11g) — the account-deletion closure: when apps/mobile ships an auth surface and tools/store-tunables.json accountDeletion is the seeded { surface: 'action', actionId: 'session.deleteAccount', edgeFunction: 'delete-account' }, the gate reds unless that command is registered and supabase/functions/delete-account/index.ts exists and is declared in supabase/config.toml.. The deletion half ships: the delete-account Edge Function hard-deletes the caller's auth.users row via the admin API — removing the GoTrue session and refresh-token rows that reference it — and the expo-policy gate makes the surface's existence a hard requirement wherever the MOBILE app ships an auth surface (Apple 5.1.1(v)) — the closure is keyed on the consumer's write-guarded tools/store-tunables.json accountDeletion row, which carries reviewed escapes ('external' with an https url and reason, or 'none' with a reason), and it does not examine the web surface, whose DeleteAccountButton in the (protected) shell is asserted only by apps/web/__tests__/delete-account.test.ts (the unit Stop step). Three honest gaps keep this partial: disabling (banning) an account has no in-tree surface at all — it is a Dashboard or admin-API act on the operator's side; no in-tree test observes that sessions are actually gone after deletion (the cascade is the platform's schema, asserted nowhere here); and a deleted user's outstanding access JWT still verifies until expiry, the same self-contained-token residual recorded on 7.4.1.

requirements.text: Verify that the application gives the option to terminate all other active sessions after a successful change or removal of any authentication factor (including password change via reset or recovery and, if present, an MFA settings update).
requirements.note: No surface in the tree offers to terminate other sessions after a password change, password recovery, or MFA settings update: the seeded /security page (web factors-panel.tsx, mobile security.tsx) enrols and unenrols TOTP factors with no session sweep offered afterwards, no password-change or recovery flow ships at all (no resetPasswordForEmail or updateUser call exists on either surface), and no post-credential-change hook or UI exists. The one adjacent fact: both sign-out buttons call auth.signOut() with no scope argument, and supabase-js's documented default scope is 'global' (every session of the user is revoked server-side) — but that is a plain sign-out, not an option presented after a factor change, and no test asserts the scope. supabase-js exposes the primitive the requirement wants (signOut with the 'others' scope), so the harness could ship the option; as of this release the consumer must build it.

requirements.text: Verify that all pages that require authentication have easy and visible access to logout functionality.
requirements.proof: apps/web/e2e/authenticated.spec.ts — the sign-out control must exist and must end the session in the server render.
requirements.note: Control: web-e2e (quality-gate.yml job web-e2e) — apps/web/app/(protected)/layout.tsx renders SignOutButton in the one shared shell every authenticated page renders through, and the sign-out spec exercises it by testID.. On the web the argument is structural: every route under (protected) renders through one shell layout (apps/web/app/(protected)/layout.tsx) whose header carries the sign-out button, so a page cannot opt out of it, and the browser lane fails if the control disappears or stops working (testID sign-out). Mobile is why the grade is partial: sign-out ships as the session.signOut entry in the command palette (apps/mobile/src/features/actions/registry.ts) — reachable from anywhere, but discoverable rather than visible, and no check asserts a persistent on-screen logout affordance. Nothing machine-checks 'easy and visible' on either platform; the shared layout's structure is the argument, not a gate. The `web-e2e` job is (path-filtered), so this is proven periodically or per-touching-PR rather than on every commit.

requirements.text: Verify that application administrators are able to terminate active sessions for an individual user or for all users.
requirements.note: No administrator surface in the tree terminates another user's sessions, singly or globally: the template ships no admin console, the service-role rail is deliberately confined to the one delete-account Edge Function, and the JIT elevation machinery governs tenant-data administration, not auth-server administration. The capability exists on the operator's side of the boundary — the Supabase Dashboard and admin API can sign out a user's sessions — but an operator console the harness neither ships nor configures is not a control this register may claim. The harness could ship an ADR-governed admin function for this and does not, so the row is not-covered rather than not-applicable.

requirements.text: Verify that the application requires full re-authentication before allowing modifications to sensitive account attributes which may affect authentication such as email address, phone number, MFA configuration, or other information used in account recovery.
requirements.note: No flow in the tree requires full re-authentication before changing authentication-relevant attributes: the /security factors panel (web factors-panel.tsx, mobile security.tsx) enrols and unenrols TOTP factors on the standing session with no fresh-credential prompt, and the tree ships no email-change, phone-change, password-change or account-recovery flow at all (no updateUser or resetPasswordForEmail call on either surface), so there is no in-tree surface at which such a prompt could sit — a consumer who adds one adds this obligation with it. What is pinned is adjacent and narrower: auth.email.double_confirm_changes is held true by the auth-posture gate, so an email change made through GoTrue must be confirmed from the OLD address as well — a real anti-takeover control whose subject overlaps this requirement, but it is a confirmation loop, not re-authentication, it covers one attribute, and nothing in the tree exercises it. Where two grades were defensible the lower is recorded.

requirements.text: Verify that users are able to view and (having authenticated again with at least one factor) terminate any or all currently active sessions.
requirements.note: Users cannot view or terminate their sessions: the seeded /security page inventories MFA factors, not sessions, and no procedure in packages/api lists or revokes a user's other sessions. GoTrue holds the per-session state that would back such a surface, so the harness could ship one; as of this release the consumer must build both the session inventory and the re-authenticated termination action.

requirements.text: Verify that the application requires further authentication with at least one factor or secondary verification before performing highly sensitive transactions or operations.
requirements.proof: supabase/tests/mfa_aal2.test.sql — an enrolled user presenting an aal1 token must read ZERO rows, and the unenrolled user must be unaffected.
requirements.note: Control: schema-rls (tools/check-rls-manifest.mjs) — the RESTRICTIVE notes_mfa_aal2 policy (supabase/migrations/20260812000000_mfa_aal2.sql) and the aal2-gated JIT elevation rail (supabase/migrations/20260815000000_privilege_lifecycle_jit.sql, public.elevate()).. Two step-up mechanisms genuinely ship. The MFA rail: a user holding a verified factor must present an aal2 token — enforced at the database by a RESTRICTIVE policy, so an enrolled user's aal1 session reads and writes nothing on the governed table, proven by a pgTAP suite built specifically around the fail-open defect in the vendor's published policy. The privilege rail: administration is just-in-time — rank counts as privileged only inside an unexpired one-hour elevation minted by public.elevate(), and a lapsed owner's self-revalidation demands aal2 outright. The residuals that keep it partial: the aal2 policy governs the notes worked pattern and each consumer feature must attach the same policy to its own tables; a user who never enrolled a factor is never stepped up (mandatory enrolment is an application decision GoTrue's configuration cannot express, as tools/auth-posture.json records); and elevation is an explicit act on an already-authenticated session rather than a fresh factor presentation, except on the lapsed-owner path where aal2 is demanded.

requirements.text: Verify that session lifetime and termination between Relying Parties (RPs) and Identity Providers (IdPs) behave as documented, requiring re-authentication as necessary such as when the maximum time between IdP authentication events is reached.
requirements.negativeProof: tools/check-auth-posture.mjs (auth-posture chain step) closes supabase/config.toml's section census in both directions against the union of tools/auth-posture.json knownSections (harness-owned, sha-pinned) and tools/auth-tunables.json additionalSections (consumer-owned, write-guard-protected, seeded empty) — neither names any federation section ([auth.external.*], a third-party IdP section, or any other), so a federation block appearing in config reds the gate until one of the two registers records it in a reviewed diff (both files sit under the /tools/** CODEOWNERS rule; a consumer widening additionalSections is a reviewed human commit, not a harness release). The register keys under [auth*] are diffed the same way, so an unnamed key reds too.
requirements.note: There is no Relying Party or Identity Provider code in the tree: sessions are first-party GoTrue sessions, no OAuth/SAML/OIDC federation section exists in supabase/config.toml, and no assertion-consuming code ships on either surface, so the requirement's subject — coordinated session lifetime between RP and IdP — has no surface to attach to. A consumer enabling SSO takes this row on with the integration.

requirements.text: Verify that creation of a session requires either the user's consent or an explicit action, preventing the creation of new application sessions without user interaction.
requirements.negativeProof: The same closed section census as 7.6.1 (tools/check-auth-posture.mjs against the union of tools/auth-posture.json knownSections and tools/auth-tunables.json additionalSections) keeps an unreviewed federation section out of the config surface, and the same gate pins auth.enable_anonymous_sign_ins false by value — the one first-party path that could mint a session without a credential ceremony reds if flipped (tests/gates/check-auth-posture.test.mjs carries the 'anonymous sign-ins turned on' red case).
requirements.note: This section addresses RP/IdP code, and none exists in the tree, so the federated form of the requirement (IdP-to-RP session creation without interaction) has no code to grade. The adjacent first-party fact is worth recording: the only session-minting paths shipped are the explicit sign-in and MFA-challenge ceremonies driven by user-submitted credentials, and anonymous sign-ins are pinned off by the auth-posture gate, so no application session comes into being without an explicit user action even outside the federation framing.

requirements.text: Verify that authorization documentation defines rules for restricting function-level and data-specific access based on consumer permissions and resource attributes.
requirements.proof: tools/check-tenancy.mjs (the `tenancy` validate-chain step; its factory red-proof is tests/gates/check-tenancy.test.mjs)
requirements.note: The authorization model is documented in reviewed surfaces the agent cannot silently edit: AGENTS.md names the function-level tier ladder (publicProcedure -> authedProcedure -> orgProcedure in packages/api/src/trpc.ts) and .claude/rules/security-invariants.md defines the data-specific rules — per-table, per-operation RLS keyed on (select auth.uid()), TO authenticated, exemptions only in tools/rls-exempt.json with a written reason; tools/tenancy.json is authorization documentation as reviewed data — the closed set of tenant predicate forms that the tenancy validate step (tools/check-tenancy.mjs) enforces against every shipped policy, so the data-specific half cannot drift from what it documents; both JSON files sit under tools/**, inside the write-guard table (.claude/hooks/lib/guard-rules.mjs, rule id rls-exempt for the exemption list). The residual is why this is partial and documentation-tier: the function-level rules are prose no gate closes against the code (nothing proves every procedure is mounted on the tier the prose implies), and the seeded documentation defines the template's own rules only — a consumer's new resources arrive with permission rules these documents cannot pre-define, so the consumer inherits the obligation to extend them.

requirements.text: Verify that authorization documentation defines rules for field-level access restrictions (both read and write) based on consumer permissions and resource attributes. Note that these rules might depend on other attribute values of the relevant data object, such as state or status.
requirements.note: No field-level access model ships and no documentation defines rules for one: the worked verticals grant or refuse whole rows (owner- or org-scoped RLS), and the zod DTO contracts bound the wire shape identically for every authorized consumer rather than differentiating fields by permission. The harness could seed a documented field-level pattern (column grants, or view-based projections per role) and does not, which is why this is graded not-covered rather than not-applicable; the rules themselves would in any case be the consumer's to write, because field sensitivity is a fact about their domain model, not about this scaffold.

requirements.text: Verify that the application's documentation defines the environmental and contextual attributes (including but not limited to, time of day, user location, IP address, or device) that are used in the application to make security decisions, including those pertaining to authentication and authorization.
requirements.proof: tools/tenancy.json predicateForms + docs/adr/20260204-rate-limiting.md (the one environmental attribute a decision consults, with its trust bound); tests/gates/check-tenancy.test.mjs proves the form closure reds on an unlisted predicate shape
requirements.note: Control: tools/tenancy.json’s closed predicateForms set — the tenancy step is what keeps any contextual attribute OUT of a database authorization predicate without a reviewed form addition, so the set of attributes authorization consults is a closed, reviewed one. Regraded from not-applicable: the shipped tree DOES make one security decision on an environmental attribute. The rate-limit seam keys anonymous callers on the client IP taken from x-forwarded-for — clientKeyFromHeaders() in apps/web/lib/rate-limit-runtime.ts, consumed by the tRPC host (apps/web/app/api/trpc/[trpc]/route.ts) and by enforceActionRateLimit() ahead of identity resolution in the org Server Actions (apps/web/app/actions/orgs.ts), with rateLimitKey() in packages/platform/ratelimit falling back to c:<ip> only when no verified userId exists. That attribute IS documented: docs/adr/20260204-rate-limiting.md defines it, its trust bound (trustworthy exactly to the extent the platform overwrites the header; attacker-controlled behind self-terminated TLS, degrading anonymous limiting to nothing and weakening nothing else), and the fact that GoTrue sign-in/sign-up are outside it. No other environmental or contextual attribute (time of day, location, device) is consulted anywhere; authentication is a verified GoTrue JWT and authorization keys on auth.uid() plus live membership state, and tools/tenancy.json's closed predicate-form set (tenancy step) plus the schema-rls initPlan rule keep any such attribute out of a database authorization predicate without a reviewed form addition. Partial rather than covered because the documentation is an ADR about rate limiting, not an authorization document enumerating contextual attributes, and no gate closes 'every contextual attribute a decision consults is documented' — a consumer adding a second one inherits the obligation unassisted.

requirements.text: Verify that authentication and authorization documentation defines how environmental and contextual factors are used in decision-making, in addition to function-level, data-specific, and field-level authorization. This should include the attributes evaluated, thresholds for risk, and actions taken (e.g., allow, challenge, deny, step-up authentication).
requirements.note: Regraded from not-applicable, for consistency with 8.1.3 and 8.2.4: the tree is not free of contextual security decisions (anonymous rate limiting keys on the client IP, see 8.1.3, with thresholds in tools/rate-limit-budget.json and a deny action — TOO_MANY_REQUESTS on tRPC, an AppError on the Server Action channel), so 'nothing to document' is not true; but no authentication or authorization documentation defines how environmental or contextual factors feed decision-making — there is no attribute list, no risk threshold, and no allow/challenge/deny/step-up matrix, because there is no risk engine for such a table to describe. The one step-up that ships is operation-triggered rather than contextual: public.elevate() refuses a lapsed owner at aal1 and demands the enrolled second factor (supabase/tests/mfa_aal2.test.sql proves both the refusal and the aal2 success branch), documented in the migration text and its ADR. The database layer is closed against context joining an authorization predicate unreviewed (tools/tenancy.json forms via the tenancy step); the application layer is not machine-closed. A consumer adding risk-based decisions acquires this documentation obligation in full.

requirements.text: Verify that the application ensures that function-level access is restricted to consumers with explicit permissions.
requirements.proof: packages/api/src/envelope.test.ts — 'the auth rung THROWS': authed procedures reject an anonymous caller with UNAUTHORIZED before the input parser runs; rides the unit Stop-chain step
requirements.note: Function-level restriction ships as the procedure-tier ladder in packages/api/src/trpc.ts — authedProcedure throws UNAUTHORIZED for any caller context.ts could not verify with getUser(), and orgProcedure narrows further to the caller's resolved org seat (returning forbidden on the envelope, never touching the database — the same test file proves this) — proven by the can-fail test named as the canary. Partial for a structural reason: tier assignment is authored per procedure and no gate closes 'every procedure carries the right tier', so a consumer can mount a new procedure on publicProcedure by mistake; the backstop is one layer down, where an anonymous client's statements match no rows because every client-facing policy in supabase/schemas/*.sql is TO authenticated (the internal app_* roles carry their own narrow policies), which is data-level rather than function-level enforcement. Two guards on change are disclosed rather than claimed as coverage: any non-test diff under packages/api/src/** owes a security-reviewer PASS (tools/reviewer-triggers.json, judged by the reviewer-verdicts Stop step), and RLS (8.2.2's row) makes a mis-tiered function leak nothing across identities.

requirements.text: Verify that the application ensures that data-specific access is restricted to consumers with explicit permissions to specific data items to mitigate insecure direct object reference (IDOR) and broken object level authorization (BOLA).
requirements.proof: tests/rls/cross-tenant-isolation.test.ts (supabase-js client) and supabase/tests/rls_isolation.test.sql (pgTAP), both run by the rls-isolation Stop step (tests/rls/run-rls.mjs) against a live stack
requirements.note: Object-level authorization is enforced in the database, which both surfaces share: the schema-rls validate step (tools/check-rls-manifest.mjs) closes every table declared in supabase/schemas/*.sql into ENABLE + FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY, per-operation policies with real predicates resolving identity through (select auth.uid()), the policy-to-grant closure, an owner-leading index, and BOTH isolation registries (tests/rls/db-context.ts ISOLATION_TARGETS for the client suite, and the pgTAP rls_targets table declared in supabase/tests/rls_structure.test.sql), so a new table cannot ship outside the isolation proof — naming another object's id in a request or an RPC argument returns or affects nothing the caller does not own, which is the IDOR/BOLA mitigation the row asks for, proven by can-fail tests on every reset. Residuals stated: tools/rls-exempt.json exemptions are a human-reviewed escape hatch; service_role bypasses RLS inside ADR-governed Edge Functions (REVOKE ALL by default, per-table ADR'd grants); and the gate proves predicate realness and form, never that a policy's business meaning is the right one for a consumer's new domain.

requirements.text: Verify that the application ensures that field-level access is restricted to consumers with explicit permissions to specific fields to mitigate broken object property level authorization (BOPLA).
requirements.note: No field-level authorization mechanism ships: RLS is row-scoped, no column-level GRANT or view-per-role pattern is seeded, and the zod DTO projection in packages/contracts bounds the wire shape uniformly for every authorized caller — shape-bounding is not permission-differentiated field access, and grading it as such would be inflation. The nearest real behaviour is attribute-dependent disclosure at the schema level rather than per-permission: public.invitations stores and exposes token_digest, never a redeemable token, to the admins who may read the table. A consumer whose domain needs per-field read/write differentiation must build it; nothing in the tree prevents it, and nothing provides it.

requirements.text: Verify that adaptive security controls based on a consumer's environmental and contextual attributes (such as time of day, location, IP address, or device) are implemented for authentication and authorization decisions, as defined in the application's documentation. These controls must be applied when the consumer tries to start a new session and also during an existing session.
requirements.note: No adaptive security control based on environmental or contextual attributes exists for authentication or authorization: GoTrue's configuration surface (pinned key-by-key in tools/auth-posture.json) offers no risk engine, and no shipped code consults time, location, or device in an authentication or authorization decision, at session start or during a session. Disclosed for honesty rather than credit: the client IP IS consulted, but only as the fallback key for anonymous rate limiting (apps/web/lib/rate-limit-runtime.ts, see 8.1.3) — a throttle, not an adaptive authentication or authorization decision. The shipped step-up is operation-triggered, not contextual — public.elevate() demands aal2 from an enrolled lapsed owner — and the aal2 restrictive policy (notes_mfa_aal2, supabase/schemas/20_notes.sql) refuses aal1 sessions of an enrolled user on public.notes only, not database-wide. The requirement's own scoping is 'as defined in the application's documentation', and no documentation defines adaptive controls (8.1.3 documents one throttle attribute; 8.1.4 is not-covered); a consumer who documents adaptive controls must then implement them, on surfaces this template does not provide.

requirements.text: Verify that the application enforces authorization rules at a trusted service layer and doesn't rely on controls that an untrusted consumer could manipulate, such as client-side JavaScript.
requirements.proof: tests/rls/cross-tenant-isolation.test.ts and supabase/tests/rls_isolation.test.sql via the rls-isolation Stop step — isolation holds against a live stack whatever the client does
requirements.note: Authorization is enforced in Postgres RLS — a trusted service layer both surfaces reach through the same policies — and the untrusted-client rule is doctrine with machine teeth rather than a convention: apps/web/proxy.ts is documented as NOT an authorization boundary (CVE-2025-29927) and only rotates the session cookie; server-side identity is getUser()/getClaims(), never the signature-unverified getSession(); the mobile app is treated as an untrusted bearer of a scoped token, with the session in LargeSecureStore and no authorization decided on-device. A forged or expired JWT matches no rows regardless of any client-side state, which the live isolation twins prove on every reset. Disclosed reuse: schema-rls also grounds 8.2.2 and 8.3.3 in this register — one enforcement surface honestly answering three different questions (where enforcement lives, object-level closure, whose permissions decide) — and tools/rls-exempt.json remains the human-reviewed escape whose entries are outside this row's claim.

requirements.text: Verify that changes to values on which authorization decisions are made are applied immediately. Where changes cannot be applied immediately, (such as when relying on data in self-contained tokens), there must be mitigating controls to alert when a consumer performs an action when they are no longer authorized to do so and revert the change. Note that this alternative would not mitigate information leakage.
requirements.proof: supabase/tests/rls_isolation.test.sql (rank 30 is effective only while an unexpired elevation exists — the JIT-door assertions) and supabase/tests/mfa_aal2.test.sql (a lapsed owner's elevation is refused at aal1)
requirements.note: The database half is immediate by construction: every admin and tenant predicate routes through the closed helper forms in tools/tenancy.json (the tenancy step refuses any other shape), and since supabase/migrations/20260815000000_privilege_lifecycle_jit.sql those INVOKER helpers read public.memberships and public.admin_elevations live, hoisted to one InitPlan per statement — a revoked seat, a demotion, a lapsed 12-month revalidation, or an expired one-hour elevation stops satisfying every rank-floor predicate on the caller's next statement, with no token refresh in the path. The residual is the self-contained GoTrue JWT, exactly the caveat the requirement names: sub and aal live in the token, so a deleted or banned user's unexpired access token still resolves auth.uid() on the direct RLS path until expiry, and no alert-and-revert mitigating control ships for that window — the bounded access-token lifetime narrows it but is not the mitigation the text requires, which is why this row is partial rather than covered.

requirements.text: Verify that access to an object is based on the originating subject's (e.g. consumer's) permissions, not on the permissions of any intermediary or service acting on their behalf. For example, if a consumer calls a web service using a self-contained token for authentication, and the service then requests data from a different service, the second service will use the consumer's token, rather than a machine-to-machine token from the first service, to make permission decisions.
requirements.proof: supabase/tests/rls_isolation.test.sql — the RPCs derive the caller from auth.uid(), never from a parameter, and the caller's own claims decide every read and write; supabase/tests/audit_immutability.test.sql proves even service_role is refused on the trail by attempt, not by grant lookup
requirements.note: The default path is what the requirement asks for: the tRPC layer (packages/api/src/context.ts) verifies the caller's own bearer token or cookie session with getUser() and builds a request-scoped client that carries that token onward, so Postgres evaluates every policy against the originating subject's auth.uid() — the API tier holds no ambient privilege to substitute, because the publishable key authenticates the request to the gateway, not the caller, and RLS admits nothing on it alone. The machine identity the requirement warns about exists and is governed rather than absent: service_role bypasses RLS, is sanctioned only inside ADR-governed Edge Functions via createServiceRoleClient_BYPASSES_RLS(warrant), and migrations REVOKE ALL from it so a function reaches a table only through a per-table ADR'd grant (supabase/migrations/20260201000200_service_role_org_sweep.sql is the specimen). That governed exception is why the row is partial rather than covered: a consumer can author a new warranted function whose permission decisions are the machine's rather than the caller's, and this register can verify the discipline around each warrant, not the judgement inside it.

requirements.text: Verify that multi-tenant applications use cross-tenant controls to ensure consumer operations will never affect tenants with which they do not have permissions to interact.
requirements.proof: tests/rls/cross-tenant-isolation.test.ts and supabase/tests/rls_isolation.test.sql — org B holds exactly its own rows after cross-org UPDATE and DELETE attempts, in both directions — via the rls-isolation Stop step
requirements.note: Cross-tenant control is the tenancy gate's whole subject: every org-scoped policy predicate must match the closed reviewed form set in tools/tenancy.json arm-by-arm (a predicate arm outside the forms reds printing the exact normalized predicate it saw), the correlated-argument ban keeps membership lookups uncorrelated and per-statement, and the live twins prove on every reset that org B neither reads nor affects org A — including through RPC arguments, since the RPCs derive the caller from auth.uid() and evaluate rank floors against the caller's real seats, so naming another org is not a way in. Residuals stated: the gate closes predicate form and the tenant key against schema drift, never the business question of which rows belong to which tenant in a consumer's new domain; tools/rls-exempt.json remains the reviewed escape; and 'never affect' is proven for the data plane the tests exercise, not for side channels such as timing or shared quotas.

requirements.text: Verify that access to administrative interfaces incorporates multiple layers of security, including continuous consumer identity verification, device security posture assessment, and contextual risk analysis, ensuring that network location or trusted endpoints are not the sole factors for authorization even though they may reduce the likelihood of unauthorized access.
requirements.proof: supabase/tests/rls_isolation.test.sql (a rank-30 admin must elevate before administering — the JIT door) and supabase/tests/mfa_aal2.test.sql (a lapsed enrolled owner at aal1 cannot self-revalidate; the same owner at aal2 can)
requirements.note: The template ships no separate admin panel; administration is in-app (the org surfaces under apps/web/app/(protected)/o and (protected)/invite) and its layers are real and stacked: a verified JWT resolved per request, a rank floor read live from memberships per statement, a one-hour just-in-time elevation minted by public.elevate() (supabase/migrations/20260815000000_privilege_lifecycle_jit.sql), a 12-month revalidation / 45-day inactivity lapse that reads a stale admin as rank 20 everywhere, and an aal2 step-up guarding the lapsed-owner self-revalidation branch. The aal2 restrictive policy itself is scoped to public.notes (notes_mfa_aal2) — the seat and elevation tables are not aal2-guarded outside that one branch, so 'MFA on every admin write' is not a claim this row makes. Network location and trusted endpoints are no factor at all, so the 'not the sole factors' clause has nothing to bite on here. What the requirement lists and the tree does not have keeps this partial: no device security posture assessment and no contextual risk analysis exist on any surface, and continuous verification here means per-request and per-statement token verification, not an ongoing session-risk re-evaluation. The consoles where the most privileged administration actually happens (Supabase Dashboard, Vercel, GitHub) are the organisation's surfaces, outside this tree's reach.

requirements.text: Verify that self-contained tokens are validated using their digital signature or MAC to protect against tampering before accepting the token's contents.
requirements.note: Control: validate-chain step 'lint' — the custom ESLint rule no-unverified-session (tools/eslint-rules/index.mjs), backed by the PreToolUse write-guard getSession deny in .claude/hooks/pretool-write-guard.mjs and the security-reviewer agent. The signature verification itself is vendor code, not this tree's: @supabase/supabase-js getUser() authenticates the token against the auth server, getClaims() verifies it locally against the project's published asymmetric key, and at the RLS boundary PostgREST verifies the JWT before request.jwt.claims is populated (a forged token matches no rows). What the harness itself enforces is one layer out — that no server-graph code can accept token contents WITHOUT one of those verifying calls: the no-unverified-session ESLint rule (scoped by eslint.config.mjs to apps/web/**, packages/**, supabase/functions/** with *.test.* excluded; apps/mobile is out of scope by construction as an untrusted bearer of its own token) reds any `.auth.getSession` member call in a file not marked 'use client' — the one SDK call that decodes without verifying; the write-guard denies the same pattern at edit time across apps/web|packages|supabase; the verify.ts port structurally omits getSession; and the security-reviewer agent (MUST-BE-USED on server-side auth verification, held by the reviewer-verdicts Stop step) flags it on review. The canary exercises the helper's failed-verification branch (an error alongside attacker-supplied data yields null identity, never a partial one) and asserts the port describes getUser and nothing else. Residual: no in-tree test presents a token with a tampered signature and watches it be refused — the pgTAP RLS suites (supabase/tests/*.sql) inject request.jwt.claims directly, which is post-verification state, so they prove policy behaviour rather than signature checking; and the bearer factory (packages/platform/supabase/src/access-token.ts) forwards the token to PostgREST without decoding it, which is correct but is again vendor-side verification. Graded partial for that reason.

requirements.text: Verify that only algorithms on an allowlist can be used to create and verify self-contained tokens, for a given context. The allowlist must include the permitted algorithms, ideally only either symmetric or asymmetric algorithms, and must not include the 'None' algorithm. If both symmetric and asymmetric must be supported, additional controls will be needed to prevent key confusion.
requirements.negativeProof: validate-chain step 'lint' (no-unverified-session, tools/eslint-rules/index.mjs) reds the only SDK call that decodes a token without verifying it in the server graph; validate-chain step 'provenance' (tools/check-sources.mjs, decision group token-verification in tools/lib/provenance-rules.mjs) reds an uncited jwtVerify / createRemoteJWKSet / createLocalJWKSet / clockTolerance decision site under apps/** or packages/** *.ts(x), so a hand-rolled in-tree verifier cannot land silently; validate-chain step 'auth-posture' (tools/check-auth-posture.mjs) closes supabase/config.toml [auth*] keys and sections in both directions, so an unreviewed signing-related config surface appearing there reds the chain.
requirements.note: Algorithm selection exists only inside GoTrue (the issuer) and @supabase/supabase-js and PostgREST (the verifiers) — vendor code operated by the platform. No file in this tree creates or verifies a token signature, imports a JWT library (no jose, no jsonwebtoken — verified by grep across template/stack and template/modules), or reads an alg header, so there is no in-tree allowlist to hold and no path on which a 'None'-algorithm or key-confusion token could be honoured by code this repository ships. (The bash-guard rule dev-auth-access protects a gitignored local signing-material directory, but nothing in the shipped tree mints tokens into it.) The surface is absent, which is why this is graded not-applicable rather than covered — absence is not coverage. Residual: a consumer who adds their own JWT dependency and hand-rolls verification re-opens this surface. Nothing mechanical refuses the new dependency itself — the licenses chain step and the sbom-inventory CI job record it — but a jwtVerify/JWKS call site under apps/** or packages/** reds the provenance step until it carries a SOURCE citation, and the security-reviewer agent is the reviewing control; the algorithm allowlist that new verifier would need is still nobody's in-tree gate.

requirements.text: Verify that key material that is used to validate self-contained tokens is from trusted pre-configured sources for the token issuer, preventing attackers from specifying untrusted sources and keys. For JWTs and other JWS structures, headers such as 'jku', 'x5u', and 'jwk' must be validated against an allowlist of trusted sources.
requirements.negativeProof: validate-chain step 'lint' (no-unverified-session, tools/eslint-rules/index.mjs) — the only in-tree token reads are the verifying SDK calls, whose key source is the pre-configured project URL, and the unverified-decode call is denied in the server graph; validate-chain step 'provenance' (tools/check-sources.mjs, decision group token-verification) reds an uncited createRemoteJWKSet / createLocalJWKSet / jwtVerify site under apps/** or packages/**, which is exactly the key-source decision this requirement is about.
requirements.note: Key material is pre-configured, never token-specified: getClaims() verifies against the project's published keys at the Supabase URL pinned in environment configuration (packages/platform/supabase/src/credentials.ts validates it on the way into every public factory; public-env.ts reads NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL), getUser() round-trips to that same pre-configured auth server, and PostgREST verifies against the project's configured keys. No code in this tree parses a JWS header or fetches key material from a jku/x5u/jwk-supplied location — that defect class requires an in-tree JWT verifier, which does not exist (see 9.1.2). Whether the vendored SDK itself honours such headers is vendor behaviour this tree trusts but does not test. Graded not-applicable because the header-driven key-resolution surface is absent from the tree, not because the requirement is met by in-tree code; a consumer adding a custom verifier re-opens it — the provenance step makes an uncited JWKS resolver red until cited, but the trusted-source allowlist itself would be review-only.

requirements.text: Verify that, if a validity time span is present in the token data, the token and its content are accepted only if the verification time is within this validity time span. For example, for JWTs, the claims 'nbf' and 'exp' must be verified.
requirements.proof: tools/check-auth-posture.mjs (the `auth-posture` validate-chain step; its factory red-proof is tests/gates/check-auth-posture.test.mjs)
requirements.note: Control: validate-chain step 'auth-posture' (tools/check-auth-posture.mjs). Expiry enforcement at acceptance time is vendor behaviour: GoTrue refuses an expired token on getUser(), getClaims() validates the claims of the token it verifies, and PostgREST rejects an expired JWT before auth.uid() ever resolves — a forged-or-expired token matches no rows. None of that is re-proven by an in-tree test that presents an expired token. What the harness itself holds, and what the named control enforces, is the validity span's existence and bounds: auth.jwt_expiry is a declared tunable bounded between 300 and 86400 seconds (never disabled into a week-long token), and refresh-token rotation with a ten-second reuse interval is pinned floor posture — all diffed by value, in both directions, against the real supabase/config.toml on every chain run. Graded partial: the span is bounded and reviewed in-tree; the verification of it at runtime is delegated to the platform.

requirements.text: Verify that the service receiving a token validates the token to be the correct type and is meant for the intended purpose before accepting the token's contents. For example, only access tokens can be accepted for authorization decisions and only ID Tokens can be used for proving user authentication.
requirements.negativeProof: validate-chain step 'auth-posture' (tools/check-auth-posture.mjs) — the knownSections census over supabase/config.toml is closed in both directions and names no [auth.external.*] section, so an external OIDC provider (a second token kind entering the project) appearing in config reds the chain until reviewed into the register.
requirements.note: Exactly one class of self-contained token crosses a trust boundary in this scaffold: the GoTrue access token, consumed only through verifying SDK calls and PostgREST. The tree configures no external OIDC provider (no [auth.external.*] section in supabase/config.toml, and no signInWithIdToken/signInWithOAuth call site in stack or modules), so no provider ID token reaches application code; GoTrue refresh tokens are opaque identifiers, not self-contained; the Edge Function specimen (supabase/functions/delete-account) sets verify_jwt = true, which rejects a bearer that is not a JWT signed by the project, and then resolves the caller by getUser() on that same Authorization header — so a signed-but-not-a-user token (the legacy anon-role JWT would pass verify_jwt) still yields no identity. With a single token type serving a single purpose there is no cross-type confusion surface for in-tree code to police, which is why this is graded not-applicable rather than covered. Residual: no mechanical control enforces the single-token-type property itself beyond the config-section census — a consumer who introduces a second self-contained token type in code (service-to-service JWTs, custom ID-token handling) re-opens this surface with no type check waiting, and only the security-reviewer agent stands between that diff and the tree.

requirements.text: Verify that the service only accepts tokens which are intended for use with that service (audience). For JWTs, this can be achieved by validating the 'aud' claim against an allowlist defined in the service.
requirements.note: No code in this tree validates an aud claim against a service-defined allowlist: the session-refresh proxy calls getClaims() and deliberately discards the result, and the tRPC context derives identity via getUser() without inspecting aud. What stands in for audience restriction is key isolation — each Supabase project signs with its own keys, so a token minted by any other issuer or project fails signature verification before any claim is read — but that is an architectural property of the platform, not an in-tree control, and it cannot distinguish audiences WITHIN one project (web, mobile, and Edge Functions are deliberately one audience here). The harness could ship an explicit aud allowlist check at the packages/platform/supabase verify.ts seam, where every verified identity already flows; graded not-covered because it has not, and per doctrine the lower of two defensible grades is taken.

requirements.text: Verify that, if a token issuer uses the same private key for issuing tokens to different audiences, the issued tokens contain an audience restriction that uniquely identifies the intended audiences. This will prevent a token from being reused with an unintended audience. If the audience identifier is dynamically provisioned, the token issuer must validate these audiences in order to make sure that they do not result in audience impersonation.
requirements.negativeProof: validate-chain step 'auth-posture' (tools/check-auth-posture.mjs) — the [auth*] key and section census over supabase/config.toml is closed in both directions, so an unreviewed issuer- or signing-related configuration surface appearing there reds the chain.
requirements.note: The subject is the token issuer's key-management practice — whether one private key signs tokens for several distinct audiences, and whether dynamically provisioned audience identifiers are validated. This scaffold ships no issuer: GoTrue is operated by the Supabase platform, per project, with per-project signing keys, and every consumer of those tokens in this tree (web, mobile, the Edge Function specimen) is deliberately a single audience, so the shared-key-across-audiences condition does not arise from anything the tree contains. The harness cannot ship the issuer's audience-restriction behaviour, which is why this organisation-boundary row is graded not-applicable rather than not-covered. Residual: an operator who later points several distinct services at one project's signing keys recreates the condition this requirement guards, entirely outside the tree's sight — the closed auth-posture census sees config drift in supabase/config.toml, not the operator's wider topology.

requirements.text: Verify that tokens are only sent to components that strictly need them. For example, when using a backend-for-frontend pattern for browser-based JavaScript applications, access and refresh tokens shall only be accessible for the backend.
requirements.note: The scaffold is deliberately NOT a backend-for-frontend: sign-in happens browser-side and the browser client holds the session, a trade recorded in tools/auth-posture.json sessionTransport, which also records httpOnly as UNAVAILABLE for exactly that reason. What the auth-posture validate step does enforce is where the session lands and with which attributes: the storage-wiring closure over apps/web/app, apps/web/lib and packages/platform/supabase/src (tools/lib/session-transport.mjs — the seam whose unwired state shipped a sign-in loop for two releases) and the `secure` cookie attribute at every writer (tests/gates/session-transport.test.mjs holds the shipped-bug canaries). On mobile the session is confined to LargeSecureStore (expo-secure-store importable only under apps/mobile/src/host/**, held by the eslint no-restricted-imports groups on the lint step and the dependency-cruiser wall on the architecture step). Secret-shaped NEXT_PUBLIC_/EXPO_PUBLIC_ names are refused by the expo-public-secret-name and next-public-secret-name write-guard rules (template/base/.claude/hooks/lib/guard-rules.mjs) and by the expo-policy step's EXPO_PUBLIC_ source scan — NOT by the `secrets` step, which is a value-pattern scanner (tools/secret-patterns.json) that does not judge name shapes. Tokens therefore reach the user agent, the platform auth server, and the API host, and nothing else in the tree — but the requirement's confinement example (tokens accessible to the backend only) is the architecture this scaffold chose against, so the row cannot claim covered.

requirements.text: Verify that the client only accepts values from the authorization server (such as the authorization code or ID Token) if these values result from an authorization flow that was initiated by the same user agent session and transaction. This requires that client-generated secrets, such as the proof key for code exchange (PKCE) 'code_verifier', 'state' or OIDC 'nonce', are not guessable, are specific to the transaction, and are securely bound to both the client and the user agent session in which the transaction was started.
requirements.note: The transaction-binding machinery (PKCE code_verifier generation, storage, and exchange) is @supabase/supabase-js's implementation, not code in this tree. The harness seeds flowType 'pkce' in all three client factories (packages/platform/supabase/src/browser.ts citing RFC 9700, native.ts citing RFC 8252, cookie-server.ts with no citation on the line), but no gate holds that choice — a flip to 'implicit' reds nothing today, though editing those files does owe a security-reviewer verdict via tools/reviewer-triggers.json and the reviewer-verdicts Stop step, which is review-on-change, not enforcement of the value. The seeded sign-in path is a direct password grant on both surfaces (signInWithPassword in apps/web/app/sign-in/sign-in-form.tsx and apps/mobile/app/sign-in.tsx) that never traverses an authorization-code flow; no /auth/callback route exists under apps/web/app even though the redirect allowlist names one, so the only in-tree code that would consume a returned code is the browser client's detectSessionInUrl: true. The code-exchange path becomes live for email-link ceremonies (enable_confirmations is false in the seeded config.toml) and for any consumer-enabled external provider — the latter reds the auth-posture gate's [auth*] key census if enabled in the tree's config.toml, but a Dashboard-side enablement is invisible to it. Graded not-covered rather than partial because a seeded default with no enforcement point is not a control this register may name.

requirements.text: Verify that, if the code flow is used, the OAuth client has protection against browser-based request forgery attacks, commonly known as cross-site request forgery (CSRF), which trigger token requests, either by using proof key for code exchange (PKCE) functionality or checking the 'state' parameter that was sent in the authorization request.
requirements.note: No OAuth code flow is initiated anywhere in the seeded tree: sign-in is signInWithPassword on both surfaces and no signInWithOAuth / signInWithIdToken / exchangeCodeForSession call exists, so the CSRF defense this row asks about has no seeded flow to protect. When the code-exchange path does run (email-link ceremonies once confirmations are on, or a consumer-enabled provider), PKCE is the vendor SDK's mechanics under the seeded flowType 'pkce' default, which nothing in the tree enforces (see 10.1.2). Not graded not-applicable because the client machinery is present and one consumer decision away from live; not graded partial because the harness holds no enforcement point whose subject is this requirement. The CSRF guard that does ship gate-adjacent (packages/api/src/csrf.ts on the ambient-credential tRPC path) protects API mutations, not authorization-code token requests, and is deliberately not claimed here.

requirements.text: Verify that, if the OAuth client can interact with more than one authorization server, it has a defense against mix-up attacks. For example, it could require that the authorization server return the 'iss' parameter value and validate it in the authorization response and the token response.
requirements.negativeProof: validate-chain step auth-posture (tools/check-auth-posture.mjs, backward direction): every key under [auth*] in supabase/config.toml must be named by tools/auth-posture.json or tools/auth-tunables.json, and a consumer cannot mint a tunable — so an [auth.external.<provider>] block, an OAuth-server section, or any other auth key added to the tree's config reds the chain until a harness-reviewed release names it (tests/gates/check-auth-posture.test.mjs holds the unreviewed-key red). Limit: the census reads the tree's supabase/config.toml only; a provider or OAuth server enabled in a hosted project's Dashboard, or a consumer's own SDK call against one, is outside it.
requirements.note: The seeded client speaks to exactly one authorization server — the project's own Supabase Auth instance, whose URL is the env-validated NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL / EXPO_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL — so the multi-AS mix-up surface does not exist in the generated system (no [auth.external.*] block in supabase/config.toml, no OAuth/OIDC sign-in call site). The absence is machine-held on the tree side only: adding an external provider block to config.toml reds the auth-posture gate's [auth*] key census, while a provider enabled in a hosted Dashboard, or a consumer wiring a second authorization server in their own code, creates the surface with nothing here watching — which is why the boundary is consumer rather than harness.

requirements.text: Verify that the OAuth client only requests the required scopes (or other authorization parameters) in requests to the authorization server.
requirements.negativeProof: validate-chain step auth-posture (tools/check-auth-posture.mjs, backward direction): every key under [auth*] in supabase/config.toml must be named by tools/auth-posture.json or tools/auth-tunables.json, and a consumer cannot mint a tunable — so an [auth.external.<provider>] block, an OAuth-server section, or any other auth key added to the tree's config reds the chain until a harness-reviewed release names it (tests/gates/check-auth-posture.test.mjs holds the unreviewed-key red). Limit: the census reads the tree's supabase/config.toml only; a provider or OAuth server enabled in a hosted project's Dashboard, or a consumer's own SDK call against one, is outside it.
requirements.note: The seeded tree makes no authorization requests, and the first-party password grant it does use carries no scope parameter — there are no scopes to minimise. A consumer who enables an external OAuth provider chooses scopes in the provider configuration and their own sign-in call; that surface does not exist in the seeded tree. An in-tree [auth.external.*] enablement reds the auth-posture [auth*] key census; a Dashboard-side enablement and the consumer's own call site are outside anything this register names.

requirements.text: Verify that the resource server only accepts access tokens that are intended for use with that service (audience). The audience may be included in a structured access token (such as the 'aud' claim in JWT), or it can be checked using the token introspection endpoint.
requirements.note: No code in this tree validates an `aud` claim, and no introspection endpoint is called — the requirement's mechanism is absent. What does exist is adjacent and already claimed by 10.3.3: the no-unverified-session ESLint rule on the lint step reds any server-side supabase.auth.getSession(), so every server-side identity read is a signature-verified GoTrue token (getUser()/getClaims() against the project's own auth server or published key), which bounds acceptance to tokens the project's own issuer minted. That is issuer binding, not audience checking: in the seeded single-resource-server architecture the two coincide only vacuously, and a consumer standing up a second resource server behind the same Supabase project gets no audience separation from anything this register names. The live suite (tests/rls/cross-tenant-isolation.test.ts under the rls-isolation Stop step) proves an anonymous client — publishable key, no user token — reads zero rows from every private table; no test in the tree presents a forged, foreign-issuer, or wrong-audience token. Downgraded from partial because the only control available has verification-not-trust as its subject, not audience, and naming it here would double-count 10.3.3.

requirements.text: Verify that the resource server enforces authorization decisions based on claims from the access token that define delegated authorization. If claims such as 'sub', 'scope', and 'authorization_details' are present, they must be part of the decision.
requirements.note: Authorization decisions are enforced at the database from verified token claims: every user-scoped table's RLS policies key on (SELECT auth.uid()) — the token's `sub` — with the shape closed structurally by the schema-rls step (check-rls-manifest.mjs: ENABLE+FORCE, per-operation policies, the initPlan predicate form, the policy-to-grant closure) and the tenancy step, and proven behaviorally on a live stack by supabase/tests/rls_isolation.test.sql (pgTAP, set_config('request.jwt.claims') per tenant) and tests/rls/cross-tenant-isolation.test.ts, both run by the rls-isolation Stop step (the canary named here rides that step, not the schema-rls chain step). The `aal` claim also joins the decision where the MFA rail applies (see 10.3.4). The residual that keeps this partial: GoTrue access tokens carry no 'scope' or 'authorization_details' claims — there is no delegated-authorization vocabulary in this architecture at all — so the decision is identity (and authentication level), never a delegation scope; the requirement's 'if present' clause for those claims is simply never triggered here, and nothing in the tree would notice if it were.

requirements.text: Verify that if an access control decision requires identifying a unique user from an access token (JWT or related token introspection response), the resource server identifies the user from claims that cannot be reassigned to other users. Typically, it means using a combination of 'iss' and 'sub' claims.
requirements.note: The unique-user identifier every access decision keys on is auth.uid() — the `sub` claim of a signature-verified GoTrue JWT, a UUID from auth.users that the platform never reassigns — and it is the only identifier any policy uses: check-rls-manifest.mjs (schema-rls step) holds the policy shape, check-tenancy.mjs reds the tenant-column/user-id confusion a structural check cannot see, the API context derives actor.userId from the verified user.id (packages/platform/supabase/src/verify.ts, packages/api/src/context.ts), and the lint step's no-unverified-session rule keeps server code from trusting an unverified sub out of the cookie. The behavioral proof (the canary named here) is supabase/tests/rls_isolation.test.sql under the rls-isolation Stop step, alongside tests/rls/cross-tenant-isolation.test.ts. Issuer binding is cryptographic rather than an 'iss' string comparison: verification is against the project's own auth server or published key, so a token from any other issuer fails before a claim is read. Residual stated plainly: the architecture has exactly one trusted issuer, and a consumer who federates additional issuers must add explicit iss discrimination that nothing here provides.

requirements.text: Verify that, if the resource server requires specific authentication strength, methods, or recentness, it verifies that the presented access token satisfies these constraints. For example, if present, using the OIDC 'acr', 'amr' and 'auth_time' claims respectively.
requirements.note: Authentication strength IS checked from the presented token where the constraint exists: the restrictive policy in supabase/migrations/20260812000000_mfa_aal2.sql refuses every statement from a user holding a verified MFA factor whose token carries 'aal1' — the `aal` claim being GoTrue's acr analogue — enforced at the database on every surface including ones nobody wrote. The can-fail proof is supabase/tests/mfa_aal2.test.sql (25 live assertions that go red against the vendor's published fail-open policy), run by the rls-isolation Stop step. Partial, not covered, for two stated reasons: the rail is applied to the worked vertical (public.notes) and coverage over further tables is deliberately the consumer's sensitivity decision, not the harness's; and methods and recentness ('amr', 'auth_time') are checked nowhere in the tree.

requirements.text: Verify that the resource server prevents the use of stolen access tokens or replay of access tokens (from unauthorized parties) by requiring sender-constrained access tokens, either Mutual TLS for OAuth 2 or OAuth 2 Demonstration of Proof of Possession (DPoP).
requirements.note: Access tokens in this architecture are pure bearer tokens: Supabase Auth publishes no DPoP or mutual-TLS sender-constraining for its access tokens, so this is a platform ceiling that neither the harness nor a consumer can configure around while staying on the managed auth server. The mitigations that do ship — access-token life bounded by the auth-posture tunables (auth.jwt_expiry between five minutes and a day), refresh rotation with reuse detection pinned as posture floor, keychain-confined mobile storage — shorten the window a stolen token is useful for but sender-constrain nothing, and the row is graded on the requirement's own mechanism rather than its neighbours.

requirements.text: Verify that the authorization server validates redirect URIs based on a client-specific allowlist of pre-registered URIs using exact string comparison.
requirements.note: The pre-registered allowlist is supabase/config.toml `auth.additional_redirect_urls` — exactly two full-URL entries, the web callback and the mobile deep link — and the auth-posture validate step enforces the reviewed ceiling of two entries and reds any entry containing a wildcard (tools/auth-posture.json redirectAllowlist, bannedSubstrings ["*"]; tests/gates/check-auth-posture.test.mjs holds the wildcard red), so matching can only ever be against literal URLs; `site_url` is additionally shape-checked to https-or-loopback so a code is never handed to a cleartext origin. Partial rather than covered because the comparison itself runs inside the managed GoTrue server: the tree can keep glob patterns out of the list and hold the list's size, but it cannot prove the vendor's matcher performs exact string comparison, and the config surface is per-project rather than per-client — the seeded posture registers no OAuth clients (the platform's opt-in OAuth-server capability is unconfigured here, and any [auth*] key the register does not name reds the same gate).

requirements.text: Verify that, if the authorization server returns the authorization code in the authorization response, it can be used only once for a token request. For the second valid request with an authorization code that has already been used to issue an access token, the authorization server must reject a token request and revoke any issued tokens related to the authorization code.
requirements.negativeProof: The authorization server is Supabase GoTrue, a managed vendor component: no AS implementation exists in this tree to ship, and the CLI config surface the auth-posture gate pins carries no key governing authorization-code single-use or revoke-on-replay. Whether GoTrue enforces it is a vendor implementation property the operating organisation verifies through platform assurance (vendor documentation and attestations), not a control this register can claim, configure, or red. The harness could not ship this behavior, which is why the row is not-applicable rather than not-covered.
requirements.note: The authorization server is Supabase GoTrue, a managed vendor component: no AS implementation exists in this tree to ship, and the CLI config surface the auth-posture gate pins carries no key governing authorization-code single-use or revoke-on-replay. Whether GoTrue enforces it is a vendor implementation property the operating organisation verifies through platform assurance (vendor documentation and attestations), not a control this register can claim, configure, or red. The harness could not ship this behavior, which is why the row is not-applicable rather than not-covered.

requirements.text: Verify that the authorization code is short-lived. The maximum lifetime can be up to 10 minutes for L1 and L2 applications and up to 1 minute for L3 applications.
requirements.negativeProof: Authorization-code lifetime is internal behavior of the managed GoTrue server; no supabase/config.toml key exposes it, so the harness could neither set it nor pin it in tools/auth-posture.json. The operating organisation verifies the vendor's code lifetime through platform assurance. Not-applicable because the harness has no surface with which to ship this, not because the property does not matter.
requirements.note: Authorization-code lifetime is internal behavior of the managed GoTrue server; no supabase/config.toml key exposes it, so the harness could neither set it nor pin it in tools/auth-posture.json. The operating organisation verifies the vendor's code lifetime through platform assurance. Not-applicable because the harness has no surface with which to ship this, not because the property does not matter.

requirements.text: Verify that for a given client, the authorization server only allows the usage of grants that this client needs to use. Note that the grants 'token' (Implicit flow) and 'password' (Resource Owner Password Credentials flow) must no longer be used.
requirements.note: The seeded posture registers no OAuth clients and the tree exposes no per-client grant restriction surface — the platform's opt-in OAuth-server capability is unconfigured in supabase/config.toml and any [auth*] key the harness register does not name reds the auth-posture gate — so the requirement's mechanism cannot be shipped from this tree. The row is deliberately graded not-covered rather than not-applicable because the tension is real and must stay visible: the seeded scaffold itself authenticates through GoTrue's password grant (signInWithPassword is grant_type=password against the token endpoint on both surfaces). Read strictly against this requirement's sentence, that is the Resource Owner Password Credentials grant the chapter says must no longer be used; read against the platform's architecture it is the vendor's first-party sign-in primitive with no third-party delegation involved. Both readings are recorded; neither makes the grant restriction exist.

requirements.text: Verify that the authorization server mitigates refresh token replay attacks for public clients, preferably using sender-constrained refresh tokens, i.e., Demonstrating Proof of Possession (DPoP) or Certificate-Bound Access Tokens using mutual TLS (mTLS). For L1 and L2 applications, refresh token rotation may be used. If refresh token rotation is used, the authorization server must invalidate the refresh token after usage, and revoke all refresh tokens for that authorization if an already used and invalidated refresh token is provided.
requirements.note: Refresh-token rotation — the mitigation this requirement sanctions at L1/L2 — is pinned ON as a harness posture floor (`auth.enable_refresh_token_rotation: true` with `auth.refresh_token_reuse_interval: 10` in tools/auth-posture.json), and check-auth-posture.mjs diffs both keys by value in both directions, so a config flip or a silently-ignored misspelling reds rather than running GoTrue's default. Sender-constrained refresh tokens (DPoP/mTLS) are not offered by the platform. Two residuals stated: family-revocation on reuse of an invalidated token is GoTrue's implementation, asserted by no test in this tree; and the ten-second reuse interval is a deliberate allowance for a mobile client's concurrent refresh pair, during which one reuse of a just-rotated token is accepted — a documented deviation from strict invalidate-after-single-use, calibrated in the posture notes.

requirements.text: Verify that, if the code grant is used, the authorization server mitigates authorization code interception attacks by requiring proof key for code exchange (PKCE). For authorization requests, the authorization server must require a valid 'code_challenge' value and must not accept a 'code_challenge_method' value of 'plain'. For a token request, it must require validation of the 'code_verifier' parameter.
requirements.negativeProof: Whether the authorization server REQUIRES PKCE — demands a code_challenge, refuses 'plain', validates the code_verifier — is GoTrue server behavior with no supabase/config.toml key, so the harness could not ship or pin the server half; the tree seeds PKCE on the client side only (flowType 'pkce', itself unenforced — see 10.1.2). The operating organisation verifies the vendor's server-side PKCE enforcement through platform assurance.
requirements.note: Whether the authorization server REQUIRES PKCE — demands a code_challenge, refuses 'plain', validates the code_verifier — is GoTrue server behavior with no supabase/config.toml key, so the harness could not ship or pin the server half; the tree seeds PKCE on the client side only (flowType 'pkce', itself unenforced — see 10.1.2). The operating organisation verifies the vendor's server-side PKCE enforcement through platform assurance.

requirements.text: Verify that if the authorization server supports unauthenticated dynamic client registration, it mitigates the risk of malicious client applications. It must validate client metadata such as any registered URIs, ensure the user's consent, and warn the user before processing an authorization request with an untrusted client application.
requirements.negativeProof: validate-chain step auth-posture (tools/check-auth-posture.mjs, backward direction): every key under [auth*] in supabase/config.toml must be named by tools/auth-posture.json or tools/auth-tunables.json, and a consumer cannot mint a tunable — so an [auth.external.<provider>] block, an OAuth-server section, or any other auth key added to the tree's config reds the chain until a harness-reviewed release names it (tests/gates/check-auth-posture.test.mjs holds the unreviewed-key red). Limit: the census reads the tree's supabase/config.toml only; a provider or OAuth server enabled in a hosted project's Dashboard, or a consumer's own SDK call against one, is outside it.
requirements.note: The seeded authorization-server posture has no client registry and no registration endpoint in play: supabase/config.toml carries no OAuth-server section, and whether the platform's opt-in OAuth-server capability offers dynamic client registration is a vendor property this tree neither enables nor verifies. The conditional this requirement hangs on ('if the authorization server supports unauthenticated dynamic client registration') is therefore false for the generated system, and the tree side of that absence is machine-held — an OAuth-server or any other unreviewed [auth*] key added to config.toml reds the auth-posture gate — while a Dashboard-side enablement in a hosted project remains the operating organisation's to see.

requirements.text: Verify that refresh tokens have an absolute expiration, including if sliding refresh token expiration is applied.
requirements.note: The seeded posture pins rotation and the reuse interval but pins NO absolute refresh-token or session expiry, and tools/auth-posture.json carries no key for one. The platform's CLI config surface does expose session-lifetime keys (an [auth.sessions] block — timebox and inactivity_timeout — per the vendor's published config reference), so this is a harness gap rather than a platform ceiling: nothing in the tree sets, pins, or diffs an absolute ceiling. Worse than merely unpinned: because the auth-posture gate's [auth*] key census reds any key the harness register does not name and a consumer cannot mint a tunable, a consumer who adds [auth.sessions] to the tree's config.toml reds the chain until a harness release names the keys — the drift detection around the gap currently blocks closing it in-tree (a hosted Dashboard setting is outside the census). The row stays not-covered until an absolute expiry is actually declared as a bounded tunable and diffed.

requirements.text: Verify that refresh tokens and reference access tokens can be revoked by an authorized user using the authorization server user interface, to mitigate the risk of malicious clients or stolen tokens.
requirements.note: What ships is sign-out on both surfaces (apps/web/app/(protected)/sign-out-button.tsx and the mobile session.signOut command in apps/mobile/src/features/actions/registry.ts, both calling supabase.auth.signOut() with the SDK's default global scope, which revokes the user's refresh tokens at GoTrue), plus in-app account deletion (the delete-account Edge Function), which ends everything. The sign-out surface IS exercised by tests — apps/web/e2e/authenticated.spec.ts clicks it on a live stack and apps/mobile/__tests__/actions-modal.test.tsx asserts the command invokes signOut (mobile-unit Stop step) — but no test asserts the revocation itself (that a previously issued refresh token then fails to refresh), and no surface lists a user's active sessions or lets them revoke another device's refresh token individually. Reference access tokens do not exist in this architecture (access tokens are self-contained JWTs that remain valid until expiry regardless of revocation). A stolen-refresh-token response today is sign-out-everywhere-or-support, not a token-management UI; with revocation asserted by nothing and no per-session UI, no control is named.

requirements.text: Verify that confidential client is authenticated for client-to-authorized server backchannel requests such as token requests, pushed authorization requests (PAR), and token revocation requests.
requirements.negativeProof: validate-chain step auth-posture (tools/check-auth-posture.mjs, backward direction): every key under [auth*] in supabase/config.toml must be named by tools/auth-posture.json or tools/auth-tunables.json, and a consumer cannot mint a tunable — so an [auth.external.<provider>] block, an OAuth-server section, or any other auth key added to the tree's config reds the chain until a harness-reviewed release names it (tests/gates/check-auth-posture.test.mjs holds the unreviewed-key red). Limit: the census reads the tree's supabase/config.toml only; a provider or OAuth server enabled in a hosted project's Dashboard, or a consumer's own SDK call against one, is outside it.
requirements.note: No confidential OAuth clients exist in the generated system: the seeded posture registers no clients (the platform's opt-in OAuth-server capability is unconfigured in supabase/config.toml), and the token-endpoint calls the tree makes authenticate the user (password, refresh token, code+verifier), never a client credential.
