The subject of this requirement is absent from the seeded architecture; the tree side of that absence is held by the auth-posture [auth*] key census, and the harness could not ship client authentication for an authorization server it does not implement.

requirements.text: Verify that the authorization server configuration only assigns the required scopes to the OAuth client.

requirements.text: Verify that there is a documented policy for management of cryptographic keys and a cryptographic key lifecycle that follows a key management standard such as NIST SP 800-57. This should include ensuring that keys are not overshared (for example, with more than two entities for shared secrets and more than one entity for private keys).
requirements.note: The subject is an organisation-maintained key-management policy and lifecycle standard, which this template does not ship and the operating organisation must write. What does exist is narrower doctrine, not a policy: the always-loaded .claude/rules/encryption.md documents key birth (platform CSPRNG only), storage (one keystore door per host), wrapping (DEK wrapped by KEK, never derived) and destruction (crypto-shredding) for the keys the scaffold mints; the hardcoded-key-material write-guard rule refuses a 256-bit hex literal in a key-shaped assignment at edit time; the expo-public-secret-name / next-public-secret-name write-guard rules and the `secrets` validate step (tools/secret-patterns.json — service key, PEM bodies, keystore passwords, tokens; it carries no generic hex-key pattern) keep credential-shaped material out of the tree. Nothing documents a NIST SP 800-57-shaped lifecycle — no crypto-periods, rotation schedule, custodial roles, or an oversharing rule for operator-held secrets beyond never-in-repo and never-in-shell. Graded not-covered rather than not-applicable because the harness could ship a seed policy document and has not.

requirements.text: Verify that a cryptographic inventory is performed, maintained, regularly updated, and includes all cryptographic keys, algorithms, and certificates used by the application. It must also document where keys can and cannot be used in the system, and the types of data that can and cannot be protected using the keys.
requirements.note: Performing and maintaining an inventory is a running organisation's process, and no inventory artifact of keys, algorithms and certificates exists in this tree. The nearest artifacts are partial by construction: tools/exports-walls.json (stack tree) records the @app/crypto barrel split and its Metro-safety reason, tools/data-flow.json records what survives deletion and what an export returns (it cannot tell ciphertext from plaintext), and tools/store-tunables.json iosEncryption records the Apple export declaration for non-exempt cryptography (default nonExemptAllowed=false) — none is a key/algorithm/certificate inventory, and none documents where keys may or may not be used. Graded not-covered rather than not-applicable because the harness could ship a seed inventory file for the primitives it itself introduces (AES-256-GCM, AES-256-CTR, HKDF-SHA-256, SHA-256, X25519 when the e2ee module is enabled, the platform CSPRNGs) and has not.

requirements.text: Verify that cryptographic discovery mechanisms are employed to identify all instances of cryptography in the system, including encryption, hashing, and signing operations.
requirements.proof: tools/eslint-rules/index.mjs — the custom rule named in the note, wired in eslint.config.mjs and run by the `lint` step (factory red-proof tests/gates/eslint-custom-rules.test.mjs)
requirements.note: Control: validate step `lint` — local/crypto-primitives-one-door (tools/eslint-rules/index.mjs, wired in eslint.config.mjs). A real discovery mechanism runs on every validate: the crypto-primitives-one-door ESLint rule flags every direct reach for crypto.subtle and every node:crypto cipher/KDF/sign/keygen import (createCipheriv, scrypt, pbkdf2, hkdf, createSign, createDiffieHellman, generateKeyPair and kin) outside the two sanctioned homes, so that class of cryptography appearing anywhere else in the linted surface is red, not silent; on apps/mobile/** a no-restricted-imports group additionally reds the npm cipher libraries (aes-js, @noble/*, libsodium*, tweetnacl*, react-native-quick-crypto) outside the host seam. The weak-crypto-algorithm write-guard adds edit-time detection of named algorithm strings. What discovery does NOT reach: the rule is scoped to apps/**, packages/** and supabase/**/*.ts with tests excluded, so tools/**, scripts and test files are outside it; an npm cipher library imported on the WEB app or in a package is not flagged by any lint rule (the cipher-library group is mobile-only); digest and HMAC calls (createHash, createHmac) are deliberately not flagged, so hashing operations are only partially discovered; and SQL-side cryptography (pgcrypto/pg_catalog digest calls in migrations and seeds), the platform's own cryptography (GoTrue JWT signing, TLS, Postgres at-rest encryption), and vendored dependencies are outside its reach — inventorying those remains the operating organisation's work.

requirements.text: Verify that a cryptographic inventory is maintained. This must include a documented plan that outlines the migration path to new cryptographic standards, such as post-quantum cryptography, in order to react to future threats.
requirements.note: No cryptographic inventory exists (see 11.1.2) and no documented migration plan to new standards exists anywhere in the tree. Migration MECHANICS exist in the e2ee module — the envelope carries its version byte inside the sealed bytes, the algorithm byte reserves ALG_RESERVED_XCHACHA20 for a future cipher, and one decoder refuses unknown versions — but mechanics are not a plan, and this register does not let the presence of an agility seam stand in for a documented PQC migration path. Graded not-covered rather than not-applicable because a seed migration-plan document is a shippable artifact the harness has not shipped.

requirements.text: Verify that industry-validated implementations (including libraries and hardware-accelerated implementations) are used for cryptographic operations.
requirements.proof: tools/eslint-rules/index.mjs — the custom rule named in the note, wired in eslint.config.mjs and run by the `lint` step (factory red-proof tests/gates/eslint-custom-rules.test.mjs)
requirements.note: Control: validate step `lint` — local/crypto-primitives-one-door (tools/eslint-rules/index.mjs). The one-door rule forces application code to take primitives from the injected CryptoProvider rather than hand-rolling, and when the opt-in e2ee module is enabled its provider delegates every AEAD and KDF operation to the platform's WebCrypto (crypto.subtle) — a vendor-maintained, hardware-accelerated implementation — held to the NIST GCM validation vectors byte-exactly by packages/platform/crypto/src/webcrypto-provider.test.ts (module-conditional evidence). The honest residual is in the base tree: the mobile session store (apps/mobile/src/host/large-secure-store.ts) encrypts with aes-js, a pure-JavaScript AES that is neither industry-validated nor hardware-accelerated, chosen with documented rationale because Hermes ships no Web Crypto; its CSPRNG is the platform's (expo-crypto) but the cipher itself is software. Graded partial, and the tier stays documentation because the vector suite exists only when the module is enabled.

requirements.text: Verify that the application is designed with crypto agility such that random number, authenticated encryption, MAC, or hashing algorithms, key lengths, rounds, ciphers and modes can be reconfigured, upgraded, or swapped at any time, to protect against cryptographic breaks. Similarly, it must also be possible to replace keys and passwords and re-encrypt data. This will allow for seamless upgrades to post-quantum cryptography (PQC), once high-assurance implementations of approved PQC schemes or standards are widely available.
requirements.note: Control: Stop-chain step `unit` (tools/stop.floor.json) — runs the e2ee envelope/keyring suites when the module is installed. Conditional on the e2ee module being enabled. The agility half is real: every sealed byte-string is one versioned envelope (magic | v | alg | ivLen | iv | ct) with the version byte INSIDE the bytes so no schema column can drift from the format it claims, the algorithm byte reserves ALG_RESERVED_XCHACHA20 for a future cipher, one decoder refuses unknown versions and algorithms with distinct named reasons (envelope.test.ts proves each refusal), and primitives arrive through the CryptoProvider / X25519Provider ports so the implementation can be swapped in one place — the crypto-primitives-one-door lint rule is what keeps a second envelope format from ever appearing. The key-replacement half is only a primitive: keyring.ts ships rewrapItemKey (open the wrapped DEK under the old KEK, re-seal the SAME DEK under the new one, item ciphertext untouched; keyring.test.ts proves the rewrap suite including the old-KEK refusal), but the README states plainly that no batch runner, resume point, progress record, completion check or two-KEK-era serving strategy ships — a rotation pass is the consumer's reviewed data migration; re-encrypting the DATA under a new DEK or a new cipher is open-then-seal with no shipped path; and password replacement is Supabase Auth's platform surface, not the tree's. Base-tree crypto (the aes-js session store) has no agility seam.

requirements.text: Verify that all cryptographic primitives utilize a minimum of 128-bits of security based on the algorithm, key size, and configuration. For example, a 256-bit ECC key provides roughly 128 bits of security where RSA requires a 3072-bit key to achieve 128 bits of security.
requirements.proof: .claude/hooks/lib/guard-rules.mjs rule `weak-crypto-algorithm` — denied at the PreToolUse seam; red-proof in tests/hooks/hook-contract.test.mjs RULE_CANARIES
requirements.note: Control: write-guard rule `weak-crypto-algorithm` (.claude/hooks/lib/guard-rules.mjs). Every primitive the template itself mints clears 128 bits: the e2ee provider is AES-256-GCM only and refuses a key that is not 32 bytes (closing the observed defect where a 16-byte KEK sealed AES-128 under an envelope declaring AES-256), the session store mints 32-byte AES-256-CTR keys, digests are SHA-256, and HKDF is SHA-256. The write-guard denies sub-128-bit primitives (DES, RC4, MD5, SHA-1) at edit time. Residuals: no tree-wide gate CLOSES the tree to a strength floor — the guard is a deny-list of known-weak names, not an assertion over every primitive in use; the invitation token specimen is a ~122-bit UUIDv4 (recorded at 11.5.1); and platform-side primitives (GoTrue's JWT signing keys, TLS suites) are the vendor's choices, unverified here.

requirements.text: Verify that all cryptographic operations are constant-time, with no 'short-circuit' operations in comparisons, calculations, or returns, to avoid leaking information.
requirements.note: Nothing in the harness measures or enforces constant-time execution. The e2ee module delegates AEAD to platform WebCrypto, whose native implementations are generally constant-time, but that is the vendor's property and no gate verifies it. Two in-tree surfaces are known NOT to be constant-time: aes-js in the mobile session store is table-based software AES with data-dependent lookups (cache-timing observable in principle), and the invitation-token check compares sha256 digests via SQL equality over a b-tree index — the digest indirection blunts a timing oracle on the token value, but the comparison itself is not constant-time. Claiming coverage on unverified vendor behaviour would be inflation, so the row stays not-covered.

requirements.text: Verify that all cryptographic modules fail securely, and errors are handled in a way that does not enable vulnerabilities, such as Padding Oracle attacks.
requirements.note: Control: Stop-chain step `unit` (tools/stop.floor.json) — runs the e2ee module suites when installed. Conditional on the e2ee module being enabled. GCM has no padding, so a padding oracle has no surface; every provider failure is a null mapped to a NAMED CryptoResult refusal rather than an escaping throw; a wrong key and a tampered ciphertext are deliberately indistinguishable (keyring.test.ts: 'the wrong root key is aead_auth_failed — indistinguishable from tamper, honestly'; recovery.test.ts and recipient-wrap.test.ts make the same assertion for their seams), and each envelope decode refusal carries its own distinct reason (envelope.test.ts) so a crypto-shredded row (key_missing) is distinguishable from corruption without leaking anything an attacker can use. Base-tree residual: LargeSecureStore fails closed — any unreadable or undecryptable store reads as signed-out, never a crash — but its unauthenticated CTR means tampered ciphertext decrypts to garbage instead of failing authentication, and no error-oracle analysis exists for surfaces outside the module.

requirements.text: Verify that insecure block modes (e.g., ECB) and weak padding schemes (e.g., PKCS#1 v1.5) are not used.
requirements.proof: .claude/hooks/lib/guard-rules.mjs rule `weak-crypto-algorithm` — denied at the PreToolUse seam; red-proof in tests/hooks/hook-contract.test.mjs RULE_CANARIES
requirements.note: Control: write-guard rule `weak-crypto-algorithm` (.claude/hooks/lib/guard-rules.mjs). The write-guard denies ECB spellings (node-style 'aes-###-ecb' and WebCrypto 'AES-###-ECB'), DES/3DES, RC4, Blowfish/RC2 modes and the legacy createCipher() static-IV constructor in algorithm-argument position, so the write that introduces an insecure mode is refused at edit time; the crypto-primitives-one-door lint rule independently keeps application code from importing any node:crypto cipher API or reaching crypto.subtle outside the two sanctioned homes, whose provider exposes AEAD only. Residuals stated plainly: the guard fires on agent-made edits through the hook layer — a human commit bypasses it and no validate-chain step sweeps the tree for this class; an npm cipher library (aes-js and kin) is lint-red only on apps/mobile/**, so a web or package import of one is a reviewer's catch; PKCS#1 v1.5 padding spellings (e.g. RSAES-PKCS1-v1_5) are not in the deny pattern, though no RSA operation exists in-tree for them to attach to; and the base session store's CTR mode is a stream mode, not an insecure block mode, with its integrity gap recorded at 11.3.3.

requirements.text: Verify that only approved ciphers and modes such as AES with GCM are used.
requirements.note: Control: Stop-chain step `unit` (tools/stop.floor.json) — the e2ee provider vector suite when installed. Conditional on the e2ee module for the strong half: its provider performs AES-256-GCM only, tagLength pinned to 128, and the vector suite holds seal output byte-exactly to the GCM specification's validation test cases (tc13–tc16, the pair that catches a silently dropped AAD), so a provider drifting off the approved cipher fails a vector, not just a roundtrip; the module's key-wrap seams (recipient wrap, recovery escrow, device sync) all reuse the same AES-256-GCM envelope. The base session store uses AES-256-CTR — an approved NIST SP 800-38A mode, deliberately unauthenticated with the integrity consequence recorded at 11.3.3. Residual: the tree is protected by a deny-list (weak-crypto-algorithm write-guard) plus the one-door funnel (node:crypto / crypto.subtle everywhere it lints; npm cipher libraries on mobile only), not by an allow-list closure — nothing asserts that ONLY approved ciphers exist tree-wide, which is why this row does not claim covered.

requirements.text: Verify that encrypted data is protected against unauthorized modification preferably by using an approved authenticated encryption method or by combining an approved encryption method with an approved MAC algorithm.
requirements.note: Control: Stop-chain step `unit` (tools/stop.floor.json) — the e2ee keyring tamper suite when installed. Conditional on the e2ee module: every sealed value is AES-256-GCM AEAD with a full 128-bit tag, and the AAD binds version, algorithm, a role byte and the row identity (userId, table, itemId, field — each length-prefixed, not separator-joined, after an adversarial review broke the separator scheme), so ciphertext moved to another row, table or user FAILS AUTHENTICATION rather than decrypting in the wrong place; keyring.test.ts proves the tampered-DEK, moved-row, moved-user, role-swap and wrong-key refusals. The honest residual is the base tree's one at-rest encryption surface: LargeSecureStore is AES-256-CTR with NO authentication — a tampered session ciphertext decrypts to garbage rather than being refused; the downstream JSON parse failure reads as signed-out, which fails closed for a session, but it is not authenticated encryption and any consumer reusing that pattern for other data inherits the gap.

requirements.text: Verify that nonces, initialization vectors, and other single-use numbers are not used for more than one encryption key and data-element pair. The method of generation must be appropriate for the algorithm being used.
requirements.proof: tools/eslint-rules/index.mjs — the custom rule named in the note, wired in eslint.config.mjs and run by the `lint` step (factory red-proof tests/gates/eslint-custom-rules.test.mjs)
requirements.note: Control: validate step `lint` — local/crypto-primitives-one-door (tools/eslint-rules/index.mjs). The guarantee is structural, and conditional on the e2ee module for AEAD surfaces: sealItem mints a FRESH DEK per seal, so no key ever encrypts twice and the 96-bit random IV never meets the birthday bound that makes IV reuse under GCM catastrophic; IVs are generated inside the keyring from the provider CSPRNG and the API offers no caller-supplied-IV path, while the one-door lint rule keeps application code away from any raw cipher where an IV could be managed by hand. The base session store makes the same argument in CTR form — a fresh key per stored value is why its fixed counter start cannot reuse a keystream. Stated limits: no test asserts non-reuse directly (a mutant reusing a static IV would still roundtrip), so the tier stays documentation; and the property holds by API shape, not by a gate that measures IV uniqueness.

requirements.text: Verify that any combination of an encryption algorithm and a MAC algorithm is operating in encrypt-then-MAC mode.
requirements.negativeProof: local/crypto-primitives-one-door (validate step `lint`) — a node:crypto cipher import or a crypto.subtle reach outside packages/platform/crypto/src/** and apps/*/src/host/** is lint-red, and on apps/mobile/** the no-restricted-imports cipher-library group reds aes-js/@noble/libsodium/tweetnacl outside the host seam; the CryptoProvider port exposes no MAC primitive to compose with
requirements.note: No encryption-plus-separate-MAC combination exists anywhere in this tree, so there is no ordering to verify: the only authenticated construction is integrated AEAD (AES-256-GCM in the e2ee module, including its X25519 recipient-wrap, recovery-escrow and device-sync seams), and the port surface is aeadSeal/aeadOpen/hkdfSha256/randomBytes plus generateKeyPair/deriveSharedSecret — no MAC primitive exists to combine with a cipher. The one unauthenticated cipher surface (the CTR session store) carries no MAC at all; that is 11.3.3's recorded residual, not an encrypt-then-MAC ordering question. The stated limits of the negative proof: it reaches node:crypto and crypto.subtle in the linted globs (tests and tools/** excluded) and npm cipher libraries only on mobile, so a composition built from an npm cipher plus a hash library in the web app or a package would be a reviewer's catch, not a chain failure.

requirements.text: Verify that only approved hash functions are used for general cryptographic use cases, including digital signatures, HMAC, KDF, and random bit generation. Disallowed hash functions, such as MD5, must not be used for any cryptographic purpose.
requirements.proof: .claude/hooks/lib/guard-rules.mjs rule `weak-crypto-algorithm` — denied at the PreToolUse seam; red-proof in tests/hooks/hook-contract.test.mjs RULE_CANARIES
requirements.note: Control: write-guard rule `weak-crypto-algorithm` (.claude/hooks/lib/guard-rules.mjs). Every cryptographic hash the template itself uses is SHA-256: HKDF-SHA-256 in the e2ee keyring, recovery and recipient-wrap seams, and pg_catalog.sha256 for the invitation token digest (the never-readable-back precedent). The write-guard denies MD5 and SHA-1 in node-style string position, the WebCrypto spelling ({ hash: 'SHA-1' } / { name: 'MD5' }), and .digest('SHA-1') — the WebCrypto shape was added after review because the stack's own provider is crypto.subtle-based. Residuals: the guard fires on agent edits, not human commits, and no validate-chain step sweeps the tree for weak hash algorithms; a SQL md5() call is not a quoted algorithm argument and would not match the pattern — and one exists in-tree, supabase/seeds/scale.sql minting deterministic seed-row UUIDs from md5(), a non-cryptographic identifier use that this row records rather than hides; the push-notifications module's slice document (docs/.../push-token-id.ts.txt) derives an RFC 9562 UUIDv5 via createHash('sha1'), an identifier construction not a security digest, which the deny pattern WOULD refuse if pasted into a source file; and there is no allow-list asserting only approved functions exist — the control is a deny-list over known-broken names.

requirements.text: Verify that passwords are stored using an approved, computationally intensive, key derivation function (also known as a "password hashing function"), with parameter settings configured based on current guidance. The settings should balance security and performance to make brute-force attacks sufficiently challenging for the required level of security.
requirements.note: The tree stores no password hashes of its own — password storage in a generated application is performed entirely by Supabase Auth (GoTrue), which hashes with bcrypt using parameters the platform manages. Those parameters are not consumer-configurable through any artifact in this tree: the auth-posture gate diffs the [auth] config surface by value in both directions, but that surface carries no password-hashing parameter to pin. No harness control observes or verifies the platform's KDF or its cost settings, and crediting an unverified vendor default as coverage would be the inflation this register refuses, so the row stays not-covered with the delegation recorded.

requirements.text: Verify that hash functions used in digital signatures, as part of data authentication or data integrity are collision resistant and have appropriate bit-lengths. If collision resistance is required, the output length must be at least 256 bits. If only resistance to second pre-image attacks is required, the output length must be at least 128 bits.
requirements.proof: .claude/hooks/lib/guard-rules.mjs rule `weak-crypto-algorithm` — denied at the PreToolUse seam; red-proof in tests/hooks/hook-contract.test.mjs RULE_CANARIES
requirements.note: Control: write-guard rule `weak-crypto-algorithm` (.claude/hooks/lib/guard-rules.mjs). The only in-tree integrity digest is 256-bit SHA-256: the invitation token_digest (a second-preimage use, comfortably over the 128-bit floor) and HKDF-SHA-256 in the e2ee module; GCM's authentication is a MAC, not a digital-signature hash. The write-guard keeps SHA-1 and MD5 out of new code in all three spellings it knows. Digital signatures are not generated anywhere in the tree — JWT signing is GoTrue's and verification runs inside supabase-js via getClaims against the project's published asymmetric key, with the hash algorithm chosen by the vendor and unverified here. No rule closes the tree to appropriate bit-lengths generally; the grade rests on the small, enumerated set of in-tree hash uses plus the deny-list.

requirements.text: Verify that the application uses approved key derivation functions with key stretching parameters when deriving secret keys from passwords. The parameters in use must balance security and performance to prevent brute-force attacks from compromising the resulting cryptographic key.
requirements.negativeProof: local/crypto-primitives-one-door (validate step `lint`) denies scrypt/pbkdf2/hkdf node:crypto imports and crypto.subtle deriveKey reaches outside the provider package and host seam; the e2ee module's recovery.test.ts holds deriveRecoveryKey to HKDF-SHA-256 over a GENERATED 256-bit code (no passphrase input path exists in the API)
requirements.note: No key anywhere in this tree is derived from a password: every key is born from the platform CSPRNG (32 random bytes), and the always-loaded encryption rule forbids 'a passphrase without a memory-hard KDF' outright. The one string-to-key derivation that DOES ship (when the e2ee module is enabled) is recovery.ts deriveRecoveryKey — HKDF-SHA-256, no stretching, over a Crockford-encoded 256-bit code the module itself generates and shows once; the file's header states why that is not a password path (nothing is cheaper to brute-force than the key itself) and why passphrase-derived escrow is refused as a shipped default (WebCrypto has no Argon2id and PBKDF2-as-the-KDF would be a dishonest default), leaving it a consumer decision. This row does not lean on the factory obligations register: its `e2ee-declared-ports-unimplemented` row still anchors a ports-declared.ts file that no longer exists (node scripts/check-obligations.mjs reds it today), and RecoveryPort is now implemented, so that row is stale evidence. If a consumer implements passphrase-derived keys, this row's grade does not transfer to that implementation.

requirements.text: Verify that all random numbers and strings which are intended to be non-guessable must be generated using a cryptographically secure pseudo-random number generator (CSPRNG) and have at least 128 bits of entropy. Note that UUIDs do not respect this condition.
requirements.proof: tools/eslint-rules/index.mjs — the custom rule named in the note, wired in eslint.config.mjs and run by the `lint` step (factory red-proof tests/gates/eslint-custom-rules.test.mjs)
requirements.note: Control: validate step `lint` — local/no-insecure-random-in-crypto-scope (tools/eslint-rules/index.mjs). Where key material is born, the CSPRNG is enforced: Math.random is lint-red in the crypto scopes (the provider package and the host seams, deliberately including tests, because a fixture key from Math.random is how a weak key reaches a snapshot), the math-random-key-material write-guard catches the same act on edit fragments outside lint's globs, and the actual sources are platform CSPRNGs — crypto.getRandomValues on web, expo-crypto's native SecRandomCopyBytes/SecureRandom on device, chosen precisely because Hermes ships no Web Crypto and a polyfilled global is not trusted. Two honest residuals: the invitation token specimen is gen_random_uuid() — a version-4 UUID carrying ~122 bits, the exact case this requirement's own note excludes from the 128-bit condition (mitigated but not cured by being stored only as a sha256 digest and returned exactly once); and the lint scope covers crypto scopes, not every non-guessable string in the tree.

requirements.text: Verify that the random number generation mechanism in use is designed to work securely, even under heavy demand.
requirements.note: All randomness is delegated to kernel-backed CSPRNGs — the browser/Node WebCrypto DRBG, SecRandomCopyBytes and Android SecureRandom via expo-crypto, and Postgres's gen_random_uuid — which are designed for sustained demand and do not deplete in the blocking sense the requirement guards against. But that is a statement about vendor internals: nothing in this tree measures or verifies RNG behaviour under load, and a grade resting entirely on unverified platform properties is the inflation this register exists to refuse, so the row stays not-covered with the delegation recorded.

requirements.text: Verify that only approved cryptographic algorithms and modes of operation are used for key generation and seeding, and digital signature generation and verification. Key generation algorithms must not generate insecure keys vulnerable to known attacks, for example, RSA keys which are vulnerable to Fermat factorization.
requirements.note: In-tree key generation is CSPRNG-born symmetric keys (32 bytes) in the base tree, plus — only when the e2ee module is enabled — X25519 key pairs minted through WebCrypto generateKey in webcrypto-x25519.ts (webcrypto-x25519.test.ts proves the halves correspond and a fresh pair per call). No RSA or NIST-curve keypair is generated anywhere, so Fermat-factorisation-class weak-key attacks have no in-tree surface, but nothing gates that statement — a consumer adding RSA keygen inside the sanctioned provider package would pass every chain step. The application's real non-TLS public-key operation is JWT signature VERIFICATION, which runs inside supabase-js (getClaims verifying against the project's published asymmetric key) with algorithms Supabase chooses and rotates; no harness control asserts that algorithm set, so approval cannot be claimed here. The enforced invariant in this area — getUser()/getClaims(), never getSession() — guarantees that verification HAPPENS, which is an authentication-presence control, not an algorithm-approval one; grading it as coverage of this requirement would conflate the two.

requirements.text: Verify that approved cryptographic algorithms are used for key exchange (such as Diffie-Hellman) with a focus on ensuring that key exchange mechanisms use secure parameters. This will prevent attacks on the key establishment process which could lead to adversary-in-the-middle attacks or cryptographic breaks.
requirements.note: Control: Stop-chain step `unit` (tools/stop.floor.json) — the e2ee X25519 vector and recipient-wrap suites when the module is installed. Conditional on the e2ee module being enabled — the base tree performs no key exchange outside TLS, which this chapter scopes out. With the module, key agreement DOES ship: recipient-wrap.ts is X25519 ECIES with sealed-box semantics (a fresh ephemeral pair per wrap, ECDH against the recipient's static key, HKDF-SHA-256 binding both public keys, an AES-256-GCM wrap key), the shipped web/Node X25519Provider is WebCrypto's Secure-Curves implementation, webcrypto-x25519.test.ts holds deriveSharedSecret to the RFC 7748 §5.2 and §6.1 vectors against the real engine and proves the all-zero (low-order peer) result is refused, and recipient-wrap.test.ts proves the fresh-ephemeral, moved-recipient, tampered-ephemeral and low-order-recipient refusals plus a committed known-answer wire. Why partial and not covered: no chain step asserts an algorithm allow-list for key agreement (a consumer could add a finite-field DH inside the sanctioned provider package and stay green — the one-door lint rule only keeps createDiffieHellman/generateKeyPair OUT of application code); the mobile X25519 implementation is a priced consumer decision (docs/modules/e2ee/mobile-provider.patch.md), not shipped, so on device the parameters are whatever the consumer wires; and the factory obligations row `e2ee-declared-ports-unimplemented`, which the earlier grade cited as anchoring RecipientWrapPort as unimplemented, is stale — RecipientWrapPort is implemented and the row's ports-declared.ts anchor no longer exists.

requirements.text: Verify that full memory encryption is in use that protects sensitive data while it is in use, preventing access by unauthorized users or processes.
requirements.negativeProof: Full memory encryption is a property of the hosting hardware and hypervisor — Vercel's function runtime, Supabase's Postgres hosts, and the end user's device — and no repository artifact can create, configure, or verify it on any of those platforms; the harness could not ship it, and neither could a consumer acting through this tree, which is why the row is not-applicable rather than not-covered. No negative proof exists because there is no surface whose absence a gate could enforce. The nearest in-tree behaviour is the mobile session store's keychain split (key material outside the JS-readable sandbox), which is at-rest key scoping, not in-use memory encryption, and is not claimed as such.
requirements.note: Full memory encryption is a property of the hosting hardware and hypervisor — Vercel's function runtime, Supabase's Postgres hosts, and the end user's device — and no repository artifact can create, configure, or verify it on any of those platforms; the harness could not ship it, and neither could a consumer acting through this tree, which is why the row is not-applicable rather than not-covered. No negative proof exists because there is no surface whose absence a gate could enforce. The nearest in-tree behaviour is the mobile session store's keychain split (key material outside the JS-readable sandbox), which is at-rest key scoping, not in-use memory encryption, and is not claimed as such.

requirements.text: Verify that data minimization ensures the minimal amount of data is exposed during processing, and ensure that data is encrypted immediately after use or as soon as feasible.
requirements.proof: tools/check-tenancy.mjs (the `tenancy` validate-chain step; its factory red-proof is tests/gates/check-tenancy.test.mjs)
requirements.note: Control: validate step `tenancy` (node tools/check-tenancy.mjs) — audit value-capture closure against tools/pii-columns.json and tools/audit-columns.json. The minimization half has real base-tree machinery on one processing path: the audit trail records WHICH columns changed and never their values by default; capturing a value is a reviewed tools/audit-columns.json entry, and the `tenancy` step refuses outright a capture of any tools/pii-columns.json column, an undeclared capture, and a stale declaration naming a column no trigger passes (checkCaptureLists closes both ways). Wire strings are bounded (the dto-bounds closure) and lists keyset-limited. The `data-flow` step is NOT a processing-time control and is not claimed as one here: it closes what survives an account's deletion and what an export projects, and cannot tell ciphertext from plaintext. The encrypt-immediately half is module-deep only: when the e2ee module is enabled, sealing happens at the screen so the server never holds plaintext for module-encrypted features; outside them, data processed server-side is plaintext in memory and in Postgres, protected by RLS and the platform's at-rest encryption rather than by prompt re-encryption, and no control measures how long plaintext lives during processing.

requirements.text: Verify that only the latest recommended versions of the TLS protocol are enabled, such as TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3. The latest version of the TLS protocol must be the preferred option.
requirements.negativeProof: No TLS listener or termination configuration exists anywhere in the tree: web responses are terminated by Vercel's edge and the database/auth API by Supabase's gateway, and neither platform exposes a repo-side protocol-version surface a gate could read. No gate enforces this absence; it is an architectural fact of the managed-serverless deployment.
requirements.note: TLS protocol version selection happens at the managed platforms' terminating edges, so there is no artefact in this tree that could be held to 'TLS 1.2/1.3 only, latest preferred' — the harness could not ship this control even if it wanted to. Verifying the deployed endpoints would require a live handshake probe, which is exactly the kind of network-resolving check the harness's hermeticity rule refuses; the operator verifies their deployed hostnames with an external TLS scanner on their own cadence.

requirements.text: Verify that only recommended cipher suites are enabled, with the strongest cipher suites set as preferred. L3 applications must only support cipher suites which provide forward secrecy.
requirements.negativeProof: Same absence as 12.1.1: no TLS termination surface exists in the tree, and neither Vercel nor Supabase exposes cipher-suite configuration to the repository. No gate enforces the absence.
requirements.note: Cipher-suite selection, including the L3 forward-secrecy clause, is a property of the platforms' terminating edges and is not configurable from anything this tree contains. The residual is the same as 12.1.1: only an external scan of the deployed endpoints can evidence this, and that is the operator's act, not a gate's.

requirements.text: Verify that the application validates that mTLS client certificates are trusted before using the certificate identity for authentication or authorization.
requirements.negativeProof: No code path in the generated system reads, trusts, or derives identity from a TLS client certificate: caller identity is a GoTrue JWT verified server-side via getUser()/getClaims() (template/base/.claude/rules/security-invariants.md) and authorization is RLS keyed on auth.uid(). No gate asserts this absence — it is a fact about the tree, machine-checked by nothing.
requirements.note: The requirement is conditional on an application using mTLS certificate identity, and this application uses none — its authorization boundary is RLS over verified JWTs, enforced in one place for both surfaces. If a consumer adds an mTLS surface (for example a partner API behind a terminating proxy), nothing in the harness validates the trust chain for them; the requirement becomes live and unowned at that moment.

requirements.text: Verify that proper certification revocation, such as Online Certificate Status Protocol (OCSP) Stapling, is enabled and configured.
requirements.negativeProof: Certificate lifecycle — issuance, renewal, revocation, stapling — is performed entirely by the platforms that terminate TLS (Vercel, Supabase); no certificate or revocation configuration exists in the tree, and no gate enforces the absence.
requirements.note: OCSP stapling is a property of the terminating server, which this repository does not run and cannot configure. Evidencing it requires inspecting a live handshake, which the hermeticity rule refuses to build into a gate; the operator inherits whatever revocation posture their platform ships and can only verify it externally.

requirements.text: Verify that Encrypted Client Hello (ECH) is enabled in the application's TLS settings to prevent exposure of sensitive metadata, such as the Server Name Indication (SNI), during TLS handshake processes.
requirements.negativeProof: ECH is negotiated between the client, the DNS HTTPS record, and the terminating edge — all owned by the platforms and the operator's DNS, none represented by any artefact in this tree. No gate enforces the absence.
requirements.note: The application has no TLS settings of its own in which ECH could be enabled; the capability depends on the CDN edge and on HTTPS DNS records at the operator's registrar/DNS provider. This is the row least reachable from a code tree in the whole chapter, and it is recorded as such rather than mapped to something adjacent.

requirements.text: Verify that TLS is used for all connectivity between a client and external facing, HTTP-based services, and does not fall back to insecure or unencrypted communications.
requirements.proof: apps/web/e2e/security-headers.spec.ts (quality-gate.yml job web-e2e, run by tools/check-web-e2e.mjs) + tests/gates/check-security-headers.test.mjs (RED: HSTS max-age weakened) + tests/gates/check-expo-policy.test.mjs (RED: NSAllowsArbitraryLoads / non-loopback ATS domain / usesCleartextTraffic incl. plugin entry / non-https extra.apiOrigin)
requirements.note: Control: expo-policy + security-headers (validate chain). The harness holds the no-fallback half it can see. Mobile: the expo-policy chain step (tools/check-expo-policy.mjs) asserts over the RESOLVED Expo config (`expo config --json --type public`) that NSAllowsArbitraryLoads is banned, ATS exception domains are loopback-only (localhost / 127.0.0.1), usesCleartextTraffic is banned everywhere including plugin-injected entries, and extra.apiOrigin is https-or-loopback; each refusal has a named RED test in tests/gates/check-expo-policy.test.mjs. Web: the security-headers chain step (tools/check-security-headers.mjs) evaluates apps/web/lib/security-headers.ts by value against tools/security-headers.json, which pins strict-transport-security to max-age=63072000; includeSubDomains; preload (a weakened max-age is a proven RED), and the web-e2e lane spec asserts a strict-transport-security header containing includeSubDomains reaches a real browser response — the spec checks presence and the includeSubDomains directive, not the full value; the by-value pin is the static gate. The @app/env client schema additionally refuses any non-https public origin (loopback http:// is the single, deliberate local-dev exception). The residuals keep this partial: the gates prove committed configuration and module values, never the deployed listener — whether the platform edge accepts or redirects cleartext is Vercel and Supabase behaviour, and nothing in apps/web (proxy.ts, next.config.ts) redirects http to https itself; HSTS protects a browser only after first contact unless the operator actually submits the domain to the preload list, which is their act; and TLS itself on the wire is the platform, per 12.1.1.

requirements.text: Verify that external facing services use publicly trusted TLS certificates.
requirements.negativeProof: The tree contains no certificate material: no .pem/.crt/.key files exist anywhere under template/, the `secrets` chain step (tools/check-secrets.mjs, rule asc-api-key-material) reds any PEM private-key body committed to the tree, and the bash-guard credential-file-read rule blocks shell reads/copies of app-signing credential files (.keystore/.jks/.p8/.p12/google-services.json/GoogleService-Info.plist). Public certificate files are not themselves banned by any rule — the absence is a fact, not a gate. Both platforms provision publicly trusted certificates automatically at their edges; whether a deployed chain is publicly trusted is checkable only by a live probe, which the hermeticity rule refuses.
requirements.note: Vercel and Supabase issue publicly trusted certificates for their own and custom domains automatically, so on the default path this requirement is satisfied by the platform rather than by anything the harness ships — which is precisely why it cannot be graded as coverage. A consumer who fronts the app with their own proxy or terminates TLS elsewhere takes the requirement with them, and no artefact here would notice.

requirements.text: Verify that an encrypted protocol such as TLS is used for all inbound and outbound connections to and from the application, including monitoring systems, management tools, remote access and SSH, middleware, databases, mainframes, partner systems, or external APIs. The server must not fall back to insecure or unencrypted protocols.
requirements.proof: packages/platform/env/src/index.test.ts ('rejects a cleartext origin unless it is loopback') + packages/platform/env/src/optional.test.ts ('rejects a non-https REST URL')
requirements.note: Control: unit (Stop chain) — the @app/env origin schemas, proven refusing by their vitest suites. The outbound channels the generated system actually has are pinned to encrypted transport at boot: every public origin (Supabase URL, web origin, on both surfaces) must match the https-only ORIGIN_PATTERN in @app/env client.ts, with loopback http:// (localhost / 127.0.0.1) as the single local-dev exception, and the optional Upstash REST endpoint is refused unless https:// — both refusals are proven by named, can-fail vitest tests riding the Stop-chain `unit` step (also the `unit` CI job). The mobile tRPC origin (extra.apiOrigin) is held https-or-loopback by the separate expo-policy chain step (12.2.1). The residuals are why this is partial and not covered: SUPABASE_DB_URL is validated for postgres:// / postgresql:// scheme only — nothing enforces sslmode, so the one direct database channel could be configured without TLS and every gate would stay green; inbound TLS is the platforms (12.1.1); the platforms own internal hops, monitoring, and management planes are invisible from this tree; nothing reds a client that disables certificate validation (12.3.2); and most of the requirement enumerated surface (SSH, middleware, mainframes, partner systems) simply does not exist in the generated system.

requirements.text: Verify that TLS clients validate certificates received before communicating with a TLS server.
requirements.note: Every TLS client in the generated system — undici fetch under Node, supabase-js, the browser, the mobile runtime — validates certificates by default, but a platform default is not a shipped control: nothing in the write-guard rules, the validate chain, or CI reds NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED=0 in an environment block, or a rejectUnauthorized: false / permissive-agent option in code, so a consumer could disable validation and stay green everywhere. This is a coverable gap in the harness's own boundary — a write-guard rule plus a tree-wide check is the obvious shape — and it is graded not-covered rather than dressed up as a default.

requirements.text: Verify that TLS or another appropriate transport encryption mechanism used for all connectivity between internal, HTTP-based services within the application, and does not fall back to insecure or unencrypted communications.
requirements.negativeProof: The generated system has no internal HTTP service tier: apps/web is a single Next.js deployment that itself serves the API (app/api/trpc/[trpc]/route.ts mounts @app/api in-process via fetchRequestHandler), so web-to-API calls are in-process dispatch rather than network hops. The outbound HTTP the system does make is all to external, public https endpoints — Supabase gateway (PostgREST/GoTrue and the ADR-governed delete-account Edge Function invoked through functions.invoke on that gateway) and the optional Upstash REST limiter — enumerated in tools/resilience.json; none is an internal service of the repository own making. No gate asserts this absence — the architecture and boundaries gates hold the import graph, not the network topology.
requirements.note: The source text of this requirement is itself slightly garbled ('mechanism used for all connectivity' — a verb is missing in the official document). It activates only when internal services exist, and the scaffold deliberately has none. A consumer who decomposes the monolith into internal services takes the requirement live, and nothing in the harness will hold those new links to TLS; platform-internal traffic inside Vercel and Supabase is the platforms' own and is not visible from this tree.

requirements.text: Verify that TLS connections between internal services use trusted certificates. Where internally generated or self-signed certificates are used, the consuming service must be configured to only trust specific internal CAs and specific self-signed certificates.
requirements.negativeProof: Same absence as 12.3.3: no internal service-to-service TLS connection exists for which a trust store could be pinned, and no CA or self-signed certificate material exists in the tree (no .pem/.crt/.key files under template/). A committed private-key body would red the `secrets` chain step (asc-api-key-material) and app-signing credential files cannot be read from an agent shell (bash-guard credential-file-read), but public certificate files are not banned by any rule — the absence is a fact, not a gate.
requirements.note: There is no internal certificate estate here to trust or mis-trust; the trust decisions the system does make are the platform defaults of its https clients (see 12.3.2, graded not-covered for exactly the enforcement this row would also need). If a consumer introduces internal services with a private CA, the pinning discipline this row asks for is entirely theirs.

requirements.text: Verify that services communicating internally within a system (intra-service communications) use strong authentication to ensure that each endpoint is verified. Strong authentication methods, such as TLS client authentication, must be employed to ensure identity, using public-key infrastructure and mechanisms that are resistant to replay attacks. For microservice architectures, consider using a service mesh to simplify certificate management and enhance security.
requirements.negativeProof: There is no intra-service communication in the generated system — no microservices, no mesh, no service-to-service endpoints of the repository's own making (see 12.3.3's negative proof for the single-deployment architecture). No gate asserts the absence.
requirements.note: The nearest shipped fact is deliberately not claimed as coverage: the one elevated cross-boundary call path (the service_role key inside ADR-governed Supabase Edge Functions, reaching tables only through explicit per-table grants) is an authorization control, not endpoint authentication, and TLS client authentication exists nowhere in the system. A consumer moving to a microservice architecture inherits this requirement whole, mesh decision included.

requirements.text: Verify that all communication needs for the application are documented. This must include external services which the application relies upon and cases where an end user might be able to provide an external location to which the application will then connect.
requirements.note: tools/resilience.json is the reviewed outbound-seam register: every outbound-transport construction site (tRPC client, server-side fetch, supabase-js factory, Edge Function) needs a row and no row may outlive its site, closed both ways by tools/check-resilience.mjs — so the application's outbound communication surface is documented as gate-enforced data rather than prose. The honest residuals: the register documents outbound RUNTIME seams only — inbound needs, build/deploy-time services (EAS, Vercel, GitHub Actions, npm) and platform-internal hops (Supavisor, PostgREST) are not rows; and the scaffold has no feature where an end user supplies an external location, so that clause is unexercised rather than addressed. The register is seeded (the consumer's seams are theirs to grow); coverage of consumer additions is forced by the closure, not by this row.

requirements.text: Verify that for each service the application uses, the documentation defines the maximum number of concurrent connections (e.g., connection pool limits) and how the application behaves when that limit is reached, including any fallback or recovery mechanisms, to prevent denial of service conditions.
requirements.note: No artefact defines per-service maximum concurrent connections or documented at-limit behaviour. What exists nearby is narrower and deliberately not claimed: tools/db-limits.json records that connection count is bounded by Supavisor's pool size (platform configuration) and records WHY a role-level CONNECTION LIMIT would be inert here (it applies at login and the client roles never log in), and the rate limiter's degrade ladder (fail-open to an in-process limiter) is documented in tools/resilience.json and its ADR — but no pool number, per-service connection ceiling, or at-limit fallback is defined anywhere. The harness could seed such a register (the resilience/db-limits pattern is the shape), so this is not-covered rather than not-applicable.

requirements.text: Verify that the application documentation defines resource‑management strategies for every external system or service it uses (e.g., databases, file handles, threads, HTTP connections). This should include resource‑release procedures, timeout settings, failure handling, and where retry logic is implemented, specifying retry limits, delays, and back‑off algorithms. For synchronous HTTP request–response operations it should mandate short timeouts and either disable retries or strictly limit retries to prevent cascading delays and resource exhaustion.
requirements.note: tools/resilience.json documents, per outbound seam, timeout settings, retry counts, back-off and a written failure-handling rationale, and tools/check-resilience.mjs refuses both an undeclared seam and a posture claim the code does not implement (a non-null timeoutMs requires AbortSignal.timeout in the named file; a declared absence is legal only with a written why). The shipped posture matches the requirement's synchronous-HTTP guidance: retries are 0 on every seeded seam with the reason recorded, and the one server-to-server fetch (the rate limiter) carries a 1s deadline. The database half is tools/db-limits.json — per-role statement/idle-in-transaction/lock timeouts asserted by tools/check-db-limits.mjs, including the PostgREST reload that makes them bind. Residual: resource-release procedures for file handles and threads are absent because the serverless model holds none — an absence, not documentation — and connection-pool limits are undocumented (see 13.1.2), which is why this is partial.

requirements.text: Verify that the application's documentation defines the secrets that are critical for the security of the application and a schedule for rotating them, based on the organization's threat model and business requirements.
requirements.note: env.example and @app/env document WHICH secret-bearing variables each surface requires, and the shipped doctrine records where credentials live (only the EAS/CI/Supabase/Vercel secret stores), but no artefact classifies secrets by security criticality or defines a rotation schedule. The schedule itself is an organisation threat-model decision, yet the register that would carry it — a reviewed row per secret with a dated disposition and a lapse check, the tools/support-register.json shape the harness already uses elsewhere — is seedable and has not been seeded, so the row is not-covered rather than not-applicable.

requirements.text: Verify that communications between backend application components that don't support the application's standard user session mechanism, including APIs, middleware, and data layers, are authenticated. Authentication must use individual service accounts, short-term tokens, or certificate-based authentication and not unchanging credentials such as passwords, API keys, or shared accounts with privileged access.
requirements.note: The standard backend path authenticates with short-term verified tokens: every data-layer call runs as the `authenticated` role under a GoTrue JWT (auth.uid() resolves from request.jwt.claims), every RLS target ships policies TO authenticated with REVOKE ALL FROM anon and service_role (tools/check-rls-manifest.mjs closes policy to grant; supabase/tests/rls_structure.test.sql asserts the REVOKE took), and server-side verification is pinned to getUser()/getClaims() by the no-unverified-session ESLint rule that reds getSession() (tools/eslint-rules/index.mjs, wired in eslint.config.mjs). What the canary proves, stated precisely: tests/rls/cross-tenant-isolation.test.ts drives valid tokens for two tenants and an anonymous client through PostgREST on every db reset — cross-tenant reads return the empty set, smuggled writes are refused, and the anonymous client reads zero rows and cannot execute a tenancy RPC. It does NOT exercise a forged or expired token; that refusal is GoTrue/PostgREST JWT verification, delegated to the vendor and untested in this tree. Why partial and not covered: the requirement forbids unchanging credentials, and the scaffold's backend hops carry three — the service-role key (bounded to ADR-governed Edge Functions by the service-role-edge-functions-only lint rule and REVOKE ALL by default, but static), the Upstash REST token the rate limiter sends on every check (a static API key), and the publishable anon key every client presents; and platform-internal hops (Supavisor to Postgres, PostgREST) authenticate with the vendor's own mechanisms outside this tree's reach.

requirements.text: Verify that communications between backend application components, including local or operating system services, APIs, middleware, and data layers, are performed with accounts assigned the least necessary privileges.
requirements.note: Least privilege at the data layer is structural: every table ships ENABLE + FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY with per-operation policies TO authenticated, explicit per-operation grants beside the policies, and REVOKE ALL from service_role — so the one bypass-privileged account reaches nothing until a later ADR'd migration grants a specific table and operation. tools/check-rls-manifest.mjs closes policy to grant, and the pgTAP plus supabase-js isolation twins prove the boundary on every db reset. Per-role resource ceilings (tools/db-limits.json, asserted by tools/check-db-limits.mjs) bound the same accounts. Residual: the requirement spans ALL backend components including local and operating-system services — the platforms' own service accounts (Supavisor, PostgREST, the Vercel runtime, the Upstash token's scope) sit outside this tree and remain the operator's evidence.

requirements.text: Verify that if a credential has to be used for service authentication, the credential being used by the consumer is not a default credential (e.g., root/root or admin/admin).
requirements.note: The scaffold defines no service credential values in-tree: secrets arrive as injected environment (shape-validated per surface by @app/env), production Supabase keys are platform-generated per project, and the secrets gate plus the guard rules keep credential values out of the repository. But nothing machine-checks that a credential a consumer configures is not a default one, and the local development stack does run on the Supabase CLI's well-known local defaults (local-only; never reachable from production configuration). A default-credential deny pattern in tools/secret-patterns.json is a shippable check the harness does not ship, so this is not-covered; provisioning non-default production credentials is the running organisation's act in the platform consoles.

requirements.text: Verify that an allowlist is used to define the external resources or systems with which the application is permitted to communicate (e.g., for outbound requests, data loads, or file access). This allowlist can be implemented at the application layer, web server, firewall, or a combination of different layers.
requirements.note: Two client layers carry enforced allowlists, with the enforcement stated at its true width. Browser tier: tools/security-headers.json requires 'self' in connect-src (cspRequiredTokens) and bans the '*' token in connect-src and default-src (cspBannedTokens), value-diffed by tools/check-security-headers.mjs against what the evaluated apps/web/lib/security-headers.ts actually returns; the shipped directive is `connect-src 'self' <supabase REST origin> <supabase WS origin>` — a reviewed list — but the gate pins the PRESENCE of 'self' and the ABSENCE of the wildcard, not the membership, so a consumer appending a further host (or a scheme-source such as https:) is not a red; the list is reviewed by code review, the wildcard is refused by the gate. Mobile tier: transport is pinned by the expo-policy gate over the RESOLVED config (no NSAllowsArbitraryLoads, ATS exceptions loopback-only, cleartext banned, https-or-loopback apiOrigin) — a transport-class allowlist, not a host list. Server side is the honest gap: tools/resilience.json allowlists which FILES may construct outbound transport (both-ways closure), not which destination hosts a Server Action or Edge Function may reach, and no egress firewall exists in the scaffold's platform posture — so an allowlist exists and is gate-backed at the client layers and is absent at server egress, hence partial.

requirements.text: Verify that the web or application server is configured with an allowlist of resources or systems to which the server can send requests or load data or files from.
requirements.note: This row's subject is server-side egress specifically, and it is not covered: Vercel serverless functions and Supabase Edge Functions have unrestricted outbound network access in this scaffold, and no application-layer fetch wrapper pins destinations. The nearest shipped control is deliberately not claimed — tools/check-resilience.mjs closes outbound construction SITES (which files may open transport), never destinations, and reading a site census as a destination allowlist would be exactly the inflation this register refuses. An application-layer destination allowlist is buildable on the existing seam pattern, so not-covered rather than not-applicable.

requirements.text: Verify that where the application connects to separate services, it follows the documented configuration for each connection, such as maximum parallel connections, behavior when maximum allowed connections is reached, connection timeouts, and retry strategies.
requirements.note: The gate binds code to documentation in exactly the direction this row asks: a seam's posture claims must be backed by the symbols that implement them (a declared non-null timeoutMs requires AbortSignal.timeout in that file; a declared absence needs a written why), so the implementation cannot silently drift from its documented connection configuration. The database half is the same shape — tools/check-db-limits.mjs asserts every documented role-by-knob timeout is SET by a migration at or under its ceiling, including the PostgREST schema-cache reload without which ALTER ROLE settings never reach API traffic. Residuals: maximum parallel connections and at-limit behaviour are not documented (13.1.2) and therefore cannot be followed; and the closure covers the gate's seam taxonomy (tRPC client, server fetch, supabase-js factory, Edge Function) — a transport shape outside it (a raw WebSocket, a direct Postgres driver) would first need the gate to learn it.

requirements.text: Verify that a secrets management solution, such as a key vault, is used to securely create, store, control access to, and destroy backend secrets. These could include passwords, key material, integrations with databases and third-party systems, keys and seeds for time-based tokens, other internal secrets, and API keys. Secrets must not be included in application source code or included in build artifacts. For an L3 application, this must involve a hardware-backed solution such as an HSM.
requirements.note: The not-in-source half is enforced in depth: the hermetic secrets gate (tools/check-secrets.mjs) scans every tracked file with self-testing patterns held in rule-id lockstep with .gitleaks.toml (scanning zero files is a FAIL), the gitleaks CI job re-scans full history after push, and guard rules deny both the writes that create key material (hardcoded-key-material, expo-public-secret-name, next-public-secret-name — the two inlined-bundle prefixes refuse secret-shaped names outright) and the reads that leak it (read-env-file, credential-file-read, expo-token-leak). The vault half is posture rather than machinery: doctrine places secrets only in the EAS/CI/Supabase/Vercel secret stores and denies them from shell and repo, but whether the consumer actually manages secrets in a vault — and the L3 clause's hardware-backed HSM, which no platform in this stack offers to the application — is operator configuration no gate here can see. Built artifacts themselves are not post-build-scanned; the gate runs on the tree that produces them.

requirements.text: Verify that access to secret assets adheres to the principle of least privilege.
requirements.note: The slice of this requirement the harness can own — the coding agent's and the codebase's access to secrets — is enforced: the bash/write guards deny reading .env files (read-env-file), sourcing them (source-env-file), and reading or copying signing material and store credentials (credential-file-read, expo-token-leak, eas-credentials), all proven fireable by the hook-contract test; @app/env validates environment per surface so each surface receives only its declared variables; and the service-role key is reachable only inside ADR-governed Edge Functions (the exports-walls/boundaries closure keeps its factory off every client barrel). The larger half is the organisation's: who in the org can read the Vercel/EAS/Supabase/CI secret stores is IAM on platforms this tree cannot see, so the row cannot rise above partial.

requirements.text: Verify that all cryptographic operations are performed using an isolated security module (such as a vault or hardware security module) to securely manage and protect key material from exposure outside of the security module.
requirements.note: No vault or HSM performs this application's cryptographic operations: JWT verification runs in the serverless process (getClaims against the project's published key), invitation-token digests (pg_catalog.sha256) run inside Postgres, and neither Vercel nor Supabase offers an HSM surface a function or migration could reach. The opt-in e2ee module changes WHERE crypto happens rather than satisfying this row: key material is born and held client-side — on web through WebCrypto behind the one-door CryptoProvider, with RecipientWrap/Recovery/DeviceSync shipped in the module; on mobile only after the consumer applies docs/modules/e2ee/mobile-provider.patch.md (the expo-secure-store KeystoreAdapter is a documented patch, not shipped code) — which keeps keys off the server but is not an isolated security module performing the operations. Stated for context, conditional on enabling the module, and deliberately not claimed as coverage. An external KMS integration is buildable at the consumer boundary; nothing here ships one.

requirements.text: Verify that secrets are configured to expire and be rotated based on the application's documentation.
requirements.note: No expiry or rotation machinery exists for backend secrets: the service-role key, the Upstash token, and CI credentials (EXPO_TOKEN, deploy tokens) are static until a human rotates them in the platform consoles, and the rotation schedule this row says to follow does not exist (13.1.4 is not-covered). What IS short-lived — GoTrue access tokens under the reviewed auth-posture floors — is the user session layer, which is not this row's subject. A reviewed rotation register with a dated lapse check is a shape the harness already uses elsewhere (the reviewedUntil pattern riding the scheduled floor-review job), so shipping the documentation-and-lapse half is possible; performing rotation remains the running organisation's act, which is why the boundary is organisation and the outcome not-covered.

requirements.text: Verify that the application is deployed either without any source control metadata, including the .git or .svn folders, or in a way that these folders are inaccessible both externally and to the application itself.
requirements.negativeProof: The deployment surface this requirement configures against is absent: the web artefact is Vercel's compiled build output served by route, and the mobile artefact is an EAS/Expo bundle — neither serving model exposes a filesystem webroot containing the repository, so there is no .git folder in what serves. Stated honestly: this is an architectural absence, not an enforced one — no gate or workflow asserts it, so the negativeProof field is empty rather than dressed up — and a consumer who self-hosts (for example `next start` from a checkout behind their own web server) re-opens the question outside this register's sight.

Stated honestly: this is an architectural absence, not an enforced one — no gate or workflow asserts it, so the negativeProof field is empty rather than dressed up — and a consumer who self-hosts (for example `next start` from a checkout behind their own web server) re-opens the question outside this register's sight.

requirements.text: Verify that debug modes are disabled for all components in production environments to prevent exposure of debugging features and information leakage.
requirements.note: Debug-mode disablement currently rests on framework construction, not on a harness control: Next.js production builds strip the dev overlay and React development mode (the build gate runs the production compile), and Expo release builds exclude the dev menu. But no gate asserts the DEPLOYED environment's posture — NODE_ENV, a consumer-added DEBUG flag, a verbose logger, or a source-map exposure choice would land unexamined — and per the register's rule a framework default that nothing asserts is not a control. The scaffold ships no debug endpoints of its own. Asserting production posture at deploy time is buildable on the existing deploy-record channel, so not-covered rather than not-applicable.

requirements.text: Verify that web servers do not expose directory listings to clients unless explicitly intended.
requirements.negativeProof: There is no directory-listing surface to configure: Next.js serves compiled routes and files under public/ by exact path, PostgREST serves tables rather than files, Supabase Storage is disabled in the seeded config, and no general-purpose file server with a document root ships in the tree — the misconfiguration class requires a surface the scaffold does not produce. Nothing enforces the absence (no gate asserts it), and a consumer who fronts the app with their own reverse proxy, enables public storage buckets, or self-hosts acquires the question anew.
requirements.note: There is no directory-listing surface to configure: Next.js serves compiled routes and files under public/ by exact path, PostgREST serves tables rather than files, Supabase Storage is disabled in the seeded config, and no general-purpose file server with a document root ships in the tree — the misconfiguration class requires a surface the scaffold does not produce. Nothing enforces the absence (no gate asserts it), and a consumer who fronts the app with their own reverse proxy, enables public storage buckets, or self-hosts acquires the question anew.

requirements.text: Verify that using the HTTP TRACE method is not supported in production environments, to avoid potential information leakage.
requirements.negativeProof: The scaffold configures no HTTP server on which TRACE could be enabled: method handling is per-route (Next.js route handlers export named methods and the framework refuses the rest), and the terminating servers in the deployment model are the platforms' own (Vercel's edge, Supabase's gateway/PostgREST), whose method posture is vendor-operated and not assertable from this tree — a live probe against the deployed origin is refused by the hermeticity rule, and no in-tree configuration key exists that could flip it either way. Two edges stated: the web-e2e lane (apps/web/e2e/*.spec.ts, run by tools/check-web-e2e.mjs against a local `next start`) could assert the Next server's OWN response to a TRACE request and does not, which matters only for a self-hosted deployment where that server terminates; and the platform's production method posture is the operator's evidence to collect. Recorded as an absent configuration surface rather than a satisfied requirement.

Two edges stated: the web-e2e lane (apps/web/e2e/*.spec.ts, run by tools/check-web-e2e.mjs against a local `next start`) could assert the Next server's OWN response to a TRACE request and does not, which matters only for a self-hosted deployment where that server terminates; and the platform's production method posture is the operator's evidence to collect. Recorded as an absent configuration surface rather than a satisfied requirement.

requirements.text: Verify that documentation (such as for internal APIs) and monitoring endpoints are not exposed unless explicitly intended.
requirements.note: Control: route-manifest (tools/check-web-routes.mjs + tools/check-route-manifest.mjs) + contracts (tools/check-contract-drift.mjs action-inventory regen-diff). 'Explicitly intended' is enforced as registration on two endpoint classes and NOT on a third. Pages: every web page must declare a page.meta.ts and the generated route table is regen-diffed both ways (tools/check-web-routes.mjs), every mobile screen registers in apps/mobile/src/routes.ts (tools/check-route-manifest.mjs), and chrome rides the reviewed allowlists (tools/web-route-allowlist.json, tools/route-allowlist.json) — an unregistered documentation PAGE is a red. tRPC procedures: the contracts step regen-diffs tools/generated/action-inventory.json against the live appRouter, so a new procedure that is not committed to the inventory reds. The uncovered class is Next.js Route Handlers (route.ts) — the natural home of a /api/health or /api/docs endpoint: tools/check-web-routes.mjs treats a route.ts as plumbing and its own test asserts that adding apps/web/app/api/health/route.ts is GREEN, and the tree already ships an unregistered handler (apps/web/app/api/csp-report/route.ts) beside the tRPC mount; no gate inventories handlers. Further residuals: Supabase's Data API serves PostgREST's OpenAPI description of the exposed schemas at its REST root by platform design (bounded to public/graphql_public by supabase/config.toml [api].schemas — audit, auth_trail and private are not exposed — but not disableable from this tree); Studio is a local development-stack surface, not part of the deployed artefact; and the opt-in observability module adds no inbound monitoring endpoint (it exports spans to an OTLP endpoint), so no shipped or module surface exposes one — a consumer-added one would land as a Route Handler, in the uncovered class. Partial for the page and procedure slice; the handler class is unenforced.

requirements.text: Verify that the application does not expose detailed version information of backend components.
requirements.note: The channel most likely to leak backend version detail — error responses — is closed by enforced discipline rather than convention: procedures and Server Actions return the ActionOutcome envelope with stable codes (the app-error-only ESLint rule reds a `throw` in apps/web/app/actions/**, packages/api/src/routers/** and the vertical DALs; tests/gates/eslint-custom-rules.test.mjs proves it fires), and packages/platform/supabase/src/errors.ts maps PostgREST failures to envelope kinds and DROPS the driver message/details/hint (verified in the file), so a Postgres or driver version string inside an exception does not reach the wire by the sanctioned path. The shipped apps/web/next.config.ts also sets poweredByHeader: false. Residuals, and why partial: no gate asserts the poweredByHeader key (verified: no tool references it), so a consumer edit could re-expose the framework banner unnoticed; platform-added response headers (Vercel's, Supabase's) are outside the tree; and a browser-side supabase-js read that bypasses the DAL mapper receives PostgREST's raw error body directly from the Data API.

requirements.text: Verify that the web tier is configured to only serve files with specific file extensions to prevent unintentional information, configuration, and source code leakage.
requirements.note: Regraded from not-applicable: the template DOES ship a served-verbatim file surface — apps/web/public/ (today holding only .well-known/security.txt) is served byte-for-byte by exact path with no extension restriction, and nothing in the chain enforces an extension allowlist over it (tools/check-security-headers.mjs and tools/check-framework-floor.mjs read the security.txt CONTENT; neither censuses the directory). What remains true is the architectural separation: the web tier serves compiled route output, /_next/static and public/ — source, configuration and migrations are not in the deployment's served set, so the classic leak class (a .env or .sql inside a document root) has no path in the Vercel/Next model, and the mobile artefact is an EAS bundle with no file-serving tier. But 'not-applicable' requires the surface to be absent, and public/ is a surface a consumer can drop any extension into unexamined; an allowlist gate over apps/web/public/ (the tools/expo-permissions.json shape, one directory over) is trivially shippable and is not shipped. A self-hosted deployment behind a general-purpose file server widens the question further.

requirements.text: Verify that all sensitive data created and processed by the application has been identified and classified into protection levels. This includes data that is only encoded and therefore easily decoded, such as Base64 strings or the plaintext payload inside a JWT. Protection levels need to take into account any data protection and privacy regulations and standards which the application is required to comply with.
requirements.note: Control: data-flow (tools/check-data-flow.mjs, validate-chain step `data-flow`). The identification half is machine-closed for the schema's personal data: the data-flow step replays supabase/migrations/, walks the foreign-key graph out from auth.users, and forces every subject-data link into exactly one reviewed bucket in tools/data-flow.json (erased/severed/blocking/unreachable, plus the export projection), closed in BOTH directions — an unreviewed surviving column reds and a reviewed entry the schema no longer has reds too. What does not ship is the half the requirement actually names: classification into PROTECTION LEVELS. No protection-level taxonomy exists anywhere in the tree; tools/pii-columns.json says of itself that it 'is not a general PII inventory and does not pretend to be one' (it is the deny-list for one mechanism, audit value capture); and no register maps data classes to the regulations a consumer's product must comply with. Sensitive data OUTSIDE the schema — encoded payloads, JWT claims, anything a consumer's features create — is identified by nothing. The classification act, and its regulatory mapping, is the consumer's.

requirements.text: Verify that all sensitive data protection levels have a documented set of protection requirements. This must include (but not be limited to) requirements related to general encryption, integrity verification, retention, how the data is to be logged, access controls around sensitive data in logs, database-level encryption, privacy and privacy-enhancing technologies to be used, and other confidentiality requirements.
requirements.note: Fragments of the required documentation exist and are enforced piecewise — .claude/rules/encryption.md states the mandatory shape of any client-side encryption (AEAD only, versioned envelope, AAD binding row identity, wrapped-DEK erasure), docs/adr/20260202-audit-trail.md fixes how sensitive columns may and may not be logged, and tools/data-flow.json retained[] rows carry retention text per surviving column — but there is no per-protection-level documented requirement set, because no protection-level scheme ships (see 14.1.1), and no gate's subject is the existence or completeness of such documentation. The opt-in e2ee module's README documents the encryption requirements and their limits for encrypted features, conditional on the module being enabled. The harness COULD seed a protection-levels register with per-level requirements, which is why this is not-covered rather than not-applicable; today the documentation act belongs to the consumer building a product on the scaffold.
