requirements.text: Verify that sensitive data is only sent to the server in the HTTP message body or header fields, and that the URL and query string do not contain sensitive information, such as an API key or session token.
requirements.note: Control: auth-posture (tools/check-auth-posture.mjs via tools/lib/session-transport.mjs, validate-chain step `auth-posture`). The examples the requirement names never ride a URL, and the wiring that keeps it so is gated: the auth-posture step's session-transport closure (tools/lib/session-transport.mjs, called from check-auth-posture.mjs) asserts the browser session lands in the cookie jar with the reviewed attributes (the supabase-js DEFAULT is localStorage, and the shipped-then-fixed localStorage client is this closure's own recorded defect — tests/gates/session-transport.test.mjs proves that exact wiring reds), and the mobile tRPC client resolves the bearer token per request into the Authorization header inside httpBatchLink's headers() callback (apps/mobile/src/lib/trpc/client.ts); the publishable key rides supabase-js headers. The residual is structural and stated because it is the requirement's general clause: the mobile client's httpBatchLink sends QUERY-procedure input as a GET query string and no methodOverride is set anywhere in the tree (verified by search) — the seeded query inputs are ids and cursors, but a consumer who puts sensitive data into a query-procedure input has put it into the URL and every access log, and no gate's subject is URL or query-string content. The web app has no browser-side tRPC client (its /api/trpc route is a fetchRequestHandler), so the same residual applies to any client a consumer adds there.

requirements.text: Verify that the application prevents sensitive data from being cached in server components, such as load balancers and application caches, or ensures that the data is securely purged after use.
requirements.note: Control: security-headers (tools/check-security-headers.mjs, validate-chain step `security-headers`). The gate EVALUATES apps/web/lib/security-headers.ts and diffs the values it actually returns against tools/security-headers.json, including the authenticatedCache half: every /api/:path* response carries cache-control: private, no-store plus a Vary naming Cookie AND x-org-id (wired in next.config.ts headers(), which runs whether or not middleware does), so a shared cache — CDN, load balancer, reverse proxy — is told to store nothing from the tenant-bearing API surface, and the same-URL-different-tenant edge-key case is closed; the registered red-proof includes 'authenticated responses becoming cacheable reds' and 'Vary losing x-org-id reds'. What the control does NOT reach: caches outside the tree (a deployer's CDN or proxy configuration can ignore or strip headers), server-rendered authenticated page HTML (which rests on Next's dynamic-render defaults nothing in the tree asserts), and the requirement's purge clause — no mechanism anywhere securely purges data already cached.

requirements.text: Verify that defined sensitive data is not sent to untrusted parties (e.g., user trackers) to prevent unwanted collection of data outside of the application's control.
requirements.note: Control: observability (tools/check-observability.mjs, validate-chain step `observability`). One subject-matched enforcement point and one weaker bound. The observability step licenses vendor-telemetry-SDK imports ONLY through the reviewed sinks[] register in tools/observability.json — seeded EMPTY, and each entry must import a listed vendor, reference a named redaction symbol in code, and carry a 40+ character reason (red-proofs in tests/gates/check-observability.test.mjs: undeclared static import, dynamic import()/require(), stale sink, missing redaction reference) — so a KNOWN vendor SDK cannot be quietly wired into either surface. It is a specifier detector, not an egress detector: a vendor absent from vendorSpecifiers, or a hand-rolled fetch()/sendBeacon() to a tracker endpoint, is not caught by it. The security-headers step bounds browser CSP connect-src only loosely — the reviewed policy REQUIRES the 'self' token and BANS a '*' token (tools/security-headers.json cspRequiredTokens/cspBannedTokens); it does NOT hold connect-src to a closed set by value, so the shipped 'self' + Supabase origin + websocket twin is what the source emits today, and a consumer adding a tracker origin to connect-src turns no gate red. Residuals: the mobile app has no CSP equivalent, so its egress discipline is the sink register and review alone; registering a sink or widening connect-src is a reviewed CODEOWNERS diff, not a refusal; the opt-in observability and crash-reporting modules add third-party sinks conditional on enablement (with redaction floors, but the vendor is then trusted with what passes them); and 'defined sensitive data' presupposes the 14.1.1 classification, which is the consumer's.

requirements.text: Verify that controls around sensitive data related to encryption, integrity verification, retention, how the data is to be logged, access controls around sensitive data in logs, privacy and privacy-enhancing technologies, are implemented as defined in the documentation for the specific data's protection level.
requirements.note: Control: tenancy (tools/check-tenancy.mjs, validate-chain step `tenancy`). The logging clauses are enforced for the schema the seed ships: the audit trail defaults to metadata (WHICH columns changed, never the values), the tenancy step reds any audit.write_row(...) trigger that captures a column listed in tools/pii-columns.json and reds a stale list entry (check-tenancy.mjs, the PII_COLUMNS block), and access control around sensitive data in logs is structural — the audit schema is absent from [api].schemas in supabase/config.toml, grants USAGE to no client role, and is append-only in four layers, proven live by supabase/tests/audit_immutability.test.sql under `supabase test db` in quality-gate.yml. Canary honesty: tests/gates/check-tenancy.test.mjs proves the audit-trigger closure, WHEN-clause/skipped-operation/BEFORE-trigger reds and the writer/reader posture reds, but carries NO red-proof for the pii-columns capture check itself — that check exists in the gate but its refusal is unproven by any registered canary (the only pii-columns canary, in check-data-flow.test.mjs, proves the lower-bound closure against the DSR buckets, a different property). The remaining clauses are graded down, not claimed: encryption and PETs arrive only with the opt-in e2ee module (RecipientWrap, Recovery, DeviceSync ports and rewrapItemKey ship implemented in the module, conditional on enablement and on features being written onto it — nothing encrypts by default); retention is implemented for the audit trail alone (14.2.7); and a requirement of the form 'implemented as defined in the documentation for the specific data's protection level' can be graded no higher than that documentation, which does not ship (14.1.2) — so the per-level implementation act is the consumer's.

requirements.text: Verify that caching mechanisms are configured to only cache responses which have the expected content type for that resource and do not contain sensitive, dynamic content. The web server should return a 404 or 302 response when a non-existent file is accessed rather than returning a different, valid file. This should prevent Web Cache Deception attacks.
requirements.note: Control: security-headers (tools/check-security-headers.mjs, validate-chain step `security-headers`). The gated stance for the seeded sensitive surface is stronger than cache-correctly — it is never-cache: /api/:path* is pinned to private, no-store with Vary Cookie/x-org-id, asserted by value with a red-proof for authenticated responses becoming cacheable, which removes the cache-deception primitive (a cache storing a sensitive dynamic response under a static-looking key) for the API surface. x-content-type-options: nosniff is pinned on every response, narrowing the content-type-confusion half. The 404 clause is only weakly touched: the route-manifest step's check-web-routes.mjs requires app/not-found.tsx, which makes the unmatched-route page the app's own rather than Next's built-in — it does not itself assert that a non-existent path returns 404 rather than a different valid file (Next's router does that by default for unmatched paths, and nothing in the tree asserts the path-confusion case, e.g. a catch-all segment serving a valid page under a static-looking suffix). What the tree does not and cannot assert: the CDN in front of a deployment — Vercel's cache keying, a consumer's proxy, per-content-type cache rules — is the deployer's configuration, and server-rendered authenticated pages rest on Next's dynamic no-store defaults that nothing in the tree asserts. A deployment-level Web Cache Deception test is the operator's to run.

requirements.text: Verify that the application only returns the minimum required sensitive data for the application's functionality. For example, only returning some of the digits of a credit card number and not the full number. If the complete data is required, it should be masked in the user interface unless the user specifically views it.
requirements.note: Field-level minimization and UI masking are per-feature product judgements no template can make in advance, and no gate's subject is response minimality. What exists nearby is deliberately not claimed as this control: wire strings are bounded (.max() on every contract, escapes reviewed in tools/dto-bounds-allow.json), the DSR export projects an explicit reviewed column list per table (tools/data-flow.json export.projection, closed both ways against the schema), and RLS bounds WHO can fetch a row — none of which minimizes WHICH sensitive fields a response carries or masks them in the UI. The seed holds no data of the credit-card class, but the requirement's subject is a discipline, not a datum, and the harness could ship a masking primitive and a projection-minimality pattern — hence not-covered rather than not-applicable. The minimization act is the consumer's per feature.

requirements.text: Verify that sensitive information is subject to data retention classification, ensuring that outdated or unnecessary data is deleted automatically, on a defined schedule, or as the situation requires.
requirements.note: Control: data-flow (tools/check-data-flow.mjs, validate-chain step `data-flow`). Automatic scheduled deletion ships for exactly one data class: the audit trail. audit.events is monthly-partitioned; supabase/migrations/20260202000000_audit.sql ships audit.drop_partitions_older_than(interval, default 24 months) and schedules it monthly via pg_cron in the same file — GUARDED, so on a stack without pg_cron the function exists, a NOTICE says to schedule it manually, and no schedule runs. The named control enforces the RECORD, not the schedule: the data-flow step closes tools/data-flow.json retained[] both ways against the schema, and the audit.events entry records retention 'with a bounded window' — it does not name the partition drop or a period, and the register carries no schedule field per column, so this is a reviewed reason-per-surviving-column, not a retention classification with periods. Honest limits: the drop job itself has no red-proof (the canary proves the register closure, not the deletion), and nothing else is automatic — invitations expire but 'nothing reaps expired rows' is recorded verbatim in the register, consumer content carries no retention classification, and no general retention scheduler ships. The opt-in e2ee module adds a crypto-shred lever (deleting a row's wrapped DEK renders its ciphertext permanently unreadable), conditional on enablement — an erasure lever, not a schedule, and the ciphertext bytes survive in the table and every backup.

requirements.text: Verify that sensitive information is removed from the metadata of user-submitted files unless storage is consented to by the user.
requirements.negativeProof: The generated system accepts no user-submitted files: `[storage] enabled = false` in supabase/config.toml and no upload surface exists anywhere in the tree. tools/check-essential-eight.mjs (the second script of the `docs-sync` validate-chain step) machine-asserts both halves — it reads config.toml and scans apps/web/app, apps/mobile/app, apps/mobile/src, packages/api/src and supabase/functions for the upload shape (multipart/form-data, .formData() File reads, Blob construction, createReadStream, DocumentPicker/expo-document-picker) on BOTH surfaces, and reds if an upload surface appears while the recorded negative proofs still stand.
requirements.note: The surface the requirement governs is absent by construction, so there is no file metadata to strip and nothing to consent to. The absence is enforced rather than assumed: the moment a consumer enables [storage] or adds a route/module matching the upload shape, the docs-sync step's negative-proof scan reds (red-proofs at tests/gates/check-essential-eight.test.mjs: '[storage] is ENABLED', 'a discovered upload surface reds naming the file', 'the upload scan covers BOTH surfaces') and forces the recorded absences to be re-graded rather than silently outlived. The detector is a shape list, not a semantic scan — multipart/form-data, .formData()+File, new Blob(, createReadStream(, DocumentPicker/expo-document-picker — so an upload built from expo-image-picker plus a base64/JSON body, or a supabase-js storage.from().upload() against an externally-enabled bucket, would pass it while [storage] stays false in the committed config.toml. At the point any upload surface appears, EXIF/metadata stripping becomes the consumer's build, and this row should be re-dispositioned in the same change.

requirements.text: Verify that authenticated data is cleared from client storage, such as the browser DOM, after the client or session is terminated. The 'Clear-Site-Data' HTTP response header field may be able to help with this but the client-side should also be able to clear up if the server connection is not available when the session is terminated.
requirements.note: The mechanics exist; the control does not. Each surface stores exactly one piece of authenticated data client-side — the session: web in the cookie jar (the auth-posture session-transport closure pins that store), mobile in LargeSecureStore (per-value AES-256-CTR key in the platform keychain, ciphertext in AsyncStorage, expo-secure-store import-walled to the host seam). supabase-js signOut removes the local session on both surfaces, and the mobile sign-out command's own comment records that it clears the keychain-backed store. But nothing HOLDS any of that: no test asserts client storage is empty after termination, no Clear-Site-Data header is sent anywhere in the tree (verified by search), and no gate's subject is post-termination state — the clearing is library behavior trusted, not a control enforced, and cached page state in the browser DOM after sign-out is governed by nothing. Two grades were defensible and the lower is taken per doctrine. A sign-out E2E asserting empty storage would be the cheapest honest upgrade.

requirements.text: Verify that the application sets sufficient anti-caching HTTP response header fields (i.e., Cache-Control: no-store) so that sensitive data is not cached in browsers.
requirements.note: Control: security-headers (tools/check-security-headers.mjs, validate-chain step `security-headers`). cache-control: private, no-store rides every /api/:path* response — the surface that carries tenant rows — and the gate asserts it by VALUE: check-security-headers.mjs evaluates apps/web/lib/security-headers.ts under Node type-stripping and diffs what it returns against the reviewed tools/security-headers.json authenticatedCache policy, with a registered red-proof for authenticated responses becoming cacheable. Partial rather than covered because the pinned surface is the API routes: server-rendered authenticated PAGE responses rest on Next's dynamic-render Cache-Control defaults, which nothing in the tree asserts, and a consumer who makes a sensitive page statically cacheable would turn no gate red. The header set is also advisory to the browser by nature — it instructs, it cannot verify.

requirements.text: Verify that data stored in browser storage (such as localStorage, sessionStorage, IndexedDB, or cookies) does not contain sensitive data, with the exception of session tokens.
requirements.note: Control: auth-posture (tools/check-auth-posture.mjs via tools/lib/session-transport.mjs, validate-chain step `auth-posture`). The seed keeps exactly one sensitive datum in browser storage — the session token, the requirement's own stated exception — and the harness pins even that to the cookie jar rather than localStorage: the session-transport closure exists because the supabase-js default IS localStorage and the scaffold once shipped that wiring, and its canary proves the localStorage-backed browser client reds against a cookie-reading server. Everything else the seed persists client-side is non-sensitive (command recents through the kv seam, corrupt-payload-tolerant). On mobile — outside this requirement's browser scope but the same intent — the session lives only in LargeSecureStore, with expo-secure-store restricted to the host seam by lint and depcruise. The honest residual: the gate pins the SESSION's store, not browser storage as a class — no scan refuses a consumer feature writing other sensitive data into localStorage, sessionStorage or IndexedDB, and such a write would pass every gate.

requirements.text: Verify that application documentation defines risk based remediation time frames for 3rd party component versions with vulnerabilities and for updating libraries in general, to minimize the risk from these components.
requirements.note: The harness DEFINES remediation time frames rather than leaving them to the consumer to write: tools/lib/deploy-record.mjs carries three windows (48 hours for a critical or known-exploited advisory in the production closure, two weeks for any other production advisory, one month for a development-scoped one) and the scheduled `patch-window` job in .github/workflows/deploy-record.yml judges deployments against them; tools/framework-floor.json bounds its own review window to 31 days; production-scope rows in tools/eol.json must carry a removalTarget release; and renovate.json sets minimumReleaseAge to 5 days for the general update cadence. Where the frames are actually written down, checked against the tree: the three windows are stated in prose only in tools/essential-eight.json (the PA-06, PA-07 and PA-10 rows' note/proof text), in the header comment of .github/workflows/deploy-record.yml and in tools/lib/deploy-record.mjs; docs/harness/gates-catalog.md documents the framework-floor 31-day review window and the eol register but does not mention `patch-window` or its windows at all, and no page under docs/ (harness, security, compliance) states a remediation time frame in prose. What is NOT here: the windows are ASD's verbatim numbers, not a risk assessment the consumer performed, so the 'risk based' half is inherited rather than derived; nothing in the tree records the consumer's own tolerance for a lower-severity advisory or for a general library refresh cadence beyond the Renovate age; and the enforcement of the windows is graded under 15.2.1, not here. Graded documentation tier because the requirement's subject is the documentation, and the harness's own documentation is the only artefact that states the frames in prose. The `patch-window` job is (schedule-gated), so this is proven periodically or per-touching-PR rather than on every commit.

requirements.text: Verify that an inventory catalog, such as software bill of materials (SBOM), is maintained of all third-party libraries in use, including verifying that components come from pre-defined, trusted, and continually maintained repositories.
requirements.note: The inventory half is real and proven: the `sbom-inventory` job in .github/workflows/osv-scan.yml runs `pnpm sbom --sbom-format cyclonedx --lockfile-only` daily and tools/check-sbom.mjs closes the emitted component set against pnpm-lock.yaml in both directions (a resolved package with no component reds, a component nothing resolves reds, zero components is a hard failure), and the artefact uploads only after it passes. The `ci-provenance` opt-in module adds a second SBOM plus build attestation, conditional on enablement. The second half of the requirement is NOT covered: nothing verifies that components come from pre-defined, trusted, continually maintained repositories — there is no scoped-registry configuration, no assertion that every lockfile resolution points at an expected registry host, and no maintenance-activity signal (the eol.json census reads only the npm `deprecated` flag; see 15.1.4 and 15.2.4). The inventory is also lockfile-derived, so it enumerates dependencies rather than the shipped bundle contents, and it is only as current as the last resolution. The `sbom-inventory` job is (schedule-gated), so this is proven periodically or per-touching-PR rather than on every commit.

requirements.text: Verify that the application documentation identifies functionality which is time-consuming or resource-demanding. This must include how to prevent a loss of availability due to overusing this functionality and how to avoid a situation where building a response takes longer than the consumer's timeout. Potential defenses may include asynchronous processing, using queues, and limiting parallel processes per user and per application.
requirements.note: Three reviewed registers together document the resource posture, and each is gate-closed so the documentation cannot silently fall behind the code: tools/rate-limit-budget.json maps every mutation the router exposes to a bucket with a written reason or a reasoned exemption (the `rate-limits` step reds an unmapped mutation and a stale mapping); tools/resilience.json records the timeout, retry and backoff posture of every outbound seam with a written why (the `resilience` step reds an undeclared seam or a claim the code does not carry); and tools/db-limits.json records the per-role statement_timeout, lock_timeout and idle_in_transaction_session_timeout ceilings plus the per-org quota shape (the `db-limits` step). docs/adr/20260203-resource-limits.md and docs/adr/20260204-rate-limiting.md carry the reasoning. Residual, stated plainly: these registers classify actions by RATE and outbound seams by TIMEOUT; nothing asks a consumer to identify a feature as time-consuming or CPU-heavy in its own right, no queue or asynchronous-processing pattern ships, the web function's own execution ceiling (the host's maxDuration) is not recorded anywhere in the tree, and Server Component render time has no budget. The rate-limit-budget artefact is also claimed by 15.2.2, for a different question (does the defence exist) — disclosed here rather than counted twice silently.

requirements.text: Verify that application documentation highlights third-party libraries which are considered to be "risky components".
requirements.note: tools/eol.json is a register of exactly the risky-component class ASVS names as 'unsupported, at the end-of-life stage': the `version-sync` step reads the npm registry's own `deprecated` message out of pnpm-lock.yaml (a committed third-party artefact, no live query), reds a deprecated resolution with no reviewed row and a row matching nothing the lockfile deprecates, recomputes each row's production/development scope from the lockfile rather than believing it, and requires a production-scope row to carry a reason and a removalTarget release. tools/support-register.json (vendor lifecycle statements for the online services and platforms) and tools/framework-floor.json (a major line with no floor row is judged unsupported) extend the same idea, and every row is write-guarded and CODEOWNERS-reviewed. Residual: the census sees only what npm marks deprecated at resolve time — a poorly maintained package that nobody deprecated, one with a history of significant vulnerabilities, or an abandoned transitive dependency is invisible to it, and there is no maintenance-activity or advisory-history signal; the register is only as fresh as the last resolution (hence the 31-day review window and the scheduled floor-review lapse check); and 'in the production dependency closure' is a ceiling on exposure, not a measurement of what the bundle ships.

requirements.text: Verify that application documentation highlights parts of the application where "dangerous functionality" is being used.
requirements.note: No documentation surface in the tree records where the ASVS-defined classes of dangerous functionality (deserialization of untrusted data, raw file or binary parsing, dynamic code execution, direct memory manipulation) are used, and no gate would notice one appearing in a consumer's feature. What the harness does hold is adjacent, and is recorded so it is not mistaken for coverage: tools/security-definer-allow.json is a gate-closed register (the `schema-rls` step) of every SECURITY DEFINER function — the one SQL construct that runs as its owner and bypasses the caller's policies — each with a reviewed reason, a pinned `SET search_path = ''` and no identity-shaped parameter; the RLS-bypassing service-role client is confined by the `service-role-edge-functions-only` lint rule to ADR-governed Edge Functions; and raw HTML rendering is banned outright by the `dangerously-set-inner-html` write-guard rule. Those are registers of PRIVILEGE, not of the parsing and execution classes this requirement means, and grading them as coverage would be reading an adjacent control as the requested one. A consumer adding a file-upload parser or a dynamic-code path has nowhere in this tree to declare it.

requirements.text: Verify that the application only contains components which have not breached the documented update and remediation time frames.
requirements.note: The `patch-window` job in .github/workflows/deploy-record.yml downloads the latest deploy-record manifest, joins the DEPLOYED resolution set against OSV advisory publication dates, and reds when an affected resolution is still deployed after the window (48 hours critical, two weeks production, one month development-scoped) has elapsed — judged against what is deployed, never against what main resolves today. Two clockless per-commit halves back it: the `version-sync` step holds every tools/framework-floor.json package at or above its patched release as read from the resolved lockfile (a transitive resolution below the floor reds too), and the `scan-pr` / `scan-full` OSV jobs catch newly introduced and standing advisories. Residual, and it is the channel's own honesty: patch-window is scheduled and network-bound by subject, so the verdict is periodic rather than per-commit; it measures only deployments that EMITTED a manifest through the deploy-record channel, and a console or CLI deploy outside it is invisible; the framework floor covers the packages listed in the floor file, not the whole tree; and 'updating libraries in general' beyond vulnerability windows rests on Renovate PRs being merged, which nothing in the tree measures. The `patch-window` job is (schedule-gated), so this is proven periodically or per-touching-PR rather than on every commit.

requirements.text: Verify that the application has implemented defenses against loss of availability due to functionality which is time-consuming or resource-demanding, based on the documented security decisions and strategies for this.
requirements.note: Four defences ship and each has a can-fail proof: the `rate-limits` step closes tools/rate-limit-budget.json against the generated action inventory in both directions and asserts both seams are wired (the tRPC host passes the rateLimit port; every budgeted Server Action calls enforceActionRateLimit), diffing bucket limits by VALUE against the code; the `db-limits` step holds per-role statement_timeout / lock_timeout / idle_in_transaction_session_timeout ceilings and the per-org quota trigger's fail-closed shape (FOR EACH STATEMENT with a transition table, never a RESTRICTIVE policy over a STABLE count); the `contracts` step requires every wire z.string() to carry .max(); and the `query-shapes` step requires every DAL read to be bounded, index-served and under the PostgREST max_rows ceiling. Residual: the rate limiter binds the two application seams only — a client posting straight to PostgREST with the publishable key, and sign-in/sign-up at GoTrue, are bounded only by the database ceilings; the limiter FAILS OPEN when its backend is unavailable (degrading to a per-instance limiter, which on a serverless host approaches no limit); no queue, worker or asynchronous-processing pattern ships for genuinely long-running work; and Edge Function and Server Component execution time is not budgeted. The rate-limit-budget artefact is also claimed by 15.1.3 for the documentation question — disclosed.

requirements.text: Verify that the production environment only includes functionality that is required for the application to function, and does not expose extraneous functionality such as test code, sample snippets, and development functionality.
requirements.note: Two steps address two halves of 'extraneous'. The `dead-code` step (`pnpm exec knip --strict`) reds unused files, exports and dependencies. Checked against the installed knip: `--strict` isolates workspaces and considers only direct dependencies; it is `--production` (not passed) that drops test files from the entry set, and knip.json lists test globs as entries — so in the mode the chain runs, test-only reachability DOES keep code alive, and docs/harness/gates-catalog.md's 'production mode' description of this step is not what the command does. That matters here because 'test code' is one of the requirement's named extraneous classes and the step as run does not distinguish it; the `build` step exports the mobile bundle and reds server markers, privileged DSN names and secret-shaped strings in the emitted client bundle (proven by tests/gates/build-check.test.mjs), so server-graph code cannot ride into the client artefact. Residual, and it is specific: the mobile app ships a development measurement screen, app/perf-harness.tsx, in the production route set behind an `if (!__DEV__)` guard that renders only an unavailability note — a reviewed tools/route-allowlist.json entry records why, but it IS development functionality present in the release binary, and no gate proves a dev-only route is absent from a release build; nothing asserts that Next.js development-only routes, test fixtures or the seeded exemplar vertical are excluded from a production deployment; and knip judges reachability, not whether reachable code is REQUIRED. The canary named proves the runner reds a failing step, not that a specific dev surface is caught.

requirements.text: Verify that third-party components and all of their transitive dependencies are included from the expected repository, whether internally owned or an external source, and that there is no risk of a dependency confusion attack.
requirements.note: No control in the tree asserts the source registry of any resolution. pnpm-workspace.yaml configures no scoped registry and pins no registry host; no gate reads the resolution URLs or integrity fields out of pnpm-lock.yaml to assert they point at an expected host; and although every internal package is meant to be declared with the `workspace:` protocol (which keeps pnpm from ever consulting a registry for an @app/* name), no gate enforces that protocol, so a mistyped internal specifier would resolve from the public registry if that scope were squatted. What narrows the window without addressing the requirement: CI installs with `--frozen-lockfile` (the `static` job), so a resolution cannot change without a lockfile diff; the `dependency-update` bash-guard rule denies `pnpm update` in-session so bumps arrive only as Renovate PRs; and the daily SBOM closure (15.1.2) proves the inventory matches the lockfile — none of which says where a component came from. Grading any of that as coverage would be reading pinning as provenance.

requirements.text: Verify that the application implements additional protections around parts of the application which are documented as containing "dangerous functionality" or using third-party libraries considered to be "risky components". This could include techniques such as sandboxing, encapsulation, containerization or network level isolation to delay and deter attackers who compromise one part of an application from pivoting elsewhere in the application.
requirements.note: Because 15.1.5 is not covered there is no documented set of dangerous-functionality sites to wrap, and nothing in the tree isolates a consumer-declared risky component (a production-scope tools/eol.json row carries a removal date, not a sandbox). The harness DOES isolate its own most dangerous capability, and it is recorded so it is not mistaken for this requirement: the RLS-bypassing service-role client is confined to Supabase Edge Functions (a separate Deno isolate) by the `service-role-edge-functions-only` lint rule, migrations REVOKE ALL from service_role so a function reaches a table only through an explicit ADR'd per-table grant, and the `boundaries`, `architecture` and `build` steps keep the factory structurally out of the mobile bundle. That is encapsulation of a PRIVILEGE the harness itself introduced, graded elsewhere; it is not additional protection around parsing, deserialization or dynamic-execution code, and it does not extend to anything a consumer adds. Graded consumer boundary because the sandboxing decision (a separate function, a separate service, network isolation) is one the consumer makes per feature.

requirements.text: Verify that the application only returns the required subset of fields from a data object. For example, it should not return an entire data object, as some individual fields should not be accessible to users.
requirements.note: Control: the security-reviewer verdict, demanded by the reviewer-verdicts Stop step. The pattern is taught and reviewed, not gate-enforced. The seeded notes vertical selects an explicit column constant (NOTE_COLUMNS), re-parses every row against the zod NoteRecord contract at the DAL's exit (rows are typed `unknown` at the port so the compiler cannot skip the parse), and returns a mapped DTO — and rows.test.ts asserts the projection equals the row schema's keys exactly and is not a wildcard, which is the canary named here and it covers the EXEMPLAR only. The security-reviewer agent's rubric bans `select('*')` and a raw row escaping past the row-to-DTO map on packages/verticals/*/src/data/** and packages/api/src/**, and the `reviewer-verdicts` Stop step reds a turn where a diff on those paths did not receive that reviewer's PASS; the torvalds-reviewer carries the same rule. Residual: no chain step reads the `.select(...)` argument (the query-shapes recorder captures the columns but judges only boundedness, indexes and ordering), so a new vertical that selects `*` and parses to a DTO that happens to include an internal column is caught only if a reviewer notices; tRPC procedures declare no `.output()` schema, so field subsetting rests on the DAL map rather than a wire-boundary check; and reviewer judgment is documentation-tier evidence by definition.

requirements.text: Verify that where the application backend makes calls to external URLs, it is configured to not follow redirects unless it is intended functionality.
requirements.note: The one server-side fetch to an external URL in the seeded tree — the Upstash pipeline call in packages/platform/ratelimit/src/index.ts — passes no `redirect` option and therefore follows redirects by the platform default; the Supabase clients talk to the project's own URL through the SDK, and the Edge Function is enumerated but carries no redirect posture either. tools/resilience.json is the natural place for such a posture (it already enumerates every outbound seam with a reviewed timeout/retry/backoff row and reds an undeclared seam), but its schema records no redirect field and the `resilience` step asserts nothing about one. The mobile lint ban on global fetch outside the tRPC client is a client-side rule and does not reach the server. Nothing in the tree, therefore, prevents a consumer's server-side fetch from following an attacker-controlled redirect.

requirements.text: Verify that the application has countermeasures to protect against mass assignment attacks by limiting allowed fields per controller and action, e.g., it is not possible to insert or update a field value when it was not intended to be part of that action.
requirements.note: The tenant and owner columns — the fields whose mass assignment breaks authorization — are gate-held: the `org-id-from-session-only` lint rule reds an org field in any zod contract and an org_id assigned from request input (RuleTester red-proofs in the named canary); the database refuses a smuggled tenant/owner value even if the application let it through — an INSERT policy carries a WITH CHECK by SQL grammar (and an UPDATE policy's USING doubles as its check when none is written), the `schema-rls` step reds a vacuous `true` predicate and a per-row identity call, and the `tenancy` step requires every predicate arm (USING and WITH CHECK alike) to carry one of the reviewed tenant-scoping forms in tools/tenancy.json; note that no step asserts a WITH CHECK is PRESENT on an UPDATE policy — schema-rls only does so for the MFA restrictive rail; and the security-reviewer rubric requires the owner id to come from the verified actor and never the wire. Every procedure that takes input parses it through a zod object from @app/contracts (the `contracts` step requires those contracts to bound every wire string, which is how it knows they are zod), and zod's default object parsing strips undeclared keys, so an unexpected field does not survive to the handler; the seeded update path additionally builds its patch from an explicit field list rather than spreading the input. Residual: no gate asserts that a mutation's DAL write is built from an allowlist rather than `...input` — that is the reviewer's half — and no gate requires a procedure to declare an `.input()` schema at all, so a consumer's `.input(z.any())` or a Server Action reading `formData` directly would pass the chain.

requirements.text: Verify that all proxying and middleware components transfer the user's original IP address correctly using trusted data fields that cannot be manipulated by the end user, and the application and web server use this correct value for logging and security decisions such as rate limiting, taking into account that even the original IP address may not be reliable due to dynamic IPs, VPNs, or corporate firewalls.
requirements.note: The only place the peer address is read is clientKeyFromHeaders in apps/web/lib/rate-limit-runtime.ts, which takes the first hop of x-forwarded-for and, in its own docstring, records that this is trustworthy exactly to the extent the platform overwrites the header — on Vercel it does; behind a self-terminated TLS edge it is attacker-controlled. The design limits the blast radius rather than trusting the value: a verified userId always outranks the client key in the rate-limit identity, so a forged address can only degrade ANONYMOUS limiting and never spend another caller's budget, and the audit trail treats request_id as correlation while actor_id (from the verified JWT) is the field with integrity. None of that is an enforcement point: the `rate-limits` step diffs bucket limits and procedure-to-bucket resolvers by value but does not evaluate the client-key resolver, no test exercises x-forwarded-for handling, and nothing asserts the deployment sits behind a proxy that sets rather than appends. The correctness of the original-IP field is a platform property the tree cannot see, which is why the boundary is shared and the outcome is not-covered rather than partial.

requirements.text: Verify that the application explicitly ensures that variables are of the correct type and performs strict equality and comparator operations. This is to avoid type juggling or type confusion vulnerabilities caused by the application code making an assumption about a variable type.
requirements.note: The type half is held hard: the `types` step runs `tsc -b` in strict mode with noUncheckedIndexedAccess, exactOptionalPropertyTypes, verbatimModuleSyntax and isolatedModules across every project (tsconfig.base.json), and the `lint` step applies typescript-eslint's strictTypeChecked and stylisticTypeChecked presets to every .ts/.tsx file — the no-unsafe-* family, restrict-plus-operands, no-base-to-string and restrict-template-expressions (with only number and boolean permitted) refuse `any` flowing into typed positions, so untrusted JSON must be narrowed through zod before it is used, and every wire input is a zod contract. The strict-equality half is NOT enforced: neither `eqeqeq` nor any core ESLint rule is enabled (js.configs.recommended is not extended and Biome's linter is off), so loose `==` is permitted wherever TypeScript's own no-overlap comparison error does not fire — `null == x` and same-type coercions pass the chain. The canary proves the runner reds on a failing tsc/eslint step, not that a specific confusion is caught; the seeded rules are upstream presets rather than harness-authored red-proofs, hence system-generated-artefact rather than simulated-activity.

requirements.text: Verify that JavaScript code is written in a way that prevents prototype pollution, for example, by using Set() or Map() instead of object literals.
requirements.note: No rule in the tree targets prototype pollution: `no-proto`, `no-prototype-builtins` and `no-extend-native` are core ESLint rules and the config extends no core preset; there is no ban on object literals as maps, on `__proto__` / `constructor.prototype` keys, or on recursive-merge helpers over untrusted input; and no guard rule watches for them. Two indirect mitigations exist and are recorded so they are weighed correctly rather than counted: strictTypeChecked's no-unsafe-assignment forces `JSON.parse` output to be narrowed (in practice through zod, whose object parsing copies only declared keys into a fresh object, so a `__proto__` key in a payload does not survive the boundary), and the mobile kv/recents seam reads corrupt payloads as empty. Both are consequences of type discipline, not a prototype-pollution control, and a consumer's `Object.assign(target, parsed)` or a deep-merge over query parameters would pass every step.

requirements.text: Verify that the application has defenses against HTTP parameter pollution attacks, particularly if the application framework makes no distinction about the source of request parameters (query string, body parameters, cookies, or header fields).
requirements.note: The seeded API surface is shaped so that parameter sources do not merge — tRPC v11 reads a query's input from one JSON-encoded `input` search parameter and a mutation's from the body, never both, and validates it as one zod object; Server Actions receive their arguments as a typed payload; the acting org is a transport selector (the x-org-id header or the /o/[orgSlug] segment) that the `org-id-from-session-only` lint rule refuses to accept from the payload — but those are framework and design properties, and no gate, test or reviewer rubric names parameter pollution. Duplicate JSON keys resolve last-wins inside JSON.parse before zod sees them, duplicate query keys in a Route Handler are whatever `URLSearchParams.get` returns first, and nothing asserts either behaviour. A consumer adding a Route Handler that reads searchParams and body into one object has no control watching.

requirements.text: Verify that shared objects in multi-threaded code (such as caches, files, or in-memory objects accessed by multiple threads) are accessed safely by using thread-safe types and synchronization mechanisms like locks or semaphores to avoid race conditions and data corruption.
requirements.note: The JavaScript tier runs no threads — the web server, the tRPC router and the Edge Functions execute on a single event loop per instance and no worker_threads are used — so the failure this requirement describes appears here as MODULE-SCOPE STATE shared across concurrently interleaved requests, and one instance of it is gate-held: the `no-module-scope-supabase` lint rule reds a Supabase client constructed at module scope (a hoisted client carries one request's identity into another's render), with a RuleTester red-proof in the named canary; the mirror rule on mobile is `useState(factory)`. On the database side, PostgreSQL's MVCC is the synchronization mechanism, and the `db-limits` step plus the `pg-advisory-session-lock` write-guard rule keep the one explicit lock primitive transaction-scoped (see 15.4.3). Residual: no rule reviews OTHER module-level mutable state — the in-process rate-limiter fallback keeps per-instance counters by design, and a consumer's module-level cache or memoized map is unreviewed; nothing asserts thread-safety of anything because there is nothing threaded to assert it over, and that absence is stated rather than graded as coverage.

requirements.text: Verify that checks on a resource's state, such as its existence or permissions, and the actions that depend on them are performed as a single atomic operation to prevent time-of-check to time-of-use (TOCTOU) race conditions. For example, checking if a file exists before opening it, or verifying a user’s access before granting it.
requirements.note: The two check-then-act paths the harness owns are both forced into a single statement. Authorization: RLS is the boundary, so 'verify access, then grant' is one statement — the policy predicate and WITH CHECK are evaluated inside the INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE that depends on them (the `schema-rls` step requires a permissive policy per operation with a non-vacuous predicate, the `tenancy` step requires the USING/WITH CHECK arms to carry a reviewed tenant-scoping form, and the security-reviewer rubric forbids an application-side owner filter that would re-introduce a separate check). Quota: the `db-limits` step requires the per-org quota to be an AFTER INSERT ... REFERENCING NEW TABLE ... FOR EACH STATEMENT trigger, and REDS the alternative that fails open by TOCTOU — a RESTRICTIVE policy over a STABLE count, which the planner hoists to one evaluation against the PRE-statement count so a multi-row insert passes wholesale (the named canary's 'RESTRICTIVE counting policy' case). The seeded invitation redeem (accept_invitation in the tenancy spine migration) is one guarded `DELETE ... WHERE token_digest = ... AND expires_at > now() RETURNING` — expiry check, used check and consume in a single statement, so two sessions racing the same token cannot both proceed; that is a pattern in the seeded SQL, not something any gate asserts. Residual: no static check recognises a check-then-act pattern in application code (a `select` followed by a dependent `insert` in one procedure is invisible to the chain), file-existence races are out of scope because the app writes no files, and the mutation lane covers the authorization seams but is not a race detector.

requirements.text: Verify that locks are used consistently to avoid threads getting stuck, whether by waiting on each other or retrying endlessly, and that locking logic stays within the code responsible for managing the resource to ensure locks cannot be inadvertently or maliciously modified by external classes or code.
requirements.note: The only explicit lock primitive in the stack is PostgreSQL's advisory lock, and it is held to the transaction: the `pg-advisory-session-lock` write-guard rule denies pg_advisory_lock at the moment of the edit and the `db-limits` step closes the whole source tree for it (a session-scoped lock on a pooled backend outlives the request that took it, so an error path leaks a lock that blocks every later caller and no pool release clears it — the named canary's 'session-scoped advisory lock' case reds and the xact form is proven green). Waiting is bounded rather than trusted: tools/db-limits.json sets a per-role lock_timeout (2s anon, 3s authenticated, 5s service_role) alongside statement_timeout and idle_in_transaction_session_timeout, the gate reds a dropped or RESET setting and a value that disagrees with the contract, and the runtime twins in supabase/tests/rls_structure.test.sql and tests/rls/resource-limits.test.ts prove the ceilings are in force through PostgREST. Residual: nothing enforces that locking logic stays inside the resource-owning module (there is no lock-owning module in the seeded tree, and a consumer's could take the xact lock from anywhere), the JavaScript tier has no locks to be consistent about, and 'retrying endlessly' is bounded only where tools/resilience.json records a retry count — the register refuses undeclared and false postures, not high ones.

requirements.text: Verify that resource allocation policies prevent thread starvation by ensuring fair access to resources, such as by leveraging thread pools, allowing lower-priority threads to proceed within a reasonable timeframe.
requirements.note: The pooled resource in this architecture is the database backend behind Supavisor's transaction-mode pool and PostgREST, and fair access to it is what the `db-limits` step enforces: per-role statement_timeout and idle_in_transaction_session_timeout ceilings (so one caller cannot hold a pooled backend indefinitely — proven in force through PostgREST by tests/rls/resource-limits.test.ts, and the named canary reds a dropped, RESET or contract-disagreeing setting), the per-org quota so one tenant cannot consume the shared table without bound, and the `rate-limits` step's per-identity buckets on the application seams. It also reds the two 'obvious' knobs that bind nothing here (temp_file_limit and CONNECTION LIMIT), so a reviewer never reads a dead number as a policy. Residual, stated plainly: there is no thread pool in the JavaScript tier — the web host's function concurrency and any per-instance fairness are the platform's, unrecorded in the tree; the ceilings bound traffic arriving through PostgREST and not a direct connection; there is no priority tiering of any kind, so 'lower-priority threads proceed' has no analogue; and the rate limiter fails open to a per-instance limiter when its backend is unavailable.

requirements.text: Verify that an inventory exists documenting the logging performed at each layer of the application's technology stack, what events are being logged, log formats, where that logging is stored, how it is used, how access to it is controlled, and for how long logs are kept.
requirements.note: No log inventory ships. The nearest artefact is docs/runbooks/log-forwarding.md, whose per-stream table names five streams (audit.events, auth_trail.events, GoTrue's auth.audit_log_entries, the Supabase platform pipeline, the Vercel platform pipeline) with where each lives and what it carries, and states that platform retention is plan-capped at roughly 90 days; it does not record log formats, the access-control posture per stream, or a retention figure per stream, and it omits the application log lines the @app/observability seam and the mobile src/lib/log.ts seam emit to stdout. Retention for the two database trails exists only as operator-invoked DDL (audit.drop_partitions_older_than and the auth_trail twin), not as a documented figure. Nothing in the validate chain, the Stop chain or CI asserts that an inventory exists or that it is complete, so there is no enforcement point to name; the harness could ship an inventory skeleton for the streams it creates, and the deployed inventory (platform logs, drains, sinks, retention) is the operator's to complete.

requirements.text: Verify that each log entry includes necessary metadata (such as when, where, who, what) that would allow for a detailed investigation of the timeline when an event happens.
requirements.note: The two database trails carry the metadata: audit.events records occurred_at (timestamptz), org_id, actor_id (derived inside the SECURITY DEFINER writer audit.write_row from private.caller_id() and re-checked by the INSERT policy's WITH CHECK, never supplied by the caller), action, table_name, row_id, changed_columns and a correlation-only request_id (read from the x-harness-request-id header only; x-request-id is deliberately ignored); auth_trail.events records occurred_at, user_id, event_kind, factor_id and GoTrue's hook payload. The tenancy validate step (tools/check-tenancy.mjs) reds any org-scoped table whose migration lacks an AFTER INSERT OR UPDATE OR DELETE trigger executing audit.write_row, an audit trigger with a WHEN clause, a writer body that never sets actor_id or derives no verified identity, or an actor_id column with a DEFAULT; the canary pgTAP suite (run by the rls-isolation Stop step and the runtime-rls CI job, NOT by the tenancy step) proves the trigger fires for a real write and that the row's actor_id names the acting user. What this does NOT reach: source IP and user agent are recorded nowhere (the hooks and the trigger have no access to them); request_id on an audit row is forgeable by a client talking straight to PostgREST, so it is correlation and not evidence; the audit trail records mutations only and nothing about reads (SELECT auditing needs pgaudit configuration a migration cannot express); the application log seam (@app/observability) deliberately emits no timestamp and carries who/where only when the caller passes them as fields, so a call site that omits them yields a record an investigator cannot place; and the mobile seam (apps/mobile/src/lib/log.ts) prints raw arguments in development and nothing in release.

requirements.text: Verify that time sources for all logging components are synchronized, and that timestamps in security event metadata use UTC or include an explicit time zone offset. UTC is recommended to ensure consistency across distributed systems and to prevent confusion during daylight saving time transitions.
requirements.note: The database trails stamp occurred_at as timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(), which PostgreSQL stores normalised to UTC and renders with an explicit offset, so the format half holds for those two streams by construction; no gate or suite pins the column type, so a migration that changed it to timestamp without time zone would not red. The @app/observability seam emits NO timestamp on purpose (its header records that a phone's clock is user-settable and that the only trustworthy timestamp is the one the ingesting system stamps on arrival), which delegates both the format and the synchronisation of application log lines to whatever collector the operator wires. Time-source synchronisation of the logging components themselves — the Vercel function hosts, the Supabase Postgres host, and the mobile device — is outside anything this repository can configure or observe; the device clock in particular is untrusted, which is why the seam owns elapsed time (a difference) and not wall-clock time. There is therefore no enforcement point to name, and the row records the facts rather than a control.

requirements.text: Verify that the application only stores or broadcasts logs to the files and services that are documented in the log inventory.
requirements.note: The observability gate makes off-device log egress a reviewed register: every import of a telemetry-vendor SDK across apps/, packages/ and supabase/functions/ (static, side-effect, dynamic import() and require()) must match a row in tools/observability.json sinks[], each row must name the file, the vendor, a redaction symbol the file actually references, and a 40+ character reason, and the register is closed both ways so a stale row reds too; the shipped register declares zero sinks, so as shipped no log record leaves the process except through the host's stdout, and the observability-sinks write-guard rule keeps the register a human-reviewed edit. The can-fail proof is factory-side (tests/gates/check-observability.test.mjs spawns the real gate against an unregistered @sentry import and a sink that never references its redaction symbol). What this does NOT reach: the scan is over import specifiers, so telemetry sent by a raw fetch() to an ingest URL, or a vendor SDK reached through a transitive dependency, is invisible; there is no log inventory (16.1.1) for the register to be reconciled against, so the register IS the de facto inventory of broadcast destinations rather than a check against one; the stdout lines are collected by the platforms into pipelines the repository does not describe; and the two database trails are rows, not broadcasts, and are covered by 16.4.2.

requirements.text: Verify that logs can be read and correlated by the log processor that is in use, preferably by using a common logging format.
requirements.note: The @app/observability default sink (consoleSink) emits one JSON object per line (JSON.stringify({...fields, level, message})) and the redaction pass is also the serialisation pass, so every record is JSON-safe by construction (functions, symbols, undefined and bigint become tags rather than throwing; cycles become '[circular]'); the suite that rides the unit Stop step proves the JSON-safety property at the record level. The two database trails are structured rows with fixed columns and a keyset-friendly (occurred_at, id) order, readable by any SQL consumer, and audit.events carries request_id as a correlation key. What this does NOT reach: no log processor is chosen or wired, so 'the log processor that is in use' is the operator's, and whether it parses the JSON lines is theirs to verify; consoleSink itself is exercised by NO test in the tree (the suite captures records at the sink boundary through a test sink, before stringification), so the one-JSON-line-per-record format is asserted nowhere; the test titled 'never the envelope' passes no field named level, so the claim that a caller field cannot re-file a record is by construction of the record shape, not proven; the mobile seam prints raw arguments to the Metro console in development and drops everything in release, so mobile emits no common-format log at all; correlation between application log lines and traces (a trace_id on each record) is a documented patch in the opt-in observability module (docs/modules/observability/otel-server.patch.md), not shipped code, and enabling the module ships only a span-name manifest test (span-routes.test.ts); and GoTrue's own auth.audit_log_entries and the platform pipelines have formats this repository does not define.

requirements.text: Verify that when logging sensitive data, the application enforces logging based on the data's protection level. For example, it may not be allowed to log certain data, such as credentials or payment details. Other data, such as session tokens, may only be logged by being hashed or masked, either in full or partially.
requirements.note: Two mechanisms, each with a can-fail proof. First, the @app/observability seam redacts at the seam rather than at call sites: every field whose normalised key contains token, password, authorization, apikey, secret or cookie is replaced with '[redacted]' at every depth before any sink sees the record, an Error is reduced to {name, message} with no stack, and the suite (unit Stop step) proves redaction happens before the sink and reaches nested arrays. Second, the audit trail captures metadata by default and the tenancy validate step reds an audit.write_row(...) trigger that captures by value a column listed in tools/pii-columns.json (and reds a tools/audit-columns.json entry that contradicts the PII list), which is a protection-level rule expressed as reviewed data. What this does NOT reach: redaction matches on the field NAME and cannot see a credential inside an innocently named value (a database URL with a password in its authority, a free-text note), which the seam header states as its limit; the eslint no-console rule that forces mobile code through the seam applies only to apps/mobile/**, so a bare console call in apps/web, packages/** or an Edge Function is not lint-red (supabase/functions/delete-account/index.ts writes driver messages with console.error today); the mobile seam does no redaction of its own and prints raw arguments in development; session tokens are dropped rather than hashed or masked, so the seam offers no masked form for correlation; and the crash-reporting module's redactText policy (DSNs, bearer tokens, JWT-shaped blobs, e-mail addresses, home paths) exists only if a consumer enables that module and applies its patches.

requirements.text: Verify that all authentication operations are logged, including successful and unsuccessful attempts. Additional metadata, such as the type of authentication or factors used, should also be collected.
requirements.note: auth_trail.events records password_success, password_failure, mfa_success and mfa_failure with user_id, factor_id (which factor an MFA attempt exercised) and GoTrue's hook payload, written by GoTrue itself through the [auth.hook.password_verification_attempt] and [auth.hook.mfa_verification_attempt] hooks, which is the only seam that sees a failed attempt from a caller who never got a session. The control that can go red today is the runtime proof: tests/rls/auth-trail.test.ts (the rls-isolation Stop step, CI job runtime-rls) drives a REAL failed signInWithPassword over HTTP and reads the password_failure row back, and supabase/tests/auth_trail.test.sql (same step) proves the writer privilege path and vocabulary. The auth-posture validate step also pins both hooks' enabled flags and pg-functions URIs by value, BUT that pin is ramped: on any install whose .harness/manifest.json baseVersion predates 1.0.0 (which is every install the current 0.11.1 installer produces) a disabled or repointed hook is printed as a dated NOTE and the step stays green until the install runs harness 1.1.0, and no factory-side test in tests/gates/check-auth-posture.test.mjs exercises the [auth.hook] keys — so it is named here as context, not as the control. Ceilings the ADR (docs/adr/20260816-auth-event-trail.md) states and this row inherits: an attempt against an e-mail with no user row fires nothing (GoTrue looks the user up first), so enumeration sweeps are visible only in the platform's HTTP logs; the password hook covers the password grant only, so OAuth, magic-link and OTP sign-ins do not traverse it; sign-out, token refresh, password change and factor enrolment are not in the trail's vocabulary; on hosted Supabase the auth hooks are plan-gated, so a consumer on a plan without hooks has an unwired trail while every gate stays green; and the trail lives in the same database as the system it observes (see 16.4.3).

requirements.text: Verify that failed authorization attempts are logged. For L3, this must include logging all authorization decisions, including logging when sensitive data is accessed (without logging the sensitive data itself).
requirements.note: A refused authorization is not logged anywhere in the shipped tree. RLS is the authorization boundary and a policy refusal surfaces as SQLSTATE 42501, which packages/platform/supabase/src/errors.ts maps to appError.rlsDenied on the wire and nothing records; an RLS-filtered read returns an empty set by design (deliberately indistinguishable from absence) and leaves no trace; the orgProcedure rung's forbidden(org_context_required) is returned and not logged; and the audit trail fires AFTER INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE, so a write the policy refused never reaches the trigger. The L3 clause is unreachable as designed: audit.events records mutations only and nothing about reads (the gates catalog's first stated honest loss — SELECT auditing needs pgaudit configuration a migration cannot express). The platform's Postgres logs will carry 42501 messages, but that is the platform pipeline the repository does not describe or protect. The harness could ship a denial log at the DAL mapping seam or the tRPC error formatter, so this is a gap rather than an inapplicability.

requirements.text: Verify that the application logs the security events that are defined in the documentation and also logs attempts to bypass the security controls, such as input validation, business logic, and anti-automation.
requirements.note: There is no documented set of security events to log against (16.1.1), and the bypass classes the requirement names are mostly silent: a tRPC .input() zod failure throws BAD_REQUEST and is not logged; a rate-limit refusal (TOO_MANY_REQUESTS) is thrown before the handler and not logged — only the limiter's DEGRADED state and its missing-credentials fallback are logged via log.error in apps/web/lib/rate-limit-runtime.ts; a version-skew CONFLICT and a CSRF rejection are refused and not logged; business-logic refusals ride the ActionOutcome envelope and are not logged. The one bypass signal that IS logged is a Content-Security-Policy violation, which apps/web/app/api/csp-report/route.ts writes as a csp_violation warn record through the redacting seam with a size cap and a field allowlist, but no test exercises that route (apps/web/__tests__/security-headers.test.ts asserts only that the report-only header points at it), so nothing here can go red. The harness could ship logging at the middleware throw sites and the CSRF/skew refusals; the security-events documentation is shared with the operator.

requirements.text: Verify that the application logs unexpected errors and security control failures such as backend TLS failures.
requirements.note: Unexpected errors are collapsed, not logged. toOutcome/toOutcomeAsync in @app/errors turn any throw into appError.unknown() and hand the cause to an OPTIONAL onThrow observer, and no production caller in the shipped tree passes one, so the cause is dropped; apps/web/lib/safe-action.ts's handleServerError returns a message-free AppError and does not log (its comment says the diagnostic copy belongs in the server log the seam owns, but no call is made); the tRPC route handler wires no onError; apps/web has no instrumentation.ts onRequestError. The one security-control failure that is logged and proven is the rate limiter's degradation: packages/platform/ratelimit fires onUnavailable exactly once per degraded decision (its suite proves it) and the web runtime logs the DEGRADED report and the missing-Redis fallback through the seam. Backend TLS failures specifically are not distinguished anywhere; a failed outbound call is whatever the runtime default makes it (tools/resilience.json declares seven of eight seams as posture-absent by design). The mobile ErrorBoundary calls log.error on a caught render error, but the mobile seam is a no-op in release builds, so that line reaches nothing in production. The crash-reporting module's server-sentry.patch.md documents an onRequestError plus tRPC onError funnel, and that is documentation until a consumer applies it, so no module is named on this row.

requirements.text: Verify that all logging components appropriately encode data to prevent log injection.
requirements.note: The @app/observability consoleSink serialises each record with JSON.stringify, so a caller-supplied string containing CR/LF or control characters is escaped rather than starting a new line, and the record's own level and message are spread LAST so a field named level cannot re-file a warn line as debug (the sink's comment names this ordering as its log-injection defence). The CSP report route, the one endpoint that logs attacker-controlled input, caps the body at 8 KiB (MAX_BODY_BYTES), keeps only six allowlisted fields (REPORTED_FIELDS), and truncates each string to 512 characters before it reaches the seam. The database trails take structured columns through parameterised trigger inserts, so free-text injection has no surface there beyond the jsonb payload. Evidence, honestly stated: the unit Stop step runs the seam's suite, which proves the record is JSON-safe by construction and that redaction precedes the sink, but NO test in the tree exercises consoleSink or passes a CR/LF payload or a field named level, so the encoding property itself rests on JSON.stringify's language guarantee and on inspection of the spread order, not on a can-fail assertion; and no test exercises the CSP route's caps (apps/web/__tests__/security-headers.test.ts asserts only that the report-only header points at it). What this does NOT reach: the mobile seam forwards raw arguments to console.* in development with no encoding, and a consumer who swaps in a vendor sink through the crash-reporting or observability module inherits that vendor's encoding; the Edge Function's console.error lines interpolate driver messages into template strings with no encoding; and platform-produced logs (PostgREST, GoTrue, Vercel request logs) are encoded by the platforms.

requirements.text: Verify that logs are protected from unauthorized access and cannot be modified.
requirements.note: The two database trails are append-only in four layers — no UPDATE/DELETE policy, no client grant (the schemas are absent from [api].schemas and grant USAGE to no client role, so the tables do not resolve over PostgREST), a BEFORE UPDATE OR DELETE row trigger that binds even a BYPASSRLS role, and a BEFORE TRUNCATE statement trigger on the parent and every partition — and the tenancy gate reds a migration that removes any layer, grants service_role on the trail, or drops audit from nonPublicSchemas. supabase/tests/audit_immutability.test.sql (32 assertions, run under the rls-isolation Stop step and the runtime-rls CI job) has service_role ATTEMPT read, forge, modify, delete and truncate and asserts each refusal, and proves the read path admits a rank-40 admin and refuses a rank-20 member of the same org; supabase/tests/auth_trail.test.sql proves the same layers on auth_trail.events, which has no reader role at all. What this does NOT reach: GoTrue's own auth.audit_log_entries carries no append-only layer and none can be added because GoTrue re-migrates its schema; application log lines written to stdout are protected only by whatever the platform pipeline and the operator's sink guarantee; the trails are protected IN PLACE and live in the same database as the system they observe, so a database-level compromise reaches them (16.4.3); the postgres role that runs migrations can drop a partition, which is the intended retention path and also the erase path; and audit.events is readable by rank-30+ members of the owning org through org_audit_events(), which is a designed access, not an unauthorised one, but it means the trail's confidentiality is a rank decision the consumer owns.

requirements.text: Verify that logs are securely transmitted to a logically separate system for analysis, detection, alerting, and escalation. The aim is to ensure that if the application is breached, the logs are not compromised.
requirements.negativeProof: This requirement applies in full to every deployed application; not-applicable here records only that no artefact in this repository can discharge it, and the boundary sits with the operator. Central collection means the record survives compromise of the system that produced it, and every stream this tree produces stays on the platform that produced it: the two database trails are rows in the product's own Postgres, the application log lines go to the platforms' stdout pipelines, and GoTrue's entries live in GoTrue's schema. Forwarding is configured in provider consoles the repository deliberately does not reach — the runbook records Supabase log drains as Dashboard-only (its stated check: drain appears in the Management API specification only as an enum value, never as a path) and plan-gated, Vercel drains as API/Terraform-addressable outside this repo, and the database trails as needing a scheduled export the operator runs — and a gate that resolved drain state from a live vendor endpoint is refused by the hermeticity rule. A search of template/base, template/stack and template/modules finds no drain configuration, export job or forwarding code; docs/runbooks/log-forwarding.md is the recorded surface (what to forward per stream, where each drain is, and the four properties the sink must hold: independent credentials, its own immutability, chosen retention, a tested read path); the Essential Eight rows on the word 'centrally' (RAP-20, RAP-21, AC-11, AC-12, UAH-20, MFA-16) already sit at this boundary for the same reason. Nothing here can go red, and the row must not be read as coverage.
