requirements.text: Verify that a generic message is returned to the consumer when an unexpected or security-sensitive error occurs, ensuring no exposure of sensitive internal system data such as stack traces, queries, secret keys, and tokens.
requirements.note: Three seams keep internals off the wire, each with a can-fail test in the unit Stop step: toOutcome/toOutcomeAsync collapse any throw to {kind: 'unknown', code: 'unknown'} and the suite asserts the thrown text ('driver exploded: connection string localhost:5432') is absent from the serialised envelope; mapPostgresError drops PostgREST's message, details and hint (which quote column names, constraint definitions and sometimes the offending value) and packages/platform/supabase/src/errors.test.ts asserts none of the three reaches the error channel; and apps/web/lib/safe-action.ts's handleServerError returns a fixed, message-free appError.unknown so a Server Action's throw never carries Next's development-mode message. The web-security-reviewer's checklist names 'never returns a raw driver/stack string' for Server Actions and the route handler, and the reviewer-verdicts Stop step requires its PASS on those paths. What this does NOT reach: an error thrown from INSIDE a tRPC procedure body that the DAL did not wrap is shaped by the errorFormatter in packages/api/src/trpc.ts, which spreads tRPC's default shape unchanged (message retained, and data.stack when NODE_ENV is not production) and only appends appCode/retryAfterSeconds — it strips nothing, and the route wires no onError; the envelope rule (lint local/app-error-only) makes such throws a lint error only under three globs; a .input() zod failure returns zod's issue text as BAD_REQUEST, which is a contract message and not internals but is not generic; and the mobile ErrorBoundary renders this.state.error.message verbatim in its fallback, which is a client-side render error rather than server internals but is not a generic message either.

requirements.text: Verify that the application continues to operate securely when external resource access fails, for example, by using patterns such as circuit breakers or graceful degradation.
requirements.note: The resilience validate step makes the outbound-seam posture reviewed data: every outbound-transport construction site (the tRPC client, a server fetch, a supabase-js factory, an Edge Function) must have a tools/resilience.json row, a row's timeout/retry/backoff claims must be backed by the symbols that implement them (a non-null timeoutMs requires AbortSignal.timeout in the file), and the register is closed both ways; the can-fail proof is factory-side (tests/gates/check-resilience.test.mjs). Ramp caveat: on an install whose .harness/manifest.json baseVersion predates 1.0.0 (every install the current 0.11.1 installer produces) the gate withholds every finding as a dated NOTE and reports ok until the install runs harness 1.1.0, so the register reds today only in the harness's own tests and on a manifest-less tree. The one graceful-degradation mechanism that is shipped AND tested (unit Stop step) is the rate limiter: packages/platform/ratelimit falls back to a shared per-process limiter when the Redis backend is unreachable, marks each decision degraded, fires onUnavailable once per degraded decision, and its suite proves all of that; the limiter's REST call carries a 1 s AbortSignal.timeout so it cannot hang a request; and mapPostgresError classifies only SQLSTATE classes 08/53/57 as retryable 'unavailable' so a client never retries a permanent failure. What this does NOT reach, and it is most of the requirement: seven of the eight shipped rows declare {timeoutMs: null, retries: 0} with a written reason (the platform's function deadline or the OS socket stack owns the ceiling), so the register documents an absence rather than a posture; no circuit breaker exists anywhere; the gate proves declared posture and symbol presence, never runtime behaviour under a failing dependency; and the limiter's degradation is deliberately FAIL-OPEN (requests are allowed while degraded and a host cannot opt into failing closed), which keeps the application operating but is the reviewed opposite of 'securely' for that one control — the 16.5.3 row states the same fact from the other side.

requirements.text: Verify that the application fails gracefully and securely, including when an exception occurs, preventing fail-open conditions such as processing a transaction despite errors resulting from validation logic.
requirements.note: The single-error-channel doctrine is the mechanism: a domain failure is a returned outcomeErr(appError.X()) and a throw anywhere under apps/web/app/actions/**, packages/api/src/routers/** or packages/verticals/**/src/data/** is a lint error (local/app-error-only, factory-proven in tests/gates/eslint-custom-rules.test.mjs), while toOutcome/toOutcomeAsync collapse a throw to a FAILED envelope and never a success (proven in the errors kernel suite, including the async form whose rejection would otherwise escape). Validation runs at the boundary before domain code (tRPC .input() zod parsing; next-safe-action's schema parse for Server Actions), the DAL reads PostgREST's error before its data so an RLS denial cannot render as an empty success, and the per-org quota is a FOR EACH STATEMENT ... REFERENCING NEW TABLE trigger precisely because the RESTRICTIVE-policy-over-STABLE-count alternative fails open on a multi-row INSERT — the db-limits gate reds a FOR EACH ROW quota trigger. What this does NOT reach: the lint rule's three globs leave every other file free to throw; the rate limiter FAILS OPEN by design when its backend is unavailable and a host cannot opt into failing closed, so one security control's failure mode is the reviewed opposite of this requirement's default and must be read as such; nothing proves transactional atomicity of multi-step writes beyond the database's own semantics; and no test injects an exception mid-procedure over a real HTTP round trip.

requirements.text: Verify that a "last resort" error handler is defined which will catch all unhandled exceptions. This is both to avoid losing error details that must go to log files and to ensure that an error does not take down the entire application process, leading to a loss of availability.
requirements.note: No last-resort handler that both preserves availability AND logs the details exists on either surface. apps/web ships no app/error.tsx, no app/global-error.tsx and no instrumentation.ts onRequestError, and the tRPC route handler wires no onError, so an unhandled server exception is whatever Next.js and tRPC do by default with nothing of this repository's recording it; safe-action's handleServerError catches a Server Action's throw but discards the cause. apps/mobile mounts a root ErrorBoundary in app/_layout.tsx that catches render exceptions and offers a reset (the availability half for the render tree), but its log.error goes through src/lib/log.ts, which is a no-op in release builds, so the details are lost in production, it does not catch exceptions outside render (event handlers, async work), and no test exercises the boundary. The crash-reporting module documents an onRequestError plus tRPC onError funnel (docs/modules/crash-reporting/server-sentry.patch.md) and the sink swap for the mobile seam, but both are patches a consumer applies by hand and stay documentation after enablement, so no module is named as a control. The harness could ship the web boundaries and a logging onError, so this is a gap rather than an inapplicability.

requirements.text: Verify that the Traversal Using Relays around NAT (TURN) service only allows access to IP addresses that are not reserved for special purposes (e.g., internal networks, broadcast, loopback). Note that this applies to both IPv4 and IPv6 addresses.
requirements.negativeProof: The generated system operates no TURN or STUN service: the tree carries no coturn or relay configuration, no ICE-server list, and no RTCPeerConnection, getUserMedia, DTLS, SRTP or signaling call site (a case-insensitive text search of template/ for webrtc, RTCPeerConnection, RTCDataChannel, getUserMedia, mediaDevices, dtls, srtp, sdp, coturn, iceServers, stun and signaling returns nothing; the bare token "turn" was not used as a probe because it appears throughout the tree in prose about agent turns, so the TURN half of the absence rests on the coturn, iceServers and ICE-server-list probes). The client-side media-capture half of the absence is machine-held on both surfaces: the security-headers chain step diffs the evaluated Permissions-Policy against tools/security-headers.json, whose permissionsPolicyDenied list carries camera, microphone and display-capture, and the harness repo's own tests/gates/check-security-headers.test.mjs (not shipped in the template) reds when camera stops being denied; the expo-policy chain step locksteps android.permissions and iOS *UsageDescription keys bidirectionally against tools/expo-permissions.json (seeded empty) and plugins[] against tools/expo-plugins.json, and the harness repo's own tests/gates/check-expo-policy.test.mjs (not shipped in the template) reds on an unreviewed CAMERA grant and an unreviewed NSCameraUsageDescription. Guard rules security-headers-policy, expo-permissions and expo-plugins deny agent edits to those three registers.
requirements.note: This requirement applies only to systems that run their own TURN service, and the template ships none, so there is nothing for the harness to grade. The negative proof is partial and is graded documentation tier for that reason: no gate asserts the absence of a TURN server itself, and a data-channel-only RTCPeerConnection is not blocked by a Permissions-Policy that denies camera and microphone, so what the gates hold is that no media capture can be added on either client without a reviewed diff, not that WebRTC cannot appear. A consumer who deploys a TURN relay takes this requirement on in full and inherits no harness control that reaches its address filtering.

requirements.note: There is neither a media server nor a recording pipeline in the generated system, so recorder resilience under SRTP flood has no subject. The [storage] enabled = false value is seeded rather than pinned: the auth-posture chain step's section census closes over config.toml section names, not this value, so enabling storage is not machine-red and the recording-sink half of the absence is prose. Documentation tier for that reason. A consumer adding recording owns the recorder's flood behaviour and its storage.

requirements.text: Verify that the Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS) certificate is checked against the Session Description Protocol (SDP) fingerprint attribute, terminating the media stream if the check fails, to ensure the authenticity of the media stream.
requirements.negativeProof: The generated system hosts no WebRTC media server and exchanges no SDP: the tree carries no such server, no DTLS or SRTP configuration, no SDP handling, and no RTCPeerConnection or getUserMedia call site (a case-insensitive text search of template/ for webrtc, RTCPeerConnection, RTCDataChannel, getUserMedia, mediaDevices, dtls, srtp, sdp, coturn, iceServers, stun and signaling returns nothing; the bare token "turn" was not used as a probe because it appears throughout the tree in prose about agent turns, so the TURN half of the absence rests on the coturn, iceServers and ICE-server-list probes). The client media-capture half of the absence is machine-held: the security-headers chain step holds camera, microphone and display-capture denied in Permissions-Policy per tools/security-headers.json (the harness repo's own tests/gates/check-security-headers.test.mjs (not shipped in the template) reds when camera stops being denied), and the expo-policy chain step locksteps mobile permissions and usage strings against the empty tools/expo-permissions.json and plugins against tools/expo-plugins.json (the harness repo's own tests/gates/check-expo-policy.test.mjs (not shipped in the template) reds on an unreviewed CAMERA grant). Guard rules security-headers-policy, expo-permissions and expo-plugins deny agent edits to those registers.
requirements.note: No media server exists in the generated system, so there is no DTLS certificate to check against an SDP fingerprint. The absence of the server rests on prose; the gates in the negative proof reach only the client capture halves, hence documentation tier. A consumer hosting media owns fingerprint verification and stream termination on mismatch at their server.

requirements.text: The app uses secure authentication and authorization protocols and follows the relevant best practices.
requirements.note: Authentication is GoTrue with PKCE forced on the native client (packages/platform/supabase/src/native.ts), refresh-token rotation, a one-hour JWT and an exact two-entry redirect allowlist, held by the auth-posture step against supabase/config.toml in both directions (a wildcard redirect reds, proven). Authorization is RLS on auth.uid() (schema-rls and tenancy steps; the rls-isolation Stop step runs the pgTAP and supabase-js isolation suites on a live stack), and server-side identity is getUser()/getClaims() through the red-proofed no-unverified-session and service-role-edge-functions-only ESLint rules; the mobile app is an untrusted bearer and never authorizes. What this does not reach: no password-strength floor and no GoTrue [auth.rate_limit] posture is pinned (auth-posture pins the mfa, hook, rotation and redirect keys, not minimum_password_length or sign-in rate limits); client-side idle timeout and the server-side scope of sign-out are unasserted; only email/password ships, so any OAuth or passkey flow is the consumer's, reviewed by mobile-security-reviewer item 8 rather than a gate.

requirements.text: The app performs local authentication securely according to the platform best practices.
requirements.negativeProof: The scaffold performs no local (biometric or PIN) authentication: expo-local-authentication or an equivalent is nowhere in the tree, identity is remote (GoTrue) plus the database aal2 rail, and no screen gates on a device credential. What enforces the absence: the expo-policy step's bidirectional plugin closure against tools/expo-plugins.json and its usage-string review red an unreviewed expo-local-authentication plugin (its iOS Face ID usage string), and the mobile-security-reviewer owes a verdict on app.config.ts. Honest limit: an Android-only JavaScript use of a biometric library that needs no config plugin is caught by no gate. When a consumer adds local authentication this row becomes theirs to grade (keychain-bound keys, no boolean-only checks, fallback handling).

requirements.text: The app secures sensitive operations with additional authentication.
requirements.note: What ships is a session-level MFA rail rather than per-operation step-up: a user who has enrolled a TOTP factor (apps/mobile/app/security.tsx) can no longer reach the notes vertical at aal1, through a RESTRICTIVE policy over private.mfa_is_required() (SECURITY DEFINER, no FOR clause) enforced in the database so a client talking straight to PostgREST is bound too; the pgTAP suite holds the fail-open case (enrolled plus aal1 yields zero rows) and runs under the rls-isolation Stop step, and the mobile mfa-challenge route sends an enrolled aal1 session to the challenge (apps/mobile/__tests__/mfa-challenge.test.tsx). What this does not reach: no operation demands a fresh factor, biometric or re-entered password, so delete-account, export and org-admin procedures ask only for a valid JWT; MFA is opt-in per user because GoTrue has no required flag, so an unenrolled user has no additional authentication anywhere; the policy is attached to public.notes only, so a new table owes its own RESTRICTIVE policy by convention, not by gate.

requirements.text: The app requires an up-to-date platform version.
requirements.note: The harness floors targetSdkVersion (the Play submission floor of 36 in tools/store-policy.json, held by the expo-policy step) and the iOS build toolchain (the Xcode 26 floor in version-sync), but neither is the platform version the app REQUIRES to install: minSdkVersion and the iOS deploymentTarget are left at Expo SDK 57's defaults with no reviewed floor and no gate, and a targetSdk-36 build still installs on old OS releases. Adjacent controls, not the subject; a minimum-OS floor could join expo-policy's resolved-config checks.

requirements.text: The app has a mechanism for enforcing app updates.
requirements.note: The tRPC router carries a version-skew guard on the base of the procedure ladder: a client whose x-client-version major differs from the server's is refused with the stable version_skew code, an optional minSupportedClient floor forces out a specific old build within a major, every procedure inherits it (the suite asserts non-vacuous coverage across the router), and the mobile client normalises the code so screens can say update. The version-sync step holds apps/web's major to @app/api's. What this does not reach: this is an API-side refusal, not an in-app hard block with a store redirect, so the UI is not locked; the floor is null by default; a request carrying no version header passes (health tooling), so a modified client can strip it, which makes this a contract-drift control rather than a tamper control; OTA delivery is the opt-in eas-update module.

requirements.text: The app only uses software components without known vulnerabilities.
requirements.note: A clockless framework security floor over the RESOLVED pnpm-lock (tools/framework-floor.json per major line, judged in the version-sync step with a 31-day review window and the scheduled floor-review lane), the tools/eol.json vendor-deprecation census closed both ways, the OSV-Scanner lanes (scan-pr diff-aware, scan-full scheduled), the CodeQL analyze lane and the sbom-inventory lane. What this does not reach: native dependencies, because under CNG no Podfile.lock or Gradle lockfile is committed, so CocoaPods and Gradle transitives pulled at prebuild are scanned by nothing (the native lane proves prebuild determinism, not vulnerability); framework-floor covers only the packages it lists; scan-pr never reds a pre-existing pin; the binaries Expo modules link are the vendor's.

requirements.text: The app validates and sanitizes all untrusted inputs.
requirements.proof: tools/check-contract-drift.mjs (the `contracts` validate-chain step; its factory red-proof is tests/gates/check-contract-drift.test.mjs)
requirements.note: Untrusted input reaching the backend is zod-validated at the contract boundary (@app/contracts DTOs on every procedure input), the contracts step's bounded-wire-string sweep reds an unbounded z.string() in the wire contract (escape: tools/dto-bounds-allow.json), the dangerously-set-inner-html write-guard rule bans raw HTML rendering, identity is parameterised server-side by RLS, and WITH RECURSIVE needs a cycle guard. What this does not reach: validation on the device, meaning deep-link parameters, values read back from AsyncStorage or the kv seam (kv.ts treats corrupt payloads as empty by convention), server responses (tRPC types are inferred, not runtime-parsed on the client) and file or IPC inputs, is enforced by nothing; the bounded-string sweep has no committed red-proof (its anti-vacuity is documented, not tested), hence the tier.

requirements.text: The app employs current strong cryptography and uses it according to industry best practices.
requirements.note: The weak-crypto-algorithm write-guard rule denies broken constructions in algorithm-argument position (ECB, the legacy createCipher, MD5, SHA-1, DES, RC4) at edit time, and the lint step's crypto-primitives-one-door and no-insecure-random-in-crypto-scope rules (RuleTester red-proofs in tests/gates/eslint-custom-rules.test.mjs) keep primitives behind the provider seam and key material CSPRNG-born; the guard's stated limit is that it names only the constructions it knows. Honest residual in the shipped code: LargeSecureStore encrypts the session with AES-256-CTR through aes-js, an unauthenticated mode with no integrity tag in a pure-JS implementation, so a tampered ciphertext decrypts to garbage rather than being refused (GoTrue still verifies the JWT inside, so the impact is a forced sign-out, but MASVS best practice is an AEAD); the fixed counter is safe only because the key is per value. AEAD (AES-256-GCM, HKDF, X25519) with published-vector tests arrives only with the opt-in e2ee module, conditional on enablement, and its WebCrypto providers return null under Hermes: the mobile provider is a documented patch, not shipped code.

requirements.text: The app performs key management according to industry best practices.
requirements.note: Session key material is born from expo-crypto (the platform CSPRNG), stored only in the platform keychain through the one host seam, rotated on every write, and both halves are deleted together; the hardcoded-key-material and math-random-key-material write-guard rules deny a literal key or a Math.random key at edit time (proofs in tests/hooks/hook-contract.test.mjs), and no-insecure-random-in-crypto-scope lints the seam and the provider package including tests. What this does not reach: no keychainAccessible class or biometric requireAuthentication binding on the SecureStore entries (platform defaults); no hardware-backed key attestation; no rotation schedule for anything but the per-write session key; the e2ee module's key hierarchy (root to KEK to per-item DEK, the wrapped-DEK erase lever, recovery escrow under a generated code, device-sync transit, rewrapItemKey) is opt-in and conditional on enablement, and its mobile KeystoreAdapter is a documented patch. A recovery code the user loses is lost data, stated by the module itself.

requirements.text: The app secures all network traffic according to the current best practices.
requirements.note: The expo-policy step asserts over the RESOLVED config (dynamic config executed, plugins expanded): no NSAllowsArbitraryLoads, ATS exception domains loopback-only, usesCleartextTraffic banned everywhere including inside an expo-build-properties plugin entry, and extra.apiOrigin https-or-loopback; each direction has a red-proof in tests/gates/check-expo-policy.test.mjs and selftest Canary 1. The lint step bans global fetch outside the tRPC one-door client and the resilience step registers every outbound seam with a reviewed posture. What this does not reach: the Supabase project URL the mobile client dials (EXPO_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL, or extra.supabaseUrl if a consumer adds it) is scheme-checked by no gate (only extra.apiOrigin is), so a plain-http Supabase URL is refused at runtime by the ATS/cleartext posture the gate holds rather than by any check of the URL itself; a dependency's own transport (a native SDK carrying its own trust manager or URLSession configuration) is invisible to a config check; TLS version and cipher choices are the platform's; no lane captures live traffic; the web API host's HSTS is a web-side control (security-headers step) outside MASVS.

requirements.text: The app performs identity pinning for all remote endpoints under the developer's control.
requirements.note: No certificate or public-key pinning ships for either developer-controlled endpoint (the web/API origin on Vercel or the Supabase project URL): no Android network_security_config pin-set plugin, no iOS NSPinnedDomains, no expo-build-properties pinning entry, and no gate asks for one. The corpus records the Android network-security-config pin-set as a decision site, which is documentation only. Pinning against platform-hosted origins with rotating leaf certificates is a consumer decision (an SPKI set with backup pins and an update path); the version-skew guard and the opt-in eas-update module are the update channels a pin failure would need, and neither is a pin.

requirements.text: The app uses IPC mechanisms securely.
requirements.note: The one IPC entry the scaffold exposes is its custom URL scheme (expo-router plus the {{APP_SCHEME}}://auth/callback deep link). The auth-posture step holds the GoTrue redirect allowlist to exactly the web callback and that deep link with no wildcard (a wildcard reds, proven), so the provider cannot hand an auth code to another URL; expo-policy locks the scheme to tools/identity.lock.json; PKCE makes an intercepted code worthless (mobile-security-reviewer item 8); the mfa-challenge route treats a deep-link arrival with no factor as an honest dead end. What this does not reach: no gate inspects Android intent-filters or exported components, or iOS URL types a config plugin adds; no verified App Links or Universal Links ship, and a custom scheme is claimable by any installed app; deep-link route parameters are schema-validated by convention only; pasteboard and share-sheet IPC are unexamined.

requirements.text: The app uses WebViews securely.
requirements.negativeProof: No WebView ships: react-native-webview is not a dependency (searched the template tree) and no screen renders remote or string HTML. Nothing enforces that absence: react-native-webview needs no config plugin, so the expo-policy plugin closure does not see one arrive, native-deps keeps no native-module allowlist, and no lint or write-guard rule names the import. The dangerously-set-inner-html write-guard rule (proof: tests/hooks/hook-contract.test.mjs) denies the react-dom raw-HTML prop repo-wide, and .claude/rules/security-invariants.md forbids WebView source={{html}} and script injection, but the first is an adjacent web control and the second is doctrine, neither a proof of WebView absence. When a consumer adds a WebView this row is theirs (JavaScript and file-access settings, bridge exposure, URL allowlists).

When a consumer adds a WebView this row is theirs (JavaScript and file-access settings, bridge exposure, URL allowlists).

requirements.text: The app uses the user interface securely.
requirements.note: The seeded sign-in masks the password (secureTextEntry, autoCorrect off, textContentType) but no gate or test asserts it and nothing generalises it to future sensitive fields; there is no screenshot or app-switcher snapshot protection (FLAG_SECURE, expo-screen-capture, blur on background), no clipboard restriction, no notification-content policy. The designing-mobile-ui skill and the Input primitive are where such defaults would live; none of the 36 gates, the Stop chain or the reviewers' checklists names the subject.

requirements.text: The app minimizes access to sensitive data and resources.
requirements.note: The scaffold requests no Android runtime permission and declares no iOS usage string; the expo-policy step closes android.permissions and iOS usage-description keys bidirectionally against the reviewed tools/expo-permissions.json (an unreviewed grant reds, proven), the observability step reds any vendor telemetry import outside the reviewed sinks register so no third-party SDK ships by default, and ATT declarations must agree with tracking-SDK signals both ways. What this does not reach: necessity and consent are judgments, so a reviewed permission entry with a thin reason passes; no consent-management surface or SDK consent gating ships; the data flow of an added SDK is unexamined beyond the import census; the opt-in store-metadata module adds a Play data-safety mirror table but as a checklist, not a gate.

requirements.text: The app prevents identification of the user.
requirements.note: No pseudonymisation, anonymisation or unlinkability control ships. The observability redaction pass targets credential-shaped keys (token, password, authorization, apikey, secret, cookie), not identifiers, so an email or user id in a log field is emitted; the audit trail records actor_id by design; there is no analytics or fingerprinting in the tree and the observability step's vendor-import containment keeps a tracker out unless registered, but the absence of a tracker is not an unlinkability control. The pii-columns capture refusal (tenancy step) is a minimisation lever for one mechanism, the audit trail, and does not reach telemetry, exports or the wire.

requirements.text: The app is transparent about data collection and usage.
requirements.note: The expo-policy step validates declared iOS privacy manifests (Apple's category vocabulary, real reason codes, lockstep with tools/store-tunables.json privacyAccessedApiTypes), requires ITSAppUsesNonExemptEncryption to be declared, and holds ATT consistency in both directions (red-proofs 11c and 11d). The opt-in store-metadata module adds the Play data-safety mirror and iOS privacy-manifest notes as reviewed documents. What this does not reach: no privacy policy, in-app disclosure or data-collection notice ships; ios.privacyManifests is not required (absence is a NOTE); whether a declaration is complete against what the app actually collects is unjudged; the Play data-safety form itself is console-only.

requirements.text: The app offers user control over their data.
requirements.note: Deletion: the expo-policy step's account-deletion closure (Apple 5.1.1(v)) requires an app with an auth surface to register the deletion action and its backing delete-account Edge Function (red-proof 11g), and the data-flow step replays the migrations and closes every FK path from auth.users into erased, severed, blocking or retained with reviewed reasons in both directions. Portability: system.exportMyData runs as the caller under RLS and its projection is closed against the schema (packages/api/src/routers/system.export.test.ts). What this does not reach: no consent-revocation or privacy-settings surface, no data-modification UX beyond the notes vertical, no re-prompt when collection scope grows; the export gate closes column names and cannot tell ciphertext from plaintext (the e2ee residual); DSR completeness for org-controlled data is procedure-backed by the tenancy ADR's own admission.

requirements.text: The app validates the integrity of the platform.
requirements.note: No root, jailbreak or emulator detection ships and nothing asks for it; the doctrine treats the device as untrusted and puts authorization in RLS, which is a stance about where trust lives, not platform-integrity validation. The expo-policy step's identity lock and OTA-trust checks (runtimeVersion policy, updates.url bound to the locked EAS projectId) concern the app's own update channel and say nothing about the OS. MASVS-RESILIENCE is threat-model dependent (the MAS-R profile), so whether to add Play Integrity, App Attest or a detection library is the consumer's decision.

requirements.text: The app implements anti-tampering mechanisms.
requirements.note: No runtime signature, checksum or attestation check ships and no gate asks for one. Adjacent but not the subject: the expo-policy step's OTA-trust checks keep the update channel PR-reviewable and project-bound; the opt-in ci-provenance module adds build attestation and an SBOM, which is provenance of the build, not detection of a modified binary at runtime; CNG keeps native projects generated and uncommitted. A repackaged build talking to the API is refused by nothing but the same RLS every legitimate client is bound by.

requirements.text: The app implements anti-static analysis mechanisms.
requirements.note: No obfuscation ships beyond Expo's defaults: Hermes bytecode is a compile fact, not a control, and no ProGuard/R8 or string-encryption configuration is reviewed by any gate. The opt-in crash-reporting module documents release source-map upload (a leak vector if mishandled) but that is a documented patch, not enforcement. The secrets and observability steps keep credentials and vendor SDKs out of the bundle, which reduces what static analysis finds without impeding it.

requirements.text: The app implements anti-dynamic analysis techniques.
requirements.note: No debugger, hooking-framework or instrumentation detection ships and nothing asks for it. The design premise is that the app is an untrusted bearer of a scoped token and every privilege decision is made in RLS, so dynamic analysis of the client yields nothing the client was not already allowed; that is a reason the harness has not invested here, not coverage of the control, and a consumer with client-side secrets or an anti-cheat requirement owns this row.

requirements.text: The app securely stores sensitive data.
requirements.proof: dependency-cruiser.cjs rule secure-store-host-seam-only, run by the `architecture` step (depcruise over the resolved graph); factory red-proof tests/gates/check-rule-integrity.test.mjs pins the rule set
requirements.note: The scaffold's one long-lived credential, the Supabase session, lives in LargeSecureStore (apps/mobile/src/host/large-secure-store.ts): a fresh per-value AES-256 key in expo-secure-store (iOS Keychain / Android Keystore) with the ciphertext in AsyncStorage, because SecureStore truncates above roughly 2 KB. The architecture step's depcruise rule secure-store-host-seam-only and the lint step's no-restricted-imports keep expo-secure-store to apps/mobile/src/host/**, and the mobile-security-reviewer owes a verdict on that path (reviewer-verdicts Stop step). What this does not reach: no gate classifies application data as sensitive or requires it to be encrypted at rest, so a feature that caches rows in AsyncStorage or the kv seam passes every gate; SecureStore is called with no explicit keychainAccessible or requireAuthentication option, so platform defaults apply; the opt-in e2ee module adds client-side encryption rails but ships no mobile CryptoProvider or KeystoreAdapter (those are a documented patch), so under Hermes it protects nothing until the consumer applies it. Of the three layers holding the seam wall, only the write-guard's inline expo-secure-store check (.claude/hooks/pretool-write-guard.mjs, no rule id) has a committed red-proof (tests/hooks/hook-contract.test.mjs: an import outside src/host is denied, one inside is allowed); the depcruise rule and the ESLint no-restricted-imports layer named as the control have no committed test proving they red, hence the tier.

requirements.text: The app prevents leakage of sensitive data.
requirements.proof: tools/eslint-rules/index.mjs — the custom rule named in the note, wired in eslint.config.mjs and run by the `lint` step (factory red-proof tests/gates/eslint-custom-rules.test.mjs)
requirements.note: Logs: the lint step bans bare console outside apps/mobile/src/lib/log.ts, whose release-build sink is a no-op, so a shipped log line carries nothing; the secrets step and the expo-public-secret-name write-guard rule refuse secret-shaped EXPO_PUBLIC_ names that would inline into the bundle; the observability step keeps any vendor telemetry behind the redaction sink; the audit trail is metadata-only with the pii-columns capture refusal (tenancy step). What this does not reach: Android backup rules (allowBackup, fullBackupContent, dataExtractionRules) are asserted by no gate and Expo's default allows backup; keyboard cache and autocorrect on sensitive fields, clipboard, app-switcher snapshots and third-party keyboards are unenforced (the seeded sign-in sets autoCorrect off and secureTextEntry but nothing holds it); the crash-reporting redaction is a key-fragment list (token, password, authorization, apikey, secret, cookie), so a credential under another name reaches the sink. No committed test proves the no-console rule reds.

requirements.text: Products with digital elements shall be designed, developed and produced in such a way that they ensure an appropriate level of cybersecurity based on the risks.
requirements.note: The harness ships secure-by-construction defaults enforced by the 36-step validate chain (tools/harness.config.mjs VALIDATE_STEPS) that the Stop chain re-runs as its first step and CI mirrors against a frozen floor (tools/validate.floor.json); gate-integrity sha-pins the enforcement files and wiring proves the hooks are connected. What it does NOT do is perform or record the risk assessment the phrase 'based on the risks' presupposes (Article 13(2)): the level of cybersecurity is the harness author's reviewed default, not a level derived from the consumer's own product risk, and nothing in the tree carries a product risk register or risk assessment: the only threat-model text is docs/harness/README.md's 'Threat model / honest limits' section, which describes the HARNESS's own limits, not a consumer product's risks, and specs/_template.md's 'Security invariants implicated' prompt is a per-feature spec question, not an Article 13(2) assessment. Whether the default is 'appropriate' for a given product is the manufacturer's determination, which is why the row is shared and partial rather than covered.

requirements.text: On the basis of the cybersecurity risk assessment referred to in Article 13(2) and where applicable, products with digital elements shall:
requirements.note: This is the chapeau that conditions sub-points (a) to (m) on the manufacturer's Article 13(2) cybersecurity risk assessment. The harness ships no risk-assessment artefact and no template for one (the nearest surfaces are specs/_template.md, whose 'Security invariants implicated' prompt is per-feature and harness-invariant-shaped, and docs/harness/README.md's harness-scoped threat-model section — neither is a product risk assessment), and no gate that asks whether the sub-points a consumer chose to apply or not apply were decided on the basis of one. It COULD ship a seeded risk-assessment document (the same seedOnInitOnly shape SECURITY.md and security.txt use), which is why the row is not-covered rather than not-applicable: the surface is absent by omission, not by design. The 'where applicable' qualifier is likewise a manufacturer judgment recorded nowhere in the tree.

requirements.text: be made available on the market without known exploitable vulnerabilities;
requirements.note: The osv-scan workflow (.github/workflows/osv-scan.yml) runs a diff-aware OSV scan on every pull request (job scan-pr: only newly introduced vulnerabilities red a PR) and a full-tree scan daily (job scan-full), CodeQL runs security-extended queries on PR, push and a daily schedule (codeql.yml job analyze), and gitleaks plus the hermetic secrets gate scan for credentials. What none of these reach: the OSV scan covers the npm lockfile only, so vulnerabilities in the Postgres extensions, the Supabase platform components, the runner images, the native SDK toolchains and the deployed runtime are invisible; CodeQL's matrix is javascript-typescript plus actions (workflow files), so it sees the JS/TS source and the GitHub Actions YAML and nothing about SQL policies or Expo native configuration; 'exploitable' is a judgment the tooling does not make and an unfixed upstream advisory with no patched version keeps the daily scan red without any action the tree can take; and the PR half is deliberately blind to a vulnerable pin carried since before its advisory (the daily scan owns that, and it is a lane an operator must read, not a PR blocker). Renovate owns the fix path and merging remains a human act. The scan-pr job is (event-gated) — its `if:` names pull_request and merge_group, so it is proven per pull request and never on a push to the default branch.

requirements.text: be made available on the market with a secure by default configuration, unless otherwise agreed between manufacturer and business user in relation to a tailor-made product with digital elements, including the possibility to reset the product to its original state;
requirements.note: The seeded configuration is held to reviewed policy BY VALUE and in both directions: auth-posture diffs supabase/config.toml against tools/auth-posture.json (jwt_expiry, refresh-token rotation, anonymous sign-ins off, the [auth.mfa] tree, redirect allowlist ceiling and wildcard ban, section census with [realtime]/[storage] disabled), security-headers diffs the evaluated apps/web/lib/security-headers.ts against tools/security-headers.json, expo-policy asserts the resolved Expo config carries no NSAllowsArbitraryLoads/cleartext opt-in and an https apiOrigin, db-limits asserts per-role statement ceilings are set by migration, and schema-rls asserts every table ships ENABLE + FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY with REVOKE ALL from service_role. Residuals: auth-posture governs the LOCAL config.toml and cannot see a production project's Dashboard or [remotes] posture (enable_confirmations is where that gap is loudest); 'reset to its original state' has no meaning for a hosted service and no mechanism in the tree, and for the mobile app it is the operating system's uninstall, not something the product provides; and the 'unless otherwise agreed' tailor-made carve-out is a contractual fact the harness cannot record.

requirements.text: ensure that vulnerabilities can be addressed through security updates, including, where applicable, through automatic security updates that are installed within an appropriate timeframe enabled as a default setting, with a clear and easy-to-use opt-out mechanism, through the notification of available updates to users, and the option to temporarily postpone them;
requirements.proof: the eas-update module’s github/workflows/eas-update.yml `publish` job (dispatch-only), with tools/check-eas-update.mjs as the module’s own validate step
requirements.note: Control: the eas-update module’s dispatch-only `publish` workflow job (tools/check-eas-update.mjs is the module’s own step). CONDITIONAL on the eas-update module being enabled: it ships tools/check-eas-update.mjs (the consumer appends it to VALIDATE_STEPS as the 'eas-update' step) and a dispatch-only publish workflow, so JavaScript-and-asset security fixes can reach installed binaries whose runtimeVersion matches without a store round-trip; the base tree's expo-policy gate holds the OTA trust boundary (runtimeVersion exactly appVersion, updates.url embedding the locked projectId) whether or not the module is on, and the base tRPC ladder carries the version-skew guard (packages/api/src/skew.ts, proven by skew.test.ts) that rejects a stale client with a stable CONFLICT code so it must update. Nothing in base or module implements automatic security updates enabled by default with an opt-out, a user-facing notification of AVAILABLE updates, or a postpone option — on mobile those behaviours belong to the app stores and to expo-updates' launch-time check policy the consumer configures, and on web a redeploy is the update with no user choice involved. No factory canary exists for the module gate (canary null); the ci-mobile-release and ci-web-deploy modules supply the store and web release paths and are likewise opt-in. The evidence tier is documentation because in the base tree the update story is doctrine plus a product-code test, not a gate.

requirements.text: ensure protection from unauthorised access by appropriate control mechanisms, including but not limited to authentication, identity or access management systems, and report on possible unauthorised access;
requirements.note: Authorisation is RLS keyed on auth.uid() with FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY, per-operation policies TO authenticated and REVOKE ALL from service_role: schema-rls closes policy to grant statically, tenancy holds every predicate to the reviewed tenant-scoped forms, and the rls-isolation Stop step runs the pgTAP suites (supabase/tests/rls_isolation.test.sql, rls_structure.test.sql, mfa_aal2.test.sql) plus tests/rls/cross-tenant-isolation.test.ts against a live stack on every turn, proving tenant B cannot read A. Authentication posture is pinned by auth-posture (refresh-token rotation, MFA tree, no anonymous sign-ins) and the aal2 RESTRICTIVE policy is proven fail-closed by mfa_aal2.test.sql; the web-security-reviewer holds getUser()/getClaims() over getSession() and the reviewer-verdicts Stop step requires the security-reviewer's PASS when the diff touches its tools/reviewer-triggers.json paths (supabase/migrations|schemas|functions/**, packages/api/src/**, packages/platform/supabase/**, the verticals' data/ dirs, apps/web/app/actions/**, apps/web/lib/auth/** and lib/supabase/**) — supabase/config.toml is NOT a trigger path, so an auth-posture edit owes no reviewer verdict and rests on the auth-posture gate alone. The 'report on possible unauthorised access' half is where coverage thins: the auth_trail schema (supabase/migrations/20260816000000_auth_event_trail.sql, proven by supabase/tests/auth_trail.test.sql) records failed AND successful password and MFA verifications through GoTrue hooks, but by decision it has no reader, no read policy and no alerting — an operator must query the database, and nothing notifies anyone. The audit trail records mutations only, so an unauthorised READ that RLS admitted (a policy bug) leaves no trace, the rate limiter, when its backend is unavailable, degrades to an in-process limiter (packages/platform/ratelimit withFailOpen) that a multi-instance serverless platform effectively discards, and only if that fallback also fails does nothing count at all; and the GoTrue hooks that feed auth_trail are held by auth-posture's [auth.hook] block, which is RAMPED — NOTE-only until harness 1.1.0 on installs seeded before 1.0.0 — so on an upgraded install failed sign-ins may leave no record while the chain stays green.

requirements.text: protect the confidentiality of stored, transmitted or otherwise processed data, personal or other, such as by encrypting relevant data at rest or in transit by state of the art mechanisms, and by using other technical means;
requirements.note: In transit: expo-policy asserts over the RESOLVED Expo config that no NSAllowsArbitraryLoads or usesCleartextTraffic opt-in exists (ATS exceptions loopback-only) and that apiOrigin is https-or-loopback; security-headers pins HSTS by value; auth-posture reds an http:// site_url. On device the Supabase session lives only in LargeSecureStore (a per-value AES-256-CTR key in expo-secure-store, ciphertext in AsyncStorage) with the keychain import walled to apps/mobile/src/host/** by lint and depcruise. At rest, application-level confidentiality is CONDITIONAL on the e2ee module: when enabled it ships @app/crypto with AEAD-only sealing under a versioned envelope whose AAD binds row identity, X25519 RecipientWrap for sharing, a generated-recovery-code escrow, DeviceSync ports and rewrapItemKey — all with vector-pinned tests riding the unit Stop step — so the server holds neither plaintext nor a decrypting key for the columns a consumer chooses to encrypt. Residuals: without the module, at-rest confidentiality is the platform's disk encryption, which is outside the tree and unverified by any gate; even with it, encryption of a given column is a per-feature authoring act (the authoring-e2ee-feature skill), and the data-flow gate closes column NAMES against the schema and cannot tell ciphertext from plaintext; and the deployed TLS termination and certificate posture belong to Vercel and Supabase, not to anything the chain reads.

requirements.text: protect the integrity of stored, transmitted or otherwise processed data, personal or other, commands, programs and configuration against any manipulation or modification not authorised by the user, and report on corruptions;
requirements.note: Configuration and program integrity in the tree: gate-integrity recomputes sha256 over every harness-owned enforcement file recorded in .harness/manifest.json and reds naming a mismatched or missing file; the write-guard hook denies agent edits to the 98 protected paths and globs in WRITE_PROTECTED (.claude/hooks/lib/guard-rules.mjs) and applies a further 44 rules over bash commands, SQL, config and file content (26 BASH_RULES, 12 WRITE_GLOBAL_CHECKS, 4 WRITE_SQL_CHECKS, 1 WRITE_CONFIG_CHECKS, 1 MCP_RULES) — 142 rules in total, of which 98 are protected paths; migrations are append-only (the migrations gate and the migration-safety workflow's append-only job); the audit trail is append-only in four layers, proven by supabase/tests/audit_immutability.test.sql, and auth_trail mirrors it; the version-sync gate holds the committed lockfile so CI installs are frozen. Data integrity in transit rides TLS (see CRA-I.2.e); row-level integrity of user data against unauthorised modification is RLS WITH CHECK, proven by the isolation suites. Residuals: 'report on corruptions' is addressed only in the sense that a tampered enforcement file reds the next validate run and an audit-trail write attempt raises — no runtime mechanism detects or reports corruption of a user's stored data; artefact integrity for what is DEPLOYED (build attestation, signed-artifact verification) exists only in the opt-in ci-provenance (job attest, GitHub build-provenance attestations over npm packages that the module README characterises as SLSA Build L2-shaped and explicitly not L3), ci-web-deploy (job attest-web) and ci-mobile-release (job verify-and-attach) modules and is not graded here; and the e2ee module's AAD-bound envelope (a ciphertext moved to another row fails authentication) is likewise conditional on enablement.

requirements.text: process only data, personal or other, that are adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary in relation to the intended purpose of the product with digital elements (data minimisation);
requirements.note: The one minimisation control with a real enforcement point is the audit trail's metadata-only default: the trail records WHICH columns changed and never their values, value capture is a reviewed tools/audit-columns.json entry, and the tenancy gate refuses capture of any column listed in tools/pii-columns.json (and reds an entry naming a column no migration creates). Adjacent controls: the data-flow gate forces every subject-data table into a projected-or-excluded-with-reason inventory, every wire string carries a zod .max() bound (the dto-bounds discipline), and the observability gate keeps vendor telemetry behind the redaction pass. What nothing machine-checks is the requirement's actual subject — whether a column, a log field or a DTO field is NECESSARY for the product's purpose. That is a schema-design judgment the security-reviewer or architecture-reviewer may raise and no gate can, so the grade is partial on the strength of the audit-capture refusal alone and would be not-covered without it.

requirements.text: protect the availability of essential and basic functions, also after an incident, including through resilience and mitigation measures against denial-of-service attacks;
requirements.note: The rate-limits gate closes tools/rate-limit-budget.json against the GENERATED action inventory in both directions (every mutation and every Server Action mapped or reasoned-exempt, both seams asserted wired, limits diffed by value against apps/web/lib/rate-limit.ts), and packages/api/src/ratelimit.test.ts proves the router refuses before any handler runs; db-limits asserts per-role statement_timeout ceilings set by migration and the per-org quota triggers, which bind every path through PostgREST including direct supabase-js calls; the resilience gate makes every outbound seam's timeout/retry posture reviewed data. Residuals, stated where the catalog states them: the rate-limits gate carries ramps (a missing budget file on a pre-0.2.0 install, and the 0.10.0 outage-rung findings NOTE-only until 0.11.0 on installs predating the key) that are expired at this release, so the gate is live on every install now; the budgets bind the two application seams and not a client POSTing straight to /rest/v1 or to GoTrue (only the quota trigger and statement timeouts reach those); the limiter FAILS OPEN when its backend is unavailable, degrading to an in-process limiter that a serverless platform effectively discards; volumetric DDoS mitigation is the hosting platforms' edge and is outside the tree; and 'also after an incident' rests on the platform's backups, whose existence the scheduled backup-evidence job checks only when an operator wires SUPABASE_ACCESS_TOKEN and whose restore is a written record in tools/backup-posture.json (documentation tier), never a tested drill.

requirements.text: minimise the negative impact by the products themselves or connected devices on the availability of services provided by other devices or networks;
requirements.note: The resilience gate is the only control whose subject touches this requirement: every outbound transport construction site (tRPC client, server fetch, supabase-js factory, Edge Function, WebSocket/EventSource) must carry a reviewed tools/resilience.json row, and a row's claims must be true of its file (a non-null timeoutMs needs AbortSignal.timeout, retries > 0 needs a retry symbol, backoffMs needs a backoff symbol paced by a non-zero retry count), so an undeclared 'hang forever, retry never' or an unbounded retry storm against another service cannot exist unreviewed. Its stated limits are exactly this row's residual: the step is a 1.0.0 chain injection RAMPED as NOTE-only until harness 1.1.0 on installs seeded before 1.0.0 (check-resilience.mjs rampNote), so on an upgraded install its findings do not red for one release; the gate refuses undeclared and false postures, never modest or impolite ones — a reviewed row declaring aggressive retries with a written why passes; it is static and cannot see runtime behaviour or transports reached through a dependency's own internals; and nothing in the tree bounds the mobile app's outbound request rate against the consumer's own server or third parties, or the Edge Functions' egress. Whether the product is a good network citizen is therefore a reviewed decision the gate keeps visible, not one it enforces, which is why partial rather than covered.

requirements.text: be designed, developed and produced to limit attack surfaces, including external interfaces;
requirements.note: External interfaces are inventoried and closed both ways: route-manifest holds every web page and mobile screen to a registered manifest (an orphan route file reds), rate-limits closes every tRPC mutation and exported Server Action against the generated action inventory, auth-posture's section census keeps [realtime] and [storage] disabled and the redirect allowlist bounded, security-headers requires an explicit empty allowlist for each of the eight permissions-policy features named in tools/security-headers.json permissionsPolicyDenied (camera, microphone, geolocation, payment, usb, browsing-topics, interest-cohort, display-capture) — a reviewed list, not every feature — and pins frame-ancestors, the audit and auth_trail schemas are absent from [api].schemas with no client USAGE grant, and the boundaries gate over tools/exports-walls.json keeps the service-role and cookie-bound server factories structurally unreachable from the Metro bundle. Residuals: the PostgREST surface itself (every table in an exposed schema is an HTTP endpoint) is limited by RLS and grants rather than by any inventory of which tables SHOULD be exposed; the Supabase Auth, Storage and Realtime endpoints exist at the platform whether or not the local config disables them; and 'produced to limit attack surfaces' in the CRA sense includes the shipped binary's native surface (permissions, plugins), which tools/expo-permissions.json and tools/expo-plugins.json review but a reviewer can widen with a reason.

requirements.text: be designed, developed and produced to reduce the impact of an incident using appropriate exploitation mitigation mechanisms and techniques;
requirements.note: Web exploitation mitigations are asserted by VALUE: a nonce-based CSP with strict-dynamic and banned unsafe-eval, frame-ancestors none agreeing with X-Frame-Options, COOP/CORP, nosniff, HSTS, and private no-store with a Vary on the acting-org selector on authenticated responses (the cross-tenant CDN-poisoning shape); dangerouslySetInnerHTML is write-guard-banned repo-wide. Blast-radius containment on the data side is FORCE RLS with service_role revoked on every table and confined to ADR-governed Edge Functions, per-role statement ceilings and per-org quotas (db-limits), and — when the e2ee module is enabled — a server that holds no plaintext, so a database compromise yields ciphertext for encrypted columns. Residuals: the gate evaluates the module and cannot prove the DEPLOYED response carries the headers (that is the path-filtered web-e2e lane's security-headers.spec.ts, which does not run on every PR); Hermes, OS-level and Vercel-runtime mitigations are outside the tree; and no incident-response tooling (isolation, credential rotation, kill switch) ships — the harness reduces impact by construction, not by response.

requirements.text: provide security related information by recording and monitoring relevant internal activity, including the access to or modification of data, services or functions, with an opt-out mechanism for the user;
requirements.note: Every org-scoped table carries an AFTER INSERT OR UPDATE OR DELETE row trigger writing audit.events (the tenancy gate closes this: a missing trigger, a WHEN clause, a BEFORE timing, a missing operation or a statement-level trigger reds), the trail is append-only in four layers proven live by supabase/tests/audit_immutability.test.sql, and the auth_trail schema records failed and successful authentication attempts through GoTrue hooks (supabase/tests/auth_trail.test.sql) — with the caveat that the migration is seedOnInitOnly and the [auth.hook] config posture is ramped NOTE-only until 1.1.0 on installs seeded before 1.0.0, so an upgraded install has this half only once it adopts both. Three residuals, all stated in the gates catalog's 'Honest losses': the trail covers MUTATIONS ONLY and nothing about reads, so 'access to data' is not recorded (SELECT auditing needs pgaudit configuration no migration can express); there is no 'monitoring' — no forwarding, alerting or reader for auth_trail, and the runbook docs/runbooks/log-forwarding.md places central logging at the organisation boundary; and there is NO opt-out mechanism for the user, and by design (a tenant-controllable audit trail would defeat itself), which means this clause's opt-out is a product decision the consumer must take deliberately against the shipped default rather than a switch that exists. The observability module (OpenTelemetry) is opt-in and adds tracing, not access logging.

requirements.text: provide the possibility for users to securely and easily remove on a permanent basis all data and settings and, where such data can be transferred to other products or systems, ensure that this is done in a secure manner.
requirements.note: Removal: the seeded session.deleteAccount action (tools/store-tunables.json accountDeletion, backed by the delete-account Edge Function under an ADR) exists because Apple 5.1.1(v) requires it, and the data-flow gate makes its completeness mechanical — every foreign key out of the subject lands in ERASED (cascade), SEVERED (reviewed reason), RETAINED (reason plus a committed procedure file, docs/runbooks/data-subject-requests.md) or BLOCKING (allowed only with a reviewed pre-delete sweep), and it diffs supabase/schemas against supabase/migrations on referential actions so the two cannot disagree. Transfer: export.surface is the system.exportMyData tRPC procedure running AS THE CALLER under RLS with the projection closed both ways against the schema, and packages/api/src/routers/system.export.test.ts proves the authored-only filter that RLS cannot provide. Residuals: 'permanent' is bounded by the platform — deleted rows persist in Supabase backups and PITR windows whose data lifecycle the vendor does not publish (design/CONFORMANCE-FACTS.md records this as unverifiable in either direction), and audit.events rows are RETAINED by design; the export ships JSON over an authenticated procedure and the gate cannot tell ciphertext from plaintext, so with the e2ee module a consumer must decide client-side decryption at export time (the encryption rule's stated stance); and 'easily' is a UI judgment no gate makes.

requirements.text: identify and document vulnerabilities and components contained in products with digital elements, including by drawing up a software bill of materials in a commonly used and machine-readable format covering at the very least the top-level dependencies of the products;
requirements.note: The osv-scan workflow's sbom-inventory job emits a CycloneDX SBOM daily with pnpm sbom --sbom-format cyclonedx --lockfile-only (the full resolved closure, well past top-level), and tools/check-sbom.mjs CONSUMES it — the component set is closed against pnpm-lock.yaml in both directions and a zero-component emission is a hard failure — so the artefact is uploaded only after it is proven to describe this tree; the scan-full and scan-pr jobs identify known vulnerabilities in the same closure. Residuals: the SBOM covers the npm ecosystem only (native platform dependencies enter through npm packages, but Postgres extensions, the Supabase platform, runner images and the mobile toolchains are not components in it); it is a 90-day CI artefact, not a document delivered with the product or kept alongside a release; 'document vulnerabilities' exists only as scan output in a lane log, not a maintained vulnerability register with disposition; and the ci-provenance module's syft/SPDX SBOM plus attestation is opt-in and duplicates rather than extends this coverage. The `sbom-inventory` job is (schedule-gated), so this is proven periodically or per-touching-PR rather than on every commit.

requirements.text: in relation to the risks posed to products with digital elements, address and remediate vulnerabilities without delay, including by providing security updates; where technically feasible, new security updates shall be provided separately from functionality updates;
requirements.note: The deploy-record workflow's patch-window job joins the resolutions in the latest DEPLOYED manifest against OSV advisory publication dates and reds when a deployed vulnerable pin sits outside ASD's verbatim 48-hour / two-week / one-month windows — measuring what shipped, never what main resolves today. Renovate (renovate.json, write-guarded) owns the fix path and the diff-aware scan-pr job stops new vulnerabilities entering. Residuals: the job is scheduled-only and never a PR blocker (its judgment is clockful and network-bound by subject); it measures nothing until the consumer wires the deployment_status event (Vercel and EAS emit it through their GitHub integrations; repository_dispatch is the escape hatch), and a deploy performed outside that channel is invisible; 'without delay' is judged against ASD's windows because CRA sets none, which is a borrowed yardstick; remediation itself is a human merge and release; and NOTHING enforces or even records that security updates ship separately from functionality updates — the release modules cut one release per tag whatever it contains. The `patch-window` job is (schedule-gated), so this is proven periodically or per-touching-PR rather than on every commit.

requirements.text: apply effective and regular tests and reviews of the security of the product with digital elements;
requirements.note: Regular automated security testing ships and runs on a clock the consumer does not have to remember: the rls-isolation Stop step runs the pgTAP and supabase-js isolation suites every turn, CodeQL security-extended runs on PR, push and daily (codeql.yml job analyze), OSV runs on PR and daily, gitleaks on PR and on push to the default branch (gitleaks.yml, plus the lefthook pre-commit and the hermetic secrets chain step), StrykerJS mutation testing over the authorisation and transport boundary nightly (mutation.yml job stryker-full) with a set-based ratchet, and the migration-safety workflow lints every added migration. Reviews are mechanically enforced rather than advised: the reviewer-verdicts Stop step reds a turn until every reviewer whose MUST-BE-USED paths the diff touched (security-reviewer on the migration/schema/Edge Function/DAL/API/server-auth code paths in tools/reviewer-triggers.json — deliberately narrower than its prose, and not supabase/config.toml — web-security-reviewer on Server Actions, the web Supabase seam, proxy.ts, security-headers.ts and rate-limit*.ts, mobile-security-reviewer on the native config surface) has returned VERDICT: PASS. Residuals: these test the TREE, not the deployed product — no DAST, no penetration test, no runtime scan of the production origin exists in the tree; the reviewer subagents are read-only LLM reviewers whose findings are as good as their prompts, and their verdicts are recorded by a hook rather than a human; several lanes are path-filtered or scheduled and 'exists' is not 'ran' on a given commit; and manual security review cadence, third-party assessment and scope decisions are the manufacturer's process.

requirements.text: once a security update has been made available, share and publicly disclose information about fixed vulnerabilities, including a description of the vulnerabilities, information allowing users to identify the product with digital elements affected, the impacts of the vulnerabilities, their severity and clear and accessible information helping users to remediate the vulnerabilities; in duly justified cases, where manufacturers consider the security risks of publication to outweigh the security benefits, they may delay making public information regarding a fixed vulnerability until after users have been given the possibility to apply the relevant patch;
requirements.note: Nothing in the tree produces, templates or checks a security advisory: no advisory format, no changelog section for fixed vulnerabilities (the opt-in ci-mobile-release module's release-please generates a conventional-commit CHANGELOG and GitHub Release from commit types, which is a change log and carries no vulnerability description, affected-version, impact or severity fields), no gate that reds a release whose fixed OSV ids were not disclosed, and no severity vocabulary. The seeded SECURITY.md commits the consumer to coordinated disclosure and credit in prose and points Contact at the GitHub security-advisories form, which is a channel for INBOUND reports and does not by itself publish anything. The harness could ship a seeded advisory template and a release-time closure (fixed advisory ids in the patch-window manifest versus a published advisories file), which is why the row is not-covered rather than not-applicable; publishing, judging severity and impact, and deciding a justified delay are the manufacturer's acts and would remain so.

requirements.text: put in place and enforce a policy on coordinated vulnerability disclosure;
requirements.note: A coordinated vulnerability disclosure policy is seeded as SECURITY.md (private reporting, acknowledgement in 3 working days, initial assessment in 10, updates every 10, fix-before-publication default, credit by default, in/out-of-scope surfaces, and a paragraph on the consumer's own CRA Article 14 reporting duty from 2026-09-11) and its machine-readable half is apps/web/public/.well-known/security.txt (RFC 9116) with a Policy field pointing at SECURITY.md; the security-headers gate holds the clockless shape (present implies parses, Contact an https/mailto/tel URI, Expires exactly once as RFC 3339) and the scheduled floor-review job holds the calendar (an expired or over-one-year Expires). Residuals: the policy is a TEMPLATE with placeholders and target timelines the consumer must actually staff and honour — 'enforce' is an organisational fact no gate sees; security.txt is seedOnInitOnly and its absence never reds, so an install that deletes it has no machine-checked disclosure channel while SECURITY.md still reads as policy; and the evidence tier is documentation because the substance of a CVD policy is a document and the gate proves only that its pointer parses.

requirements.text: take measures to facilitate the sharing of information about potential vulnerabilities in their product with digital elements as well as in third-party components contained in that product, including by providing a contact address for the reporting of the vulnerabilities discovered in the product with digital elements;
requirements.note: The contact address ships in two forms: security.txt's mandatory Contact field (seeded to the GitHub private advisory form URL, held by the security-headers gate to be an https/mailto/tel URI, cleartext http reds) served at /.well-known/security.txt on the web origin, and SECURITY.md's private-reporting instructions naming {{SECURITY_OWNERS}}. Sharing about third-party components is facilitated only indirectly — the daily SBOM (CRA-II.1) enumerates them and SECURITY.md's scope includes 'the build and release pipeline' — with no upstream-reporting guidance or channel. Residuals: the gate judges the file only when it exists (absence never reds, by design, because a planted Expires nobody reviewed would be worse), so the machine-checked half can be removed without a red; whether the address is monitored by more than one person is the organisational point SECURITY.md itself asks the consumer to arrange; and the mobile app carries no in-product reporting surface, so a mobile-only user finds the address only via the web origin or the repository.

requirements.text: provide for mechanisms to securely distribute updates for products with digital elements to ensure that vulnerabilities are fixed or mitigated in a timely manner and, where applicable for security updates, in an automatic manner;
requirements.note: The base tree secures the update CHANNEL rather than providing the distribution: expo-policy asserts over the resolved config that runtimeVersion is exactly { policy: 'appVersion' } (the deterministic, PR-reviewable OTA compatibility boundary) and that any updates.url embeds the EAS projectId locked in tools/identity.lock.json (an update URL pointing elsewhere is a hijacked OTA channel), tools/identity.lock.json pins store identity so an update cannot be delivered to a different app, and signing material is banned from repo and shell by the write-guard (expo-token-leak, eas-credentials, credential-file-read). The distribution mechanisms themselves are opt-in modules and their grades are conditional on enablement: ci-mobile-release (EAS builds, verify-and-attach signed-artifact checks, store submission), ci-web-deploy (tag-triggered rebuild with a GitHub build-provenance attestation and in-CI verification, job attest-web), and eas-update (dispatch-only OTA publish with republish-as-rollback, honestly degrading without EXPO_TOKEN). Residuals: store delivery and its automatic-install behaviour are Apple's and Google's, and web delivery is the host's; the attestations prove the artefact came from the workflow and NOT that the source was untampered (the module READMEs characterise them as SLSA Build L2-shaped and explicitly not L3; no external assessment of that level exists in the tree); nothing in base or modules makes a security update AUTOMATIC beyond what expo-updates' launch check and the stores already do; and 'timely' is measured only by the patch-window job against ASD's windows once the deploy channel is wired.

requirements.text: ensure that, where security updates are available to address identified security issues, they are disseminated without delay and, unless otherwise agreed between a manufacturer and a business user in relation to a tailor-made product with digital elements, free of charge, accompanied by advisory messages providing users with the relevant information, including on potential action to be taken.
requirements.note: Dissemination without delay is measured (patch-window, CRA-II.2) but not caused by anything in the tree, 'free of charge' is a commercial term no artefact records, and there is no advisory-message surface at all: the version-skew guard's CONFLICT tells a stale client that it must update and nothing more, no release note or in-app message is generated from fixed advisories, and the eas-update and ci-mobile-release modules publish binaries and OTA bundles without accompanying user-facing advisory text (ci-mobile-release's release-please emits a commit-type CHANGELOG and GitHub Release, which names commits, not the action a user should take). The harness could ship an advisory template coupled to the release DAG (the same gap CRA-II.4 records), so not-covered rather than not-applicable; the decision to send an advisory, its content and the pricing term remain the manufacturer's.
